The size of each folio is 37 x 2.7 cm.
p = the picture number as mentioned in the PDF image;
f = the number as mentioned in the folio.
Words or letters enclosed in brackets [ ] are my suggestions, based on my understanding.
Dots (…) are used to indicate missing portions, damage to the folio, or unidentified characters.
"What is it?
[This refers to: p 1, 2, 3 contain illustrations; p 4, 5a are blank; 5b: *dakṣiṇāmūrtigurucaraṇāravindābhyāṃ namaḥ* | *Śaivabhūṣaṇam* | (l1.)
I salute Pārvatī and Parameśvara, the parents of the world, who are joined together like speech and its meaning, for the sake of the comprehension of both speech and meaning.
Having paid homage to the chosen deity—
having bowed to Śaṅkara, Ambikā, Gaṇapati, Skanda, and Nandīśvara—
and thereafter [to] the hosts of his lineage and the teacher who awakened my understanding...

The words of the Śiva-āgamas of the Śaivas are fashioned into an ornament adorned with jewels, composed of various colors and diverse arrangements of sounds that equal gold when placed upon the scales.
...grant all auspicious things...
(l4) Having paid obeisance to this Mahādeva, the deity who exists as the two [parents], thereafter Ambikā, Mahāgaṇapati, Skanda, Nandikeśvara, and Samayaguru... (l5)
(The Preceptors): They are Sambandha Perumāḷ, Appa Tambirān, Sundara Perumāṇār, and Māṇikkavācakar.
Thus, there are four preceptors of the *samayaguru* lineage. There are six preceptors of the *santānaguru* lineage. They are Satyajñānadarśanikas and Parañjyoti Mahāmuni.
The Lord of Koṟṟaṅguḍi, who bears the sacred names Mēykaṇṭaśivācārya,
Aruṇantiśivācārya, Maṉṉiñānaśambandhaśivācārya, and Umāpatiśivācārya. (p6a, l1)

The sixty-three [deities] consisting of the lineage of the six gurus; the sixty-three plus the nine assemblies (tīrkkūttam) make seventy-two. The term *tiruppeyar* refers to the Ācārya who stands as a source of grace (*anugraha*).
2) Having prostrated to all of them in due order, [this work] is composed by being refined with the jewels that are the words of the Śivāgamas.
This very scripture was spoken by us under the name *Śaivabhūṣaṇa*. Subsequently, the sequence of the scripture (*śāstrakrama*) was spoken as follows:
"After this [comes] that; after this [comes] that."
"The sequence has indeed been established. However, that which remains hidden within the Śiva-āgamas and is to be known, that alone I shall explain here after having analyzed it. Thus [it is said].
This sequence of the scripture—that "this follows after this"—has not been stated in this scripture. Furthermore, as for how it is [established], it is in the Śiva-āgamas.

Know this: whatever secret remains to be understood as the subject matter of the *kriyāpāda* has been explained in detail. Now, that which consists of the form of the six limbs (*sadaṅgākāra*) is being explained. (ll 6–7)

"...this work shall indeed become a sound melody traveling through the path of the ear-cavities of learned men; by the mere touch of a drop from the river Jambū, everything becomes indeed Jāmbūnada gold. Thus it is said.
(p6b, l1) This scripture has entered, even if only slightly, into the ears of the Śaiva teachers who are both learned and beyond numbering.

By the mere entry [of this work], through both its words and its meaning, it shall certainly be auspicious, free from any defect. Just as by the touch of a drop of water from the river of the essence of jambū fruits...
Even all things such as clods of earth became excellent *apāñcī* gold... 8. Afterwards, it remained without being mentioned in the assembly.

"The karma performed in a previous birth (*pūrvajanmakṛtakarma*) is indeed the cause for accomplishing every task; likewise, my state of being a servant to the devotees of Śiva is the cause for the excellence of my scriptural knowledge," so it is said.
If one asks what is the cause for each individual action that brings about all results, it is the ripening of past karma (*karmaparipāka*). In that same way, why did I compose this *grantha*? (16)

Even if this is the reason for [your objection], what is our reason? Know that we compose this *śāstra* for the purpose of bestowing the *adimaitiram* (the state of being at the feet) upon all those who are devoted to Śiva. 9. Hereafter, it is stated that there are seven types of *Śaivas*.
It is said that there are seven kinds of Śaivas: first, the beginningless Śiva; then the twice-born (brāhmaṇas); then the great king; then both the vaiśya and the anuśaiva;
then the śūdra, who is indeed the antaśaiva; and below him is the śaṅkaraprāvara.
Subsequently, it is shown in the Śaiva Āgama that there are those of the lowest caste (*antyaja*) who are Śaivas (*antyaśaiva*). As for what these are, they are: 1.
*anādiśaiva* (the beginningless Śaivas), 2. *ādiśaiva* (the Śaivas by birth), 3. *śivabrāhmaṇa* (Śaiva Brāhmaṇas).
1. Great Śaivas who are great Brāhmaṇas; 4. Anuśaivas who are Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas; 5. Avāntaraśaivas who are Śūdras; 6. Pravaraśaivas who belong to mixed castes (*saṅkarajāti*). (l4)

O noble ones born [of this lineage], 7. others are the *antyaśaivas*. Thus, know that the Śaivas are said to be of seven kinds in some Āgamas, and of ten kinds in the Śivāgamas such as the Kāmika (l5). 10. Hereafter, the definition of the *śuddhaśaiva* remains to be told.

But among them, those who follow the Śiva-āgamas as taught [therein], whose initiations are radiant, who are devoted to the excellent conduct of the Śaivas, and who are always in accordance with the Vedas—
Those who are averse to base conduct, observant of restraints, constant in their daily rites,
and who have relied upon the assembly of their former lineage— they are remembered as the pure Śaivas.
Those people who, through initiation by Śiva, have become distinguished...

May they remain in the Kali age as those who possess the excellent Śaiva conduct that is not opposed to the Mārga, who turn their backs on base actions, who are disciplined, who never neglect their daily obligatory rites (*nityakarman*), who are virtuous, and who are devoid of the names and designations of previous births. May they be so! O Kālī!

Thus they are known as the Śuddhaśaivas. 11. (l3) Furthermore, the conduct of the *ativarṇāśrama* (those beyond the castes and stages of life) has been described. By virtue of being devoid of the conduct of the castes and stages of life, they become here those who belong neither to a caste nor a stage of life (*atīta-varṇāśramiṇaḥ*). [They may wear] saffron or white garments. (l4)

Those who uphold [this] are indeed the pure Śaivas. As stated in the Kiraṇāgama: "Apart from the conduct (ācāra) existing within the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, and apart from the conduct existing within the four stages of life (āśrama)—namely, studenthood (brahmacarya), householdership (gṛhastha), forest-dwelling (vānaprastha), and renunciation (saṃnyāsa)—[one should follow] that which is declared in the Śiva Āgamas."

Those great souls who are pure Śaivas, possessing the conduct and practices beginning with *caryā*, are known as *ativarṇāśramins*. For them, both saffron-colored cloth (*kāṣāyavastra*) and white cloth (*śubhravastra*) may be worn; this is stated in the Kiraṇāgama.

Know this: among these modes of conduct for those beyond the [four] castes and stages of life (*ativarṇāśramācāra*), the *kuṭīcaka* form of renunciation (*sannyāsa*) alone is the most excellent. 12. Subsequently, the means of livelihood for the pure Śaiva community remains to be told. (p8a, l1) "How is the livelihood of the Śaivas here? Likewise, how is their acquisition through agriculture like that of Brahmins, or how is the office of a monastery head (*māṭhāpatya*)? Having understood this, the ascetic was granted [to them], thinking, "How indeed can he be a true saint? (13).

The gift of knowledge shines forth through the affection of the virtuous king and through the increase of the ascetic’s dharma; for the disciples, the ascetic [performs] the commerce of performing his own prescribed duties—just as Brahmins practice agriculture—and acts as the head of the monastery (*maṭhapati*). Thus, others bestow upon him the reputation of being a good man.
It is given by those who have studied with satisfaction;
it is given by kings who are upholders of justice; it comes as the fruit of *dharma*; it is given as a teacher’s fee (*guru-dakṣiṇā*) by disciples; [it is] wealth appropriate for oneself. (15)
It comes through business activity. Know that these types of income that come in this manner constitute the means of livelihood for the Śuddhaśaivas.

And in the Śaiva tradition, the rule for renunciation (saṃnyāsa) is fourfold; the wise man who knows well [these]—are these indeed the types of renunciants? Is the Kuṭīcaka also one who possesses a wife, even while following the dharma of renunciation? What is it?
Thus, Śaiva-saṃnyāsa is of four kinds: vidvat-saṃnyāsa, vidiṣu-saṃnyāsa, bahūdaka-saṃnyāsa, and kuṭīcaka-saṃnyāsa. (p8b, l1)

It exists. Know that within it, there is also the *kuṭīcaka-saṃnyāsa*, which is endowed with the duties of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa-dharma*) such as wearing ochre-colored garments (*kāṣāya-vastra*) and so forth. (12) Know that this *kuṭīcaka-saṃnyāsa* alone is the most excellent among the intermediate types of Śaivas. 14.

...the sixteen rites (ṣoḍaśakriyā) [are] not to be spoken of... (l3) For these, the sixteen pure rites are prescribed by means of the mantras proclaimed therein; their fitness for the study of the Śiva-āgamas and so forth, as well as the status of an Ācārya, [is established]. (l4) Those who are endowed with the purificatory initiation (saṃskāradīkṣā) and are Śaivas of the foremost birth, they alone are rightly [qualified] according to the stated doctrine; for if it were not thus, they would not be fit for anything whatsoever. Whatever [is] Śiva... (Note: The provided text contains Tamil script fragments interspersed with Sanskrit. The translation focuses on the Sanskrit portions to maintain linguistic consistency.)
Those for whom the sixteen saṃskāras, beginning with *garbhādhāna*, are performed by means of the mantras of the divine Āgamas—
they alone are the pure Śaivas.
Know that they alone are the twice-born (dvijāti), in accordance with the words of the Āgamas.
As stated in the Kāmika:
"The four beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, as well as those considered to be born in the natural order (anuloma)... (7).
And the office of teacher (ācāryatva) for those rites is proclaimed.
And in the Sarvajñānottara: "O Six-faced One, Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those born of pure lineages may [attain] the status of an Ācārya in due order from among their own castes."

"The birth of those born in the natural order (anuloma) as well as those born in the inverse order (pratiloma) is declared here by Manu, in accordance with the teachings of the *Suprabhedāgama*. This refers to the sequence of origin for the six names of the *anulomas* and the six names of the *pratilomas*, as stated in this passage from the *Suprabhedāgama* and the *Manuvijñāneśvara*.
It remains unspoken. (l3.
In the *Suprabhedāgama*:
"Having obtained a red maiden according to the prescribed rite along with the mantras, the Brahmin..."
Of him who is known to be of the same caste, [the son] born of women not lower than himself is honored.
He too shall be known as a Brāhmaṇa, and his ritual activity shall be Vedic;
however, from the union of a Pīta woman with a Brāhmaṇa, one named Ambaṣṭha is born.
Initiated by a twice-born man himself, he is ever intent upon his daily duties;
by the command of one of equal caste, he always practices medicine.
Born from a Śūdra maiden by a Brāhmaṇa, he is known as a Pāraśava.
There, one should worship Kālī according to the path prescribed in the Kula scriptures.
In every house, in the afternoon, one should cook [the food];
thus one should perform the daily rites until the end of life.
The son born to a king from a Vaiśya maiden is called a Gurujña;
his livelihood consists of acting as a royal priest and officiating at sacrifices.
The son born to a king from a Śūdra maiden is known as an Āgrya.
Service to the Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, Shudras, and the aged is declared to be his duty.
By the king’s command, he shall punish those deserving of punishment without hesitation.
From the conjunction with *pīta* (yellow), he is named Jāścūcuka;
his livelihood consists of vegetables, crows, wood, round objects, water, and various types of goods.
In the Manu-vijñāneśvara:
"From a Kṣatriya on a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Sūta; from a Vaiśya, a Māgadha is recorded;
but from a Śūdra, a Caṇḍāla is born, who is excluded from all ritual acts."
"From a Kṣatriya [she bears] an Āgadhaka, from a Vaiśya a Śūdra, and from a Śūdra a Kṣattṛ;
and from a Śūdra she indeed gives birth to an Āyogava as her son. (Verse 3). As for the six *anuloma* castes: one born to a Brāhmaṇa from a Kṣatriya woman is known as a Mūrdhāvasikta.
He is also called Savarṇa and Vaidehika.
One born from a Śreṣṭhin woman is called Ambaṣṭha; his profession is that of a physician skilled in warding off diseases.
[From] a Śūdra woman... (l5)

A certain wicked man named Pārāśava was born in the house of a Vaiṣṇava woman; he performed these Bhadrakālī-pūjās and festivals according to the Yāmala-Padmādhipa, and during the afternoon, he went from house to house begging for alms in order to eat.
One born to a Kṣatriya from a Brāhmaṇī woman is called a Sūta; one born to a Vaiśya from a Brāhmaṇī woman is called a Vaidehika; and one born to a Śūdra from a Brāhmaṇī woman is called a Caṇḍāla.
From a Brāhmaṇī woman, three types of sons are born from Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra fathers:
the Sūta, the Vaidehika, and the Caṇḍāla.
Furthermore, from a Kṣatriyā woman, a son born from a Vaiśya father is called a Māgadha; and from a Kṣatriyā woman, a son born from a Śūdra father is a Kṣatta.
And so it is.
From a Śūdra father and a Śreṣṭhinī mother is born the Āyogava; thus, these six beginning with the Sūta are known by the name Pratiloma.
For them, there is also a common assembly... (l4)
This is the teaching of the *Āgama*. One should also accept it as such. Understand that this is the meaning of both this *Āgama* teaching and the teaching of Manu-vijñāneśvara:
"Those born from the upward-seed (*ūrdhvabīja*) [of the father] and the downward-field (*adhaḥkṣetra*) [of the mother] belong to the anuloma [castes]."

"Those born from a superior field (mother) and an inferior seed (father) are *pratiloma*. This refers to those born from men of high caste and women of low caste; they are called *kṛtaviśrama*. Thus, there are two types: *anuloma* and *pratiloma*.
Know that those born from women and men of different castes are of mixed origin (saṅkarajātayaḥ).
In some places on earth, due to the nature of the Kali age, there will be various wonders;
there shall be many divisions of caste among those born from human wombs.
Know that they are fit for the study of the Śivāgamas and other scriptures, as well as for those who are devoted to Śiva. Therefore,
[this constitutes] the initiation of purification (*saṃskāradīkṣā*).
Know that those who have received the *viśeṣa-dīkṣā* are qualified for the pursuit of Śiva (*śivārcanā*) as well as for the study of the Śivāgamas and other scriptures.

(15) Furthermore, it has been stated that even in the case of the *saṃskāra-dīkṣā* prescribed in the Śivāgamas, there exists the distinction of being twice-born (*dvijatva-viśiṣṭatvam*). If [the goal] is to be accomplished here by means of the rites prescribed in the Smṛtis...

If, at that time, the act of speaking the words of the gods [as prescribed] for the sake of the twice-born were not beneficial, how could there be the status of a twice-born? If this were so, and the deity [were not established], how could it be accomplished in the case of Śilāda and others?

Therefore, the status of being twice-born is indeed established as having the authority of scriptural testimony. (Note: The text provided contains fragments of Sanskrit and Tamil. The translation above renders the intelligible Sanskrit portions. The Tamil portion "(என)" translates to "thus" or "so," which has been integrated into the flow of the argument.)
That which was said... the statement indeed... having attained the status of a twice-born... by the wicked Mahādeva... at the sacred moment... solely by means of the words of the Āgamas (l5)...
in accordance with that... there exists a statement—no, it does not exist... (l6).
Having performed... by the twice-born... [the path] to the world of [Viṣṇu]...
(l7)... as it was declared... the direction of wood (kāṣṭhā)... in the world... and (p11b, l1).
... it is said that iron... [the state of] being... the Sāṃkhya system. Furthermore, regarding those previously mentioned who have attained liberation through the lotus-born [Brahmā]...

as if liberated... therefore... (l2) ...for all those born [in this way], there is indeed no counting... in this... having reached the end... and all these [are like] gold... and... (Note: The provided text fragments appear to be highly fragmented and contain numerous ellipses. The translation above reconstructs the most probable meaning based on the surviving Sanskrit terminology and context.)

Sura... mava ... sva ... dā (l3) ... meva | ... nadyudakapra... to ... naṣṭatasmādasta tvamatra bhavata... (l4) ...ntā ... ramucyate'tra tu yagāsanyāsinaḥ karmaṇā śreṣṭhāṃ kiñca... ryathā lavaṇatāṃ prāpnoti | taddevakośyāṃ kiṃ tu ||
"Mahas... (l5) ...de...litaḥ, and all [are] Sādāśiva; therefore, for those born in the sacrifice of the aforementioned lineage... (l6) ...become.
This refers to the conjunction with fire (*agnisaṃyoga*) for the sake of the next birth (*janman*).

After arriving, just as in the east the name *svarūpā* (the mode of one's own nature) departs and another name, *svarūpaṃ* (one's own nature as water), arrives; so too, after the *saṃyoga* (conjunction) of the *rasakūpikā* (well of rasa) with the two wives... thereafter, the *svarūpaṃ* that was previously present as the *rasasvarūpa* (the essence of rasa) also departs.
Just as gold, when heated intensely...
(p12a, l1) ...and likewise, the water that falls upon a pearl-oyster loses its former name of "water" and, taking on another color, receives the name "pearl. (l2)

Just as one's own body, the forest, and Mount Mahāmeru possess a golden hue; just as the clouds possess the salty water of the ocean and the excellent clear water [of the rivers]; so too, in the great Ānandāvalī, all things such as the earth and stones possess the nature of river-water.
(3) ... [as if they were] like that. All objects, beginning with the earth and stones, within the great Ānandāvalī, are like the water of the rivers.
Like the Aparañci golden river...
I am a Brāhmaṇa who knows that; once, while engaged in a particular ritual act, I went to wear the sacred thread (kūḍumi). These people have now become renunciants (saṃnyāsikas). (14–15)
...and like the supreme Śreṣṭhara who is free from attachment, and like salt for all that is opened up, in the city of Kāśī...

(l6) ...all those who have received the great instruction (mahopadeśa), like the atom (aṇu) which is always diamond-like, and likewise for all those who have received the Śiva-saṃskāra, together with their previous births...
Know that [his] former name, lineage (*gotra*), and designation (*nāmadheya-rūpa*) shall become otherwise. 19.
Thereafter, by means of the *pūrva...* [and] ... through that, [there is] the realization of the *pratyavāya*... (p12b, l1).
It remains unspoken.
In the *Svacchanda*:
"Likewise, regarding the person dwelling in the stage of Śiva, that which causes displeasure... [as previously stated].
In the ocean of hell, however, [the duration] flows until the end of Brahmā’s single *pūṣā*;

for one who is worthy of worship, it lasts for five days, and likewise until the end of three *rudra*-days; thereafter, having attained the state of the Teacher, he remains in the stage called *Sādākhya* for three years. Thus it is said.

Having received the initiation (*dīkṣā*) of Śiva-saṃskāra and wearing the *vibhūti* and *rudrākṣa* as the marks of Śiva, that devotee of Śiva—[who was] Yogamāyā, [the one] who transcends darkness... [he who] remembered his previous birth... by the King [who was] the humblest of the Śakas...
in the presence of Brahmā... (l4)

He who said that those who do not observe the five days of Viṣṇu’s festival shall lie in hell for five days, and even longer than that in the state of *maukaviḷ* (the state of being a ghost), and furthermore, he who said that they shall lie in hell for five days on the day of Nīlarudra, and even longer than that... [in] the *lāḷi* of Nīlarudra for three days.
Thinking, "Will I remain lying in hell even for this much [time]? he honored the great elders who were Śaiva teachers and holders of the lineage of the Guru-pīṭha...
in the year of the Sādākhyatattva, three... (17)
Know that it is stated in the *Svacchandabhairava-āgama* that [those who act otherwise] shall lie in hell for a year. 20.

Even for Śūdras, initiation indeed brings about the attainment of the state of Śiva, the status of the twice-born (*dvijatva*), and furthermore, excellence; nevertheless, it is declared that they still possess the very nature of being limbs of the Veda (*nigamāṅgatva*). Therefore, their status as twice-born is not lost, just as in the case of women.

"O twice-born one, everywhere it is like that of a renunciant; such is the Vedic injunction regarding the respective regulations. Thus it is said. By the power of Śiva-initiation, those known as Mahāśūdras, born from the fourth caste, became endowed with the status of the twice-born.
... they are never fit for the meditative *śrauta* rituals. ... For them, the status of being twice-born (*dvijatva*) shall never be attained. Just so... (v.
14) ...the mantra-based twice-born status of Brāhmaṇa women and these Brāhmaṇa renunciants [is established]... and they must indeed perform the study of the Vedas in their hands...
In general... (l5) ...to the [temples] of the Lord of Vāvaru...
and also to the south. Not being such [as described], due to the delusion of his mind, the Caturthaśaivanāthan... (l6)
He requested the Śivāgama and the Drāviḍaśāstra for himself... [If one] performs the Śrauta rites, know that there is no sin (pratyavāya) whatsoever for him. 21.
The so-called Śaivas... [are] the Pāṭhas; indeed, the primordial Āgamas are declared by a number of twenty-eight through the stream [of tradition].

(p13b, l1) Because of the performance of worship and other rites starting from the root-meditation (*mūladhyāna*), and by means of verses beginning with the *anuṣṭubh* meter... for the ten births of the twice-born and others in the Śaiva sacrifice. May all be auspicious.
The most compassionate Śrī Mahādeva, the Supreme Lord, [bestowed] the Caryāpāda— which grants *sālokya* as its ultimate goal— to those who were perfected through the initiation of Śiva. Sāmīpya...

The four quarters— namely, the *kriyāpāda*, *caryāpāda*, *yogapāda*, and *jñānapāda*— are intended as the means (*nimitta*) for attaining the four goals of life (*caturvarga*), namely dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; and for the sake of protecting all the worlds, the sevenfold initiation of Śiva (*śivadīkṣā*) is required.

The rites beginning with *karṣaṇa* (plowing) and ending with *pratiṣṭhā* (consecration), as well as those beginning with *pratiṣṭhā* and ending with *utsava* (festival)—these rituals must be performed... [according to] the *Kāmikāgama*, through meditation... (l6) 28. Also, by means of the divine *Āgamas* and verses (*padya*) composed in the *anuṣṭubh* meter, in that sequence of sacred tradition...

Tiruvuḷḷam pa... (l7) Furthermore, in that Śaivavāreṇṉil, among the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, those six persons who were born in the lineage of those four, making a total of ten persons— (p14a, l1) for these eleven persons...
Know who is qualified to study these Śivāgamas. 22.

Next, the conduct appropriate to one's own caste (*svajātyācāra*) is mentioned: "Even one who is distinguished by Śiva-initiation (*dīkṣā*) and established in the Śiva-order (*śivāśrama*), should always perform that which is declared suitable for his noble birth (*sujāti*) and consistent with good conduct (*sadācāra*), avoiding any confusion; such a wise man is indeed the foremost among the Śaivas. Thus it is said. [Regarding] one distinguished by Śiva-initiation...
Even while living,
whatever Śivāśramin gives— provided it is appropriate for his own caste, suitable for that particular region, free from confusion with the customs of other times, and is wholesome— (l3–l4)
Know that [the one] among the sixfold [traditions] who follows the Śaiva-samayācāra is a Vaidika-Śaiva.

23. Now, the gradation of statements is being declared: the gradation of statements here has been proclaimed... as it is proclaimed in the world... therefore that which is undesirable is indeed better than that; therefore, from this, the word of the Creator [is superior]. The statement of Indra is [inferior] to that.

"...for that purpose, it is better [to follow] that Raudrānta-virama-aiśvara-pravilīna-aiśvara. Thus [it is said]. It is stated in the Pauṣkarāgama that there is a gradation of statements; according to this, just as in the world there is the word of those who are generally considered authoritative...

The word of the Ṛṣis, being scriptural (ārṣa), is superior; even more so is the word of Brahmā; even more so is the word of Viṣṇu; even more so is the word of Rudra; and even more so is the word of Īśvara.
The word *vacanam* is redundant; thus, it should be read as *vacanam adhikam*. In this manner, one should understand the sequence of the gradations of speech (*vacanatāratamyakrama*).

This final rite (*antyeṣṭi*) is stated to be an ancillary (*aṅga*) of initiation (*dīkṣā*); here, O Noble One, worship (*pūjā*) is said to be an ancillary of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*);
some [act] is declared to be an ancillary of bathing (*snāna*); and the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) would be an ancillary of fasting (*upavāsa*). (L3) What [is the case here]?

For the *naimittika* initiation, the *antyēṣṭi-kriyā* together with the *sapindīkaraṇa* is an auxiliary; for the *pratiṣṭhā* rite, the characteristics of the preceptor (*ācārya-lakṣaṇa*) are an auxiliary; and for the auspicious bath (*puṇyakāla-snāna*), giving gifts according to one's capacity (*yathāśakti-dāna*) is an auxiliary to the bath;
[and for] the fast (*upavāsa*)—(l5)
Fasting is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the *pārāyaṇa*, and thus these are known as the auxiliary rites for occasional duties (*naimittika-karmāṅga*).

44. Regarding those which are optional rites (*kāmya-karmāṇi*), obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*), and occasional rites (*naimittika-karmāṇi*): [as for] the optional... for it is said that there is a specific concluding rite (*udyāpana*) for each of them, according to the method prescribed therein. What [is this]?

As for the optional times (*kāmyakāla*): apart from the two types of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites mentioned previously, there are the Somavāra-vrata, Umāmaheśvara-vrata, Kedāra-vrata, Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī-vrata, Śuklāṣṭamī-vrata, Vināyaka-vrata, and Vināyaka-... (p23b, l1).

The fourth vow (caturthī-vrata), the sixth-day vow (ṣaṣṭhī-vrata), the Sunday vow (bhānuvāra-vrata), the Tulākāverī vow, bathing in the Gaṅgā up to bathing at Setu, bathing in sacred rivers (puṇyanadī-snāna), and so forth—all these are known as optional rites (kāmyakarmāṇi). For all such vows, there is the concluding rite (vratodyāpana) for that... [purpose].
It performs [the rite]. Know that it is stated in the Śivāgamas that this is an ancillary (aṅga) to that vow. 45. Afterwards, bathing is said to be of eight kinds. First, regarding those baths: (l4)
For the celibate student (brahmacārī), there may be the Bhasmaka, Māntra, Mānasa-divya, Māruta, Gaurādya, and Pārthiva;
having performed these eight mantras and the Ṛk-text, one should daily perform the fourfold bath beginning with the water-bath (udakasnāna).

This is the complete cleansing of all limbs with moist cloth according to the Kapila [tradition]. (l5) What is it? It is said that there are eight kinds of baths; and what are they? They are: the Varuṇa bath, which is the water bath; the Āgneya bath...

The fourfold bath consisting of *bhasmasnāna* (ash-bath), *mantrasnāna* (mantra-bath), and *mānasasnāna* (mental bath) is known as the *nityasnāna* (daily obligatory bath). The four [types of baths] consisting of *divyasnāna* (celestial bath), *mārutasnāna* (wind-bath), *gauravasnāna* (respectful bath), and *pārthivasnāna* (earth-bath)— these four...

There are eight types of bathing, including the *naimittika-snāna* (occasional bathing). Even when one does not perform formal bathing, if one rubs all the limbs with a wet cloth, it is called *kāpila-snāna*.
Know that such various classifications of bathing are described in manifold ways within the Śivāgamas.

Furthermore, the previously mentioned ritual bathing (*jalasnāna*) is of two kinds: with mantras (*samantraka*) and without mantras (*amantraka*). Among these, the bathing with mantras (*samantrakasnāna*) is prescribed for Brahmins and those who have received Śiva-initiation (*śivadīkṣā*).
It may also be performed for those who are without mantras and have not received Śiva-initiation.

Regarding the *āgneya-snāna* (fire-bath), which consists of rubbing the head and all limbs with holy ashes (*bhasma*), it is said that this alone may be performed for one observing a vow; furthermore, this *āgneya-snāna* is likewise of two types: with mantras (*samantraka*) and without mantras (*amantraka*).
It is of two kinds:
(15) that which is performed with the awareness of what is appropriate and what is inappropriate, and that which is performed together with mantras.
As for mental bathing (mānasa-snāna), it is as follows: (16)
Performing the visualization of bathing well within the mind as a mental instruction from the Guru is called *mānasa-snāna* (mental bathing).
Thus, these four types of bathing constitute *nitya-snāna* (daily obligatory bathing).
Now, *divya-snāna* (divine bathing): [17]
When it is slightly warm, facing east in the rain of *netrāñjana*, one recites the *Īśāna-mantra* and the *Tatpuruṣa-mantra* and walks seven steps; this is the "divine bath" (*divya-snāna*).
Whether it is the "hot bath" (*āmoṣṇa-snāna*) or the "lukewarm bath" (*apomānya-snāna*), when the animals bathe by themselves... [of] those animals.
The dust particles within a pond, driven by the wind,
move toward it so that they may fall upon its entire body, covering it completely;
this is known as *māruta-snāna* (wind-bath), which is also called *vāyavya-snāna*.

Earth-bath (*pārthiva-snāna*): Having taken sacred earth from rivers that are specially distinguished by the presence of Śiva’s sacred sites (*śivasthala*) within great Śiva-sites, and having placed it at the very location where one is staying, one sprinkles that earth upon one's head after kneading it with water whenever necessary. Or else—
Having rolled it up and applied it as a *tripuṇḍraka* like holy water (*tīrtha*), one wears *vibhūti* over it;
this is known by the great name "bathing on earth" (*pārthivasnāna*).

Gaurava-snāna (the bath of honor) consists of bathing all the limbs, beginning with the head, by rubbing the two *śrīpādas* (holy feet) of one’s own *ācārya* with sandalwood paste and water, or by merely touching them; or else, by sprinkling [the water] upon the head and [entering] within.
Receiving [the remains of the offering] is also the *gaurava-snāna* (bath of honor).
Thus, across all [categories], there are eight types of baths, beginning with the *jala-snāna* (water bath) and ending with the *gaurava-snāna*.
Apart from these, [there is also the bath with] the *nirmālya* (remains of the offering) of Mahādeva.
Having brought it in a vessel, one bathes all over the body with that Śivatīrtha;

this is known as the "Nirmālya-snāna" (bath with the remains of the offering). It cures great diseases such as leprosy (kuṣṭha-vyādhi) and the like, and it also dispels all afflictions such as those caused by bhūtas, pretas, and brahmarākṣasas.
Those who do not have children will give birth to a child after performing ablutions for forty-five days; thus, know that even the *kābila-snāna* is the *daśavidha-snāna*.
46. Afterward, [one should perform] the *catuṣpādacaritra* and *dāsya*. 45(l4). 46. Subsequently, the *catuṣpādacaritra* and *dāsya*. 45(l5).
The initiate (samayin) should perform the ritual, while the son (putra) performs the worship; the practitioner (sādhaka), moreover, must accomplish the essential principles of the yoga-practice.
Indeed, every such conduct must be performed by the preceptor.

[This includes] the construction of step-wells, wells, tanks, oblong ponds, groves, gardens, and houses; the fetching of water, the gathering of flowers, the weaving of garlands, sweeping, anointing with unguents and the like, as well as the management of vehicles and the care of the feet.
One who possesses the initiation into the *samaya* is qualified for all services (*kaṅkaryas*) pertaining to the merit of Śiva.
The path of the *sahaja*, such as the *Ṣaḍadhvataraśana* beginning with the Yoga-pāda of Śiva-worship which bestows both enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*), [is the means].
The son who possesses the *saṃskāradīkṣā*, which is the *viśeṣadīkṣā* for all [types of] performance of sinful acts, including the *miśra-satsūtra*... is fit;
and this ritual path (*kriyāpakṣa*)... along with the purification of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvaśuddhi*), pertains to the entire *sahamārga* consisting of the optional rites (*kāmyakarmāṇi*).

I am one who has attained the initiation of Nirvāṇa; I am the practitioner (*sādhaka*) endowed with the consecration of a practitioner (*sādhakābhiṣeka*). (l3) As for the question of whether such a practitioner is qualified [for this], these three verses are the instruction for all the true paths (*sanmārga*).
I am one who has completed the ritual of the Great Consecration (*mahābhiṣekakriyā*), possessing the initiation of Nirvāṇa that is the nourisher [of the path]. (l4)
Know that the life stories of those who are fit to perform and cause to be performed such acts as [occupying] the seat of the preceptor (ācāryapīṭha)...
47. Now, the wearing of Śaiva ashes (śaivabhasmadhāraṇa).
It remains unspoken.
The crown of the head, the forehead, the chest, the navel, the two knees, the two arms—these six locations;
as well as the throat, the sides, and the sacral joint (trikasandhi)—thus are the eight locations for the placement of protective ornaments. (6)
Thus it is said.

The sixteen locations for wearing the *vibhūtis* (sacred ashes) are as follows: the crown of the head, the forehead, the chest, the navel, the two elbows, the two knees, the two wrists, and the two ankles. (17)
Know that the *Kāmikāgama* and the *Cintyaviśvāgama* state that there are sixteen locations for wearing the sacred ash (*vibhūti-dharasthāna*), namely: one on the forehead, two on the ears,
and one below the head at the *mucchaṇḍi* [48].
Furthermore, it has not been stated in the words of the scripture that wearing [the ash] on the Vibhūti-marks will destroy those sins: "The sin committed above the neck is on the forehead;

that committed on the neck is on the throat; the sin committed on the arms destroys food; and that acquired by the mind is on the chest. (Śrī... *dhṛtagalopari kṛtaṃ pāpaṃ tu phāle gale* ... *bhakṣyaghnaṃ bhujayostu tatkṛtamaghaṃ vatse tu cittārjitam*)
That which is remembered in the Skanda Purāṇa as "the sin of embracing [the feet] at the anus,
the knees, and so forth"— if one performs [this] in the sixteen locations previously mentioned, beginning with the head, [then] all sins... (l4)

Regarding how even sins are removed: by the statement "if worn on the head, sins above the neck are destroyed," it means that by wearing it on the forehead (*lalāṭa*), the [sins] written in sequence...
are destroyed. By wearing it on the neck, the fault of eating forbidden food (*abhakṣyābhakṣaṇa*) and so forth is removed.
By applying it to the head, the faults committed by the mind are destroyed. By applying it to the navel, the faults committed by the genitals are destroyed.
By applying it to the knees, [the faults] committed by... are destroyed.
Sins committed [elsewhere] are removed. By applying [the ash] on the *trikaṇḍī*, sins committed by a kick are removed.
By applying it on the sides and by applying it on the inner arms...
(p26b, l1) Know that it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa that the fault of embracing is thus removed. 49.
Furthermore, by means of the wearing of ashes, the attainment of the other world... (l2) ...remains unspoken as being worthy.
One should wear those ashes upon the head and apply them profusely on the forehead like a digit of the moon.
His consort... [bearing] white luster upon her breasts, with her arms extended;
and [he wears] ash applied to other parts [of his body], a bull, and a garment of bark.
If this entire supreme observance (*niyama*) is performed with silver on the edge of a mountain, it shall be [efficacious] for Brahma... (l4) ...even when combined with those respective mantras;
if worn on the forehead, it will destroy a single lunar digit (*candrakalā*). If worn on the nose...
If it is worn on the eyes, it is called Netramuṇḍa; if worn in the cavity of the nape of the neck, it is one Lāñchana; if worn on the hands, there are divine weapons such as the Māna and others;
and if worn in the topknot or in the Mucchaṇḍi and other [locations]... (15–16)
Know that all these—such as "Vṛṣabhavāhana," "Rudrāmbara," and "Kailāsavāsa"—are stated in the section concerning the Brahmakūrca [rite] in the [text] titled *Muṇḍam*. 50.
(l7. Subsequently, no further fruit for the wearing of ashes has been mentioned.
One should place pure sacred ash upon the head; on the forehead, a golden crown and the like;
on the throat, necklaces and such;
on the arms, armlets, bracelets, and rings; and divine ornaments such as waist-bands and so forth.

The umbilical region and so forth, the palanquin and so forth, the knees, the hands, the feet, and the ornaments—what fruit is there for one who wears these [as marks] on the sixteen locations beginning with the head? If it is asked what the result of such possession by the *vibhūti* is, [the answer is: the stainless...
If one wears the *vibhūti* on the head, it bestows crowns, diadems, and the like; if worn on the forehead, it makes one a sovereign ruler (*paṭṭavardhana*).
Furthermore, if worn on the neck, chest, sides, and the joints of the face, it provides pearl necklaces. (13–14)

One should know that there are divine ornaments such as this "Golden Garland" (Suvarṇārmālā) and others; likewise, there are divine cloths, divine Śrīs, divine waist-bands (kaṭisūtra) and so forth, and divine women endowed with the five ornaments (pañcālaṅkāra).
One should also know that there are divine enjoyments; and when held in the hands, there are excellent [objects] such as shoulder-cloths (tōḷvane) and the like.
There are divine ornaments.

By wearing them on the knees (16), there exist divine vehicles such as chariots, elephants, palanquins, and the like, as well as divine foot-ornaments such as anklets; all these are present—thus it is said here (17).

Know that because it is a proximate fruit (*sānnidhya-phala*), the wearing of sacred ash (*bhasmadhāraṇa*) bestows the enjoyment of great fortune in this world and liberation (*mokṣa*) in the next. 51. Now, the increasing of the sacred ash (*bhasmavardhana*).

"How may one meditate upon Bhasmadeva for the sake of attaining one's desired goal—[upon him] who has three divine faces and nine tufts of hair, yet lacks a sacred story (*tirukathai*) and three feet; who possesses a divine gait, a crimson body, and a fierce appearance (*ugraveṣa*), and is smeared with ashes (*bhasmoddhūlanam*)? Thus [one should meditate]. So it is stated in the *Makuṭakam*.
Know that it has been stated:
"Black [sandalwood] is said to remove disease; red destroys fame;
yellow leads to the destruction of prosperity; and white accomplishes all goals. (52) [13] Thus it is said.
If one wears black vibhūti, it removes disease. If one wears red vibhūti, it increases prosperity. If one wears golden vibhūti, it increases sovereignty.
White vibhūti [removes] sin.
Know that it is stated in the Kāmikāgama that [the wearing of Rudrākṣas] grants liberation to both [the wearer and the one who gives it].

53. The wearing of Rudrākṣas is the singular doctrine of Śiva; specifically, one [bead] on the crest-lock, another on the head, four rows on the Śirīṣa [forehead], two on each ear, and six on the neck.
In the pair of hands of the thirty-two arms, there are two sets of twelve;
then on the chest, eight hundred, a thousand, and likewise ten thousand for the garland of heads. (l. 7)

One should wear Rudrākṣas as follows: one Rudrākṣa should be worn on the tuft of hair (*śikhā*); forty should be worn on the head; thirty-two on the eyes; thirty-two on the forehead; sixteen each on the two arms; and one hundred and eight on the chest. [Note: The character *ttā* (8) appears to be a scribal mark.]

Know that it is stated in the Śivāgamas that one may wear [the beads] according to one's capacity, or even as a *śiromālā* (a garland for the head), or by placing twelve at each of the *maṇibandhas* (wrist-joints).
Hereafter follow the benefits of wearing *rudrākṣas*.
It has been said:
"When a Rudrākṣa bead is worn as a head-armor, the merit is ten billion-fold;
when on the ear or the neck, it is a thousand billion-fold; on the arms, it is infinite; and likewise on the wrists. (v. 4)
If one wears Rudrākṣa on the head, there is merit equal to ten million (koṭi). If worn on the ears, there is merit equal to one hundred million.

If worn on the neck, there is merit equal to one billion. If worn on the chest, there is merit equal to ten billion. If worn on the arms, there is merit equal to one hundred billion. If worn on the wrist...
Know that the fruit of wearing Rudrākṣa in this manner is infinite millions of merits, as declared in the Śivāgamas. 55.
This is the corroborating statement.
The merit in seeing [the Rudrākṣa] is one hundred thousandfold, while in touching it, it is said to be ten millionfold;
indeed, the merit of the Rudrākṣa is [greater than] even a hundred times ten million.
Through recitation, merits equal to thousands of lakṣakoṭis and hundreds of lakṣakoṭis are obtained; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
The characteristics of the rosary:
one seeking liberation [should use] a rosary of twenty-five [beads]; for nourishment, twenty-seven;
one seeking wealth should have thirty; and for a farmer, fifty-five.
With the thumb, one seeking liberation [attains it]; with the index finger, the destruction of enemies;
the middle finger is said to bring prosperity; and with the ring finger, [it brings] longevity.

"The little finger is prescribed for drawing [the thread]; thus has the characteristic of the fingers been stated. This is a statement from the Āgama. Thereafter, the Sandhyāvandanam remains to be described.

For one who has received initiation, it is prescribed that there be at least one *saṃdhyā* performed either in the morning or at midday; O sages, even a single *saṃhitā* alone is obligatory, not the seed-syllables (*bījākṣara*).
For another, however, there are two [daily rites]... that mantra with its seed-syllable.

Thus, for both the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and the teacher (*ācārya*), the entire ritual of the morning and evening twilight worship (*saṃdhyāvandana*) is declared to be complete. For one who has received the initiation into the *samaya*, there is no need for meditative visualization (*dhyāna*) or seed-syllables (*bījākṣara*). (v. 15)

...By means of the eleven mantras, one should perform the application [of ash] during the morning and midday as a single-time rite (*ekakālānuṣṭhāna*), while at all other times one must wear the sacred ash (*bhasmadhāraṇa*).

When applying it mixed with water, it should be done with the *amantravat* (without specific mantras); however, when applying the *vibhūti* alone without water, it should be done with the Śiva-mantra.

Furthermore, for that son who possesses both initiations (*dīkṣā*), it is permitted to perform the practice of wearing the sacred ash (*vibhūti-dhāraṇā*) twice a day—at both morning and evening—conjoined with the seed-syllables (*bīja-akṣara*) of meditation (*dhyāna*).
For one who possesses three initiations... [p. 29a, l. 1]

The practitioner may perform the observance of wearing the sacred ash (*vibhūti-dhāraṇa-anuṣṭhāna*) during these three times: morning, midday, and evening. For the teacher who possesses the fourfold initiation (*caturdīkṣā-ācārya*), the observances of the *sakala*, *māna*, *niyati*, and *niyama* [are to be performed] during these four times: morning, midday, evening, and midnight.
Know that this may be performed.
56. Hereafter, the sequence of Śaiva ritual practice (*śaivānuṣṭhānakrama*) remains to be explained.

"Since it is said that 'you must certainly perform the morning bath with appropriate [substances] for the sake of worshipping the Lord,' one should then, having performed the external rites and so forth outside one's own dwelling,
carry out the bath as previously described, while seated facing north and observing [the ritual gaze] and so on. (L4)
The sipping of water from a pure lotus, as well as bathing with sacred ashes and mental bathing; ||1||
The protection, the dhāraṇa, the ācamana, the kara-punyāsa with the mahāmudrā, then the filling with the nectar of prāṇāyāma, the recollection of the brahma-sandhyā and so forth,
and after that, the sprinkling with nectar, the cleansing, and the striking away of obstacles.
Again, there is the sipping of water (*ācamana*), followed once more by the process of becoming complete (*sakalībhāva*) and the enveloping with water (*ambusaṃveṣṭana*).

(6) Then, one should perform the meditation on the Gāyatrī, the appropriate libation (*santarpaṇa*), its recitation (*japa*), the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*), the root-libation and recitation for Śiva, and the libation for Īśa and the others. (7)

The auspicious performance consists of sipping water (ācamana), the libation to the limbs of the hands according to the previously stated rule, the removal of the sacred water from that site, and the recitation of the mantra of Śaṅkara. Thus it is said.
For one who has attained the status of a distinguished Śaiva, [the practice] is as declared in the Śivāgama. (p. 29b, l. 1)

Regarding the method and the sequence of performance (*anuṣṭhānakrama*): having bathed according to the prescribed injunctions and put on one's garments, one should stand near water facing either north or east. Then, one should perform *ācamana* (ritual sipping of water) with pure water while reciting the mantras in their proper order. After that, the *vibhūti-snāna* (ash-bath).

Mental bathing (*mānasa-snāna*). Wearing of ashes (*bhasma-dhāraṇa*) at each respective place. (l3) Sipping water (*ācamana*). Hand-assignment (*kara-nyāsa*). Limb-assignment (*aṅga-nyāsa*). Great mudrās (*mahāmudrā*). Regulation of breath (*prāṇāyāma*). Conceptualization of the Śiva-tīrtha. Meditation on the *sandhyā* periods beginning with the Brāhmī. Afterwards, the sprinkling with nectar (*amṛtābhiṣeka*). Purification of sin (*aghamārjana*). (l4)

The *aghamarṣaṇa* [mantra]. Again, the sipping of water (*ācamana*), the ritual of empowering the limbs (*sakalīkaraṇa*), and the immersion in water (*ambusaṃveṣaṇa*). Afterwards, meditation on the *Gāyatrī* as appropriate; the libation (*tarpaṇa*); the recitation (*japa*) of the ten-syllable *Śivagāyatrī* mantra. Afterwards, the libation with the root mantra of Śiva (*śivamūlamantra*) and its recitation. Afterwards, the libation with the mantras beginning with Īśāna and ending with Sūrya. The sipping of water (*ācamana*); the ritual placement of mantras on the hands and limbs (*karāṅganyāsa*).
The withdrawal of that sacred site (*tattīrthopasaṃharaṇa*),

its elevation (*uddhāpana*), the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*), the worship of Śiva and the Sun (*śivasūryopasthāna*), the recitation of the Śiva-mantra (*śivamantrajapa*), and the salutation of the Guru (*guruvandana*). Thus is described the sequence for the performance of the Śaiva twilight ritual (*śaivasandhyānuṣṭhānakrama*) in the Śiva Āgamas.
Know this. 59. (57–58? The meditation on the deities of the four *saṃdhyās*, beginning with Brāhmī, as well as the meditation on Gāyatrī, are described in five verses.
One should meditate upon Brāhmī at the time of dawn [as] having four arms and four faces upon the elephant of the mind.
Red in color, adorned with red ornaments, her pure matted locks bound in a crown, seated upon a swan and a lotus;
holding in her hands, from left to right, a blood-stained rosary, a water-pot, and a staff;
youthful, endowed with the qualities of sacrifice, possessing eight eyes, she is the witness to the ritual acts of Śiva. ||1||
At midday, one should worship Vaiṣṇavī, who has the luster of the moon, two eyes, and a single face; she holds in her four hands, in order, a conch, a discus, a mace, and the gesture of fearlessness,
and is mounted upon a lotus on a forest-elephant, adorned with a garland.
Meditate on her who wears ornaments, possessing two hundred crores of circles of light;
she dwells in the lotus of the bull at the time of evening twilight, is Raudrī, slightly dark-complexioned,
with her head marked by the crescent moon, three-eyed, and possessing the slight movement of youth.

One should meditate upon the Mother of the World, who possesses the qualities of sacrifice, has a single lotus-face, and carries in her hands a trident and a water-pot in the left [hands] and a vessel for fear and liberation in the right. ||3||

Furthermore, at midnight, one should contemplate that slender, manifest, supreme Śakti, who dwells there without support, who is the essence of existence, partless, full of bliss, and the fourth twilight. 4.
The meaning of these four verses is explained in sequence as follows:
the deity of the morning twilight is Brāhmī; the deity of the midday twilight is Vaiṣṇavī;
and the deity of the evening twilight is Raudrī.
Thus, these four deities—namely *ardharātra*, *sandhyā*, *devatā*, and *rūpa*—are known as the great Sandhyā-devatās. Among them, as for the meditation (*dhyāna*) on Brāhmī:
she has four faces and four *śrī-hastas*... [the four *kaunas*]—and in those four *śrī-hastas*...
On his right side are the *sruk* and *akṣamālā* (3);
on his left side he bears the staff and the discus; his divine body is red, his sacred thread is red, his divine ornaments are red, and his garland is red (4).
One should meditate upon Him as being clothed in [a garment], wearing eight eyes and a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), accompanied by His consort Prabhā, extending over a crore of *yojanas*,
and seated upon an anthill (*valmīka*) in the form of a child. This is it.
Meditation on the morning twilight devotion.
Now, the meditation on Viṣṇu:
(l6) Just as my own face-maṇḍala has four śrī-hastas, [he too] bears the conch and the gesture of fearlessness on his right side, and the discus and the mace on his left side. (l7)

One should meditate upon Him in the center of the *brahman* as follows: He is white in color, with a white halo and a white garland of pearls; He wears two sacred threads (*yajñopavīta*) and has two divine eyes;

He possesses the bloom of youth; He is seated upon Garuḍa in the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), together with His consort Prabhā, at a height of two hundred million *yojanas*. One should thus perform meditation.

The Sky. This is the meditation on the Sandhyā deity for the midday period. Now, as for the meditation on Raudrī: it consists of one face-circle, three eyes, and four triple-hands; among these, on the right side—
Wearing a rosary and a trident on his left side, and bearing a spear and the gesture of fearlessness,
with a body slightly resembling that of a bull and a youthful age with a slight beard...
wearing a sacred thread, a crescent moon, a quiver, and a crown, [he stands] upon the back of a bull.
One who meditates upon [the Lord] seated in the *padmāsana* posture at the location of the *brahmarandhra*, accompanied by His consort Prabhā, extending across three hundred million *yojanas*,
does so during the evening time (*sāyamkāla*). (15–16)

Meditation on the Sandhyā Deities. At midday, one should meditate upon the form of the Sun, which is full and complete, pervading everywhere like a four-petaled lotus; this is the auspicious meditation for one who practices it. This is the meditation on the partless (niṣkala) Sandhyā.
Thus, know that the *sandhyā* at all four junctions of time is meditation (*dhyāna*). 63.
Meditation on the Śivagāyatrī: It remains to be told.
One should meditate upon Gāyatrī, the stainless sovereign lady with a single face, whose right foot is extended across [her lap],
who stands upon the petal of her left lotus-foot, whose matted hair shines like the crescent moon,
and who possesses two hands, holding a rosary in her right.
"In her left [hand] she holds a lotus that grants fearlessness; she is adorned with a white cloth and shines with the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
(Verse 3. This is the meditation on Gāyatrī. As for my own form: a single divine face, three divine eyes, and four auspicious hands; in the right hand, a rosary... (Verse 4).
She bears the *pradhāna-mudrā* in her left hand, as well as the *abhaya-mudrā* and a lotus flower;
with her right leg slightly bent and her left leg extended upon the surface of a lotus, she sits in a comfortable posture (*sukhāsana*), her matted hair (*jaṭā*) joined with the crescent moon.
It is finished;
(l6) the white sacred thread (*śvetopavīta*), the white garland, and the excellent divine ornaments; having applied the ash-marked triple-tilaka (*bhasmatripuṇḍra*)...
possessing a complexion such as [that of] lapis lazuli... (l7)

Having meditated upon Gāyatrī as having come from the solar orb into one's own heart at that very moment, and then meditating upon her as having ascended back into the solar orb— in this manner, one should understand what is known as the Śivagāyatrī-dhyāna. 64.
The rules for the seat have not been stated.
On the ground there is suffering; on a stone, however, there may be a lack of depth [in meditation]; on grass, there is the gain of fame;
on a leaf, there is the agitation of thoughts; and on a wooden seat, there is the granting of great prosperity.

"In the bamboo [mat] there is painful poverty; in the cloth, the wasting away of disease; in the woolen blanket, happiness; in the tiger skin, prosperity; and in the black antelope skin, immortality and knowledge.
(3) Thus it is said.

There is sorrow because of being on bare ground; if one were on stone, there would be luster. If one were on a grass seat... (14) ...there would be agitation. If one were on a wooden plank, there would be great prosperity; if one were on a bamboo mat, there would be hardship.
Poverty occurs if [the seat] is made of grass. If it is made of cloth...

(15) there will be the destruction of one's left side and so forth. If it is made of woolen cloth, disease will occur. If it is made of tiger skin, both prosperity and liberation will be attained. If it is made of black antelope skin (16)...
If [this] exists, Śivajñāna will exist. Know thus the power of the seat (āsana), which remains precisely during the times of worship and other periods...
(17) ...elsewhere, the coconut... the excellent seat of the bull... the ketaki born in the forest... and so forth... it is described. Thus.
This is the statement of Smṛti. [Question: "Is it not the case that...
(p32b, l1) ...the face is fashioned from the lower jaw... the Āsana is indeed mentioned in the Āgamas. And so it is stated in some Āgamas (l2).
Know that it was stated [in the previous verse] that this is not the case.
66. Subsequently... the sequence of the Sūryapūjā is not described even within twenty verses.
(l3) Among those, the Sūryapūjā is not described in four verses.
I shall now describe the sequence for the worship of Śiva for one's own benefit, by the grace of Umānātha. Then, having approached the place of worship, the purifier should worship the Sun;
furthermore, [he should perform] the application of sacred ash (*vibhūti-dhāraṇa*), as well as the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), the water-offering (*arghya*), and the water-offering for that worship.
Therefore, one should fashion a lotus in the sky with the syllables of the mantra.
(L5) With a staff, tawny tusks, and heavy faces, the abundant seat in the center is to be worshipped; and the four feet, above the Vimalā [level], are the lotus seat.

In the eight petals starting from the east, there is the group of nine beginning with Dīptā, and the sun-throne; here is the worship of the Mūrtis with Khaṣolkin, and the meditation on Śiva-Ravi which bestows tranquility. ||2||
One should meditate upon Bhānu, radiant as saffron, with two eyes and one face, seated upon a lotus,
holding in his hands the *amṛta* vessel and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) over the right lotus,
and joined by the goddess Oṣadhī, who stands to his left and likewise to his right.
One should meditate upon this maṇḍala of the red cloth and so forth, together with the form... [of] the mantra that is directly perceived.

Therein, one performs the invocation and its subsequent rites, the mudrās, and the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the lotus-image; then follows the washing of the feet, the offering of perfumes, flowers, ornaments, and handfuls of flowers.

One should offer food and other items that are conducive to enjoyment and possess qualities such as [auspicious] characteristics; and by the worship of Caṇḍa, one's splendor increases—thus has been described the sequence of Mārkaṇḍeya’s worship. So it is said.
The worship of the Sun, the Self, the sacrificial fire, the deity, the preceptor, and the sacred thread—
this is the worship of Śiva, reckoned as constant and consisting of six supports.

Sūryapūjā, Antaryāgapūjā, Śivaliṅgapūjā, Agnikārya, Gurupūjā, and Śāstrapūjā— know that these six [are to be performed] daily, and that Sūryapūjā is mentioned first here in the Mōhaśūrottara Āgama. Therefore, [l5]...

As an ancillary part of the Śiva-pūjā, perform the Sūrya-pūjā according to the following procedure: Having gone to the Śiva-pūjā hall and seated upon the throne facing east... [having performed] the application of vibhūti and the *sakalīkaraṇa*, thereafter, by means of the six-limbed mantras of the Sun...
Having performed the Kara-aṅga-nyāsa, having prepared the *darśanārghya* and offered the arghya,
[recite] the Sūrya-mūla-mantra... thereafter, having discarded that water from the arghya vessel and washed that vessel, [perform] the Sūrya-ṣaḍaṅga-mantras.
Having prepared [the seat] for the worship of Sūrya with the *sūryamūlamantra* and [other mantras], and having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus in the form of lines like a [drawn] outline,
(l2) one should sprinkle that ground with the *astramantra* and worship Daṇḍī, Piṅgala, Vināyaka, and Śāntaguru in this manner.

In the center, having worshipped the sixfold seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*) consisting of a white lotus with four legs and pure seats such as *vimala*, [one should worship] the powers (*śakti*) beginning with *Dīptā* on the filaments (*kesara*) starting from the east,
and [the power] within the pericarp (*karṇikā*)... everywhere.
Having worshipped Mukhiśakti and worshipped the Ārghāsana, and having understood the meditation that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, he worships Kaśolkamūrti and offers the two eyes.
(15) Thereafter, having performed the invocation (āvāhana) of Sūrya with the Sūryamūla-mantra and offered the invocation-arghya, he performs the rites of stabilization (sthāpana) and so forth.
Having offered the *nirādhārārghya*,
having shown the *bimba-mudrā* and the *padma-mudrā*, having offered the *svāgatārghya*, having made the petition as follows, having illuminated the divine feet,
and having performed the *gandha-kusumāñjali*, [one should worship] with the *sūrya-mūla-mantra*.
Having offered a handful of flowers,
[he performs] the *bhogāṅga* rite:
"O God of gods, may my ritual action be the foremost auspiciousness for the world."

"Stay, O Sūrya, Lord of the World; you have been established by me through devotion. Having thus worshipped, he should offer the *daṇḍamudrā*, *govishaṇamudrā*, and *trāsanimudrā* for the six ancillaries (*ṣaḍaṅga*), and perform the worship of the enclosures (*āvāraṇapūjā*) beginning with Soma.

Having performed the *namaskāra-mudrā* (12), and thereafter having offered the *naivedya* and other items, one should perform a hymn of praise (*stotra*) and make a request; then, in the direction of worship,
one should offer the *parāṅmukhārghya* to the Sun and others (13).
Having offered these and completed the worship, one should worship the root-form of the deity on the seat with "Tejaścaṇḍāya namaḥ," offer the *naivedya* (food offerings) to Sūrya,
and having accepted the fruit of that worship,
one should dismiss Lord Tejaścaṇḍeśvara and also dismiss the *arghya* offerings of the Sūrya-pūjā; thus is the Sūrya-pūjā performed every day.
One who performs this at each of the [five] times—
know this to be the Sūryapūjākrama. 6… Next, the ritual procedure for the worship of Śiva for one's own self (ātmārthaśivapūjāvidhi) is stated:

Having performed the worship of the deity according to the ritual for worshipping Īśvara, and having sipped water (*ācamya*), one whose limbs are smeared with ashes [should perform] the northern... water and remain there; then, after performing the general *arghya* offering, the worship of the door is performed.
Having gone outside to pacify the three obstacles, one performs the inner worship in the middle of the door.
The door-panels, the worship of the two door-keepers, the great throne, and Nandin;

(1) the armor consisting of the protection by weapons, the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), and thereafter the procedure for the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*), while the external purity is understood as that which is specifically designated [for the outer ritual]. (p34b, l1)
In this rite, there should be water for the feet and so forth, as well as the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and the five nectars (pañcāmṛta);
there should be purification, the application of sandalwood paste, self-worship, and the purification of the mantra. ||2||

Thereafter, there should be the worship of Peṭṭaka-Bhīmarudra; below the worship of the door-deities, on the altar, there is the seat of power (*balāsana*). Below that, having grasped the *liṅga* with both hands and placed it [there], it is adorned below that... [and then] liberation.
Furthermore, that which has been left overnight is not worthy of offering here; indeed, one should offer curd-rice (3).

Betel, however, for the presiding deity... likewise incense and a lamp with the [right] gaze; the placement [of the hand], the removal of the worship, the excellent offering, and then the name-mantra with the little finger at the front (4).

It is stated in the Kāmika that the purification of the *liṅga* is performed with the remains of the offering (*nirmālya*), water from the *kuhaṇḍuka*, the consecration of the cloth (*vastrābhiṣeka*), and the ordinary *arghya*. 4.
Thereafter, having again worshipped the painted image (*kucitranāpaṇa*), one should perform the worship of the sixfold arising seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*).

Therein, having offered the form of the Lord’s seat along with joined palms to Śiva and the others, one performs the invocation (*āvāhana*), the installation (*sthāpana*), and the presence (*sannidhāna*). Thus, according to the ritual sequence, follows the worship of the Indragandha.
Having assembled, both the water for the feet (pādya) and the other offerings, such as incense (dhūpa) and so forth, should be given to the eight guardians of the forms (mūrtipāḥ). ||5||

The bathing with oil and other substances, the bath with sandalwood powder, the sprinkling with a stream of water by the preceptor, the wiping of the wet body with a cloth, and the mounting of the auspicious seat (bhadrāsana) upon the excellent throne.
Then follows the worship of Vighneśa, Abja, the Planets, and Ārya; then the worship beginning with Śakti and ending with Śakti;
then the worship of the seat (āsana) and the form (mūrti), as well as the placement (nyāsa) in the shape of a staff (daṇḍākṛti). ||6||

Having extracted the essence of the words of the venerable *Kāmika* and *Vātula* Āgamas, [this work] sets forth the ritual for the deposition of the tonsured (*muṇḍanyāsa*), the establishment of the thirty-eight *kalās*, the offering consisting solely of dedication to Śrīkaṇṭha, and the worship of the body of the Vidyā.
To summarize here, the meditation on Sadāśiva with attributes (*saguṇadhyāna*) is described as follows:

One should meditate here upon Sadāśiva, who bears the body of knowledge (*vidyādehavāha*), seated upon a pure lotus throne, possessing five lotus-faces, each with three eyes, and ten upraised arms on the right.
On his left, he holds in sequence a trident, an axe, a sword, a vajra, and a noose, along with fire, a bell, a lotus, the earth, and kusha grass. ||8||

Thus, regarding the face, there is the triad of visions; furthermore, here [are] the mounting, the offering of water (arghya), the installation of the vital breath (prāṇa), the presence, then its obstruction, the movement, and the arghya-offering.
[The offerings for] the throat and ears, the smearing with ashes here, and the offering of limbs to Īśa and the others.
And oneness [is achieved] by uprooting [the hair] with a closed fist; [this applies to] a cow, while for a *mahāmuṣṭhī* it is done with a large fist. ||9||

Where is the flower? "Welcome," [he says]. Then, O Lord of Speech, at the greeting, the five-faced one offers the *arghya*; then the offering of water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and *arghya*.
Then there is the worship with flowers, *akṣata*, and *dūrvā* grass, followed by the offering of incense and lamps.
Then [he performed] the offering of water for the feet and so forth, the washing of the sandals, the sprinkling, and the loosening of the sacred thread. ||10||
The internal worship with a single flower is appropriate; one should not offer mantras apart from the mantra.
And it is said [in the scripture] beginning with "Oṃ Aṃśumati," regarding the divine garments... gold...
that which [is offered]; the Lord [is worshipped] with sandalwood, ornaments, flowers, and so forth, with the threefold *añjali* according to the reality.
In the flower shop, there should be the offering of incense, lamps, and people, as well as the presentation of the *kāmamudrā*.

(p35b, l1. ...worship with the root mantra, the worship of the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga-pūjā*), and then the presentation of the five mudrās known as the *dhenu*, the *abja*, the *triśikhā*, the *mātṛkā*, and the *sruk*. (l2.)
The transformation of the river into the six perfections, and below that, the infinite...
[and] the worship of Indra and others with the vajra-weapon and so forth, together constitute the fivefold enclosure.
(12) Having offered incense and the rest, the food offering (naivedya) endowed with the six flavors is said for him. (l3)

There should be betel and the like, a multitude of incense and lamps, dūrvā grass and the like for the *athārātrika* offering, as well as protection, a mirror, a collection of umbrellas, ornaments, and the presentation of chowries and so forth. (Verse 14) There should be three handfuls of root-flowers, and again, three sets of five principal [offerings]. (Verse 13)

Having performed the great mudrā and the recitation (*jāpa*), and having protected it with the scripture (*śāstra*) and so forth, one should offer from the right hand— along with a handful of flowers— the three verses that have been recited. Following that, there should be the worship of the yoga-seat (*yogapīṭha*), which consists of the sacrifice to the mantra of the intended deity (*sādhyamantra*).
Then again, there is the worship of the teacher of knowledge (vidyādeśika), followed by the root mantra and the triple handful of flowers (tripuṣpāñjali). ||14||

A suitable hymn of praise preceded by devotion should be performed, followed by the offering of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Then, the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) is to be carried out in due order, as well as the offering of flowers and its fruit. Whatever has been prepared according to the ritual manual (*sūtra*) should be placed in the right hand of Śambhu.
Then, the hymn of praise and the eightfold worship should be performed with the [mantras] beginning with *tatpuruṣāya*, etc., and with the Brahma-mantras.

Furthermore, worship should be performed with the root mantra (*mūla*), and then the rite of raising [the deity] along with its limbs must be carried out. After that, the procedure for the worship of the deity facing away and the worship of Caṇḍeśvara should be performed.
Following that, the worship of Kapila, the offering of a morsel of food to a cow, and the salutation of the Guru are declared;
thus is the sequence for one's own purpose and the worship of Śiva established through two logical justifications. ||16||
Thus, the meaning of verse sixteen (14) has not yet been stated. By the grace of Mahādeva, the devotee of Pārvatī, [this] is the sequence of the worship of Śiva for the sake of the Self (15).

It remains to be stated. Since the worship of the Sun (Sūryapūjā) is an ancillary part of the worship of Śiva, and because it is referred to as "the section beginning with the Sun and ending with Caṇḍa," one should perform the worship of the Sun as previously described (l6).
Upon its completion, one should again perform ācamana for the sake of meditating upon the Sun, and then perform the nyāsa.

Having sipped water with the *jalam-iṣṭramāt* mantra, or having merely worn the sacred ash (*bhasma-dhāraṇa*), and having offered the *sāmānyārghya*... [he] places the *arghya* in his left hand and approaches the vicinity of the door.
Standing there, having sprinkled the eastern door, the southern door, and the western door with the *sāmānyārghya* and the *astra-mantra*, one should worship the doors by worshipping Vināyaka,
Sarasvatī, Mahālakṣmī, Nandi, Gaṅgā, Mahākāla, and Yamunā, and having also removed the three obstacles (*vighnatraya*).

Then, having entered within (l4), [having worshipped] Rukmiṇī... and having worshipped the guardians of the weapon-gates (astradvārapālas) in the manner described below, one should place [the hand] on the right side of the doors while maintaining that meditation:
vimalāya namaḥ | (l5)

Salutation to Subāhu. Having worshipped Brahmā, the lord of the site (*vāstvadhipati*), in the northwest direction within the house of worship, one should thereafter sit facing north upon a seat such as a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) at the place of Śiva-worship. Having placed the general water-offering (*sāmānyārghya*) there, one should worship Nandikeśvara together with Yaśas, facing east, upon the lower pedestal.

Thereafter, having performed the meditation on the triple moat consisting of the *astra*, the enclosure wall (*prākāra*), and the armor (*kavaca*); having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*); having prepared the special arghya water (l.

2) and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*); and having thereafter performed the purification of the ritual materials (*dravyaśuddhi*), one should worship Śivāsana upon one’s own seat and Śivamūrti within one’s own body (l. 3).

Having applied a tilaka on the forehead with sandalwood paste and performed the offering of flowers upon the head, one should perform the self-worship (ātmapūjā) and contemplate "I am Śiva" (śivoham-bhāvanā). Then, for the purification of the mantra (mantra-śuddhi), one should recite the root mantra (mūla-mantra) twelve times and the five Brahmans (pañca-brahmans) as many times as there are syllables in the Brahma-mantra.

Having dissolved the six limbs into the *piṇḍasthāna*... (15) ...this is the pronunciation of the protracted (*pluta*), long (*dīrgha*), and short (*hrasva*) vowels. This is the purification (*śuddhi*). Thereafter, having offered the heart-gesture (*hṛdayāñjali*), [one performs] the *śalaprāsāda*... (16)
Having worshipped Rudra on the eastern shoulder of the Kīya Peṭṭakku temple and having obtained his permission,

he caused the attendant deities to descend from the Peṭṭakkoyil and installed them in their respective places; having performed worship, he drew a circular enclosure (parivṛtta) upon the bathing altar (snānavedikā).
Having worshipped the Ṣaḍutthāsana upon the pedestal, he then caused the Śivaliṅgadeva of the Peṭṭakakoil to be brought forth by means of palanquins and circumambulated him on all four sides.
Having discarded [the water] with the Śivagāyatrī mantra, one who has offered the *sāmānyārghya* [should offer it] starting from Īśāna; thereafter, at that moment... (l4) [the following]:
eating betel leaf that is still warm from being held in the mouth, chewing betel nut, and offering the *naivedya*; after that, [one should perform the rite] with the Astra-mantra.

He shall cause a *stūpa* to be constructed from stone with a weight of fifteen *tanas*, and a lamp to be lit by Nēndar; having thus arranged for the maintenance of these services, he shall act accordingly in every respect.
Hereafter—(16)

Having consecrated the *satyādi* mantras upon the five faces [of the Liṅga] starting from the *taniṣṭhā*, and then taking a single fresh flower with the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger,
one should discard the *nirmālya* with the *hṛdayamantra* using the thumb, ring finger, and middle fingers; at that moment, that flower...
Having placed [the offering] upon the crown of the head with the Hṛdaya-mantra, and then reciting "Caṇḍe...

(l2), one should place those same *nirmālya* flowers in a vessel toward the northeast using the Hṛdaya-mantra; then, having washed the hands, one should [protect] the Śivaliṅga with the Astra-mantra (l3).
Having performed the consecration of the Lord with the *pādāstramantra*, one should perform the consecration with the *sāmānyārghya* using the *hṛdaya-mantra*. Then,
performing the consecration with water from a jar (*gaḍḍuka*) using the *hṛdaya-mantra*— this is the purification of the Liṅga (*liṅgaśuddhi*).
Afterward, having placed kuśa grass within the kavaca [armor], one should again invite [the deity] to ascend upon the *snānavedikā* (bathing altar).

Having performed the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) with pure water and again worshipped the sixfold seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*), one should worship the Śiva-mūrti on the Śivāsana. Having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*) by means of the root mantra, the stabilization (*sthāpana*), and the proximity (*sannidhāna*), one should perform the removal of the eye-veil (*netranirgala*) and the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the heart and other limbs, followed by the *deṇu-mudrā*.

Having offered incense and lamps for the worship of the Self, at the time of bathing, [one should perform] the invocation (*āvāhana*) with the thought that this much alone is required... [in the rivers]... afterwards, having performed the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) with the Heart-mantra and having removed the garments with the Armor-mantra (*kavaca*).
Anointing with a fragrant oil (*gandhataila*), rubbing with the *Satyājāta* mantra, rubbing with the *Mākābha* mantra, and performing an ablution (*abhiṣeka*) with pure water; then,
performing an ablution with a *jambū* fruit paste using the *Satyājāta* mantra and a turmeric paste using the *Vāmadeva* mantra.

Thereafter, having performed the *abhiṣeka* with pure water... (Kaṃ) (14), having performed the *abhiṣeka* with the five products (*pañcagavya*) by means of the root mantra, having performed the *abhiṣeka* with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), [one should perform] the *ghṛtābhiṣeka* with the Aghora mantra from among the five Brahmans. (15)

Having performed the consecration with warm water, one should thereafter perform the consecration with the heart-mantra using these: milk, curd, honey, sugar, black sandalwood paste, coconut pulp, plantain fruit, jackfruit, and mango (16).
Following this, one should perform the consecration with the juices of nutmeg, citron, and tamarind.

Having performed the consecration with the juice of *kuḷoñci* fruit and water, and thereafter having performed the consecration with pure water, having performed the consecration with fresh water, and having performed the *annābhiṣeka*, one should perform the *annābhiṣeka* for the sake of the self.
Having performed the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) by means of the words from the *Mekira-makuṭāgama*, and thereafter, at that very moment, having offered incense, lamps, and food offerings (*naivedya*),

and having performed the consecration with pure water, one should apply this paste— the saffron paste. Then, having again offered incense, lamps, and food offerings, [one should perform the consecration] with pure water using the hundred-spoked wheel (*śatadāra*).
Having performed the consecration with the mantras of the six limbs of the Mūlabrahma, one should thereafter perform the consecration with the Viśeṣārghya and Śaṅkhārghya using the Mūlamantra.
Then, having [wrapped] the sacred body with a pure, dry cloth, one should [protect it] with the Kavaca... (15)
Having offered a flower upon the head of Śakti, he shall cause [the deity] to arise facing north in the name of the Lotus Throne (padmapīṭha).
Thereafter,
in the northwest corner of the throne, he shall place Vināyaka facing south, and to its east, Mahālakṣmī.

Having worshipped the seven gurus starting from the northeast corner and proceeding toward the east, one should then worship the Śivāsana beginning with Śakti and ending with Adhiśakti; below the lower pedestal of the Lord, the Kūrmāsana is prescribed.
Then, having worshipped the Ādhāra-śakti and, above that, the Anantāsana and Ananta... [and] having worshipped dharma, jñāna, vairāgya,
and aiśvarya starting from the southeast at its feet, and adharma, ajñāna, avairāgya, and anaiśvarya in the four directions starting from the east...

Having worshipped these [deities] such as Anaiśvarya (14), one should worship the lower cover (*adhacchadana*) beneath the pedestal in the Nirṛti direction, and the upper cover (*ūrdhvacchadana*) above the pedestal in the Īśāna direction; then, upon the pedestal, one should worship the fragrance (*gandha*) and the seed-syllable (*bīja*). (15)

Having worshipped the sprout (aṅkura), the stalk (nāla), the bud (mukula), the young shoot (kaṇṭaka), the swelling node (upagranthi), the emerging petals (upadalaṅkau), the great petals (mahādalāni), the filaments (kiñjalkau),

the pericarp (karṇikā), and the seed (bīja), one should worship the lotus with the mantra "Salutation to Padmāsana" (padmāsanāya namaḥ). Then, having offered the lotus-mudrā and worshipped the firm seat (sthirāsana), one should [proceed] upon the filaments (kesara).
Starting from the east, these eight śaktis— Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā,
