Raudrī, Kālī, Kalavikaraṇī, Balavikaraṇī, Balapramathanī, and Sarvabhūtadamanī— as well as the Manonmanī-śakti in the pericarp of the Ālīśāna [lotus], [should be worshipped].

Having worshipped [the central deity], one should thereafter worship the solar maṇḍala and its presiding lord Brahmā within the circle of the pericarp-base; then, having worshipped the lunar maṇḍala and its presiding lord Viṣṇu within the circle of the tips of the filaments; and then, [one should worship] the fiery maṇḍala and its presiding lord Rudra within the circle of the tip of the pericarp.

Having worshipped [the deity] and thereafter, in the center of the *kāgrāma*, having worshipped the *śaktimaṇḍala* as well as its presiding lord, Īśvara, and having worshipped the *śivāsana* above that,
in this manner— (l5)
Regarding the method of worshipping the five seats (pañcāsanam): from Ādhāraśakti up to [the seat of] Ananta; above that, the Siṃhāsana up to the Ūrdhvachadana;
above that, the Yogāsana; the Padmāsana up to the pericarp (karṇikā); and above the pericarp, the Vimalāsana.
In this manner, having meditated upon and worshipped the five seats as the song of Śiva’s speech, one should thereafter worship the Śiva-mūrti, which consists of light and is in the form of a staff,
upon the Śivāsana; therein, according to the sequence of creation—

Having performed the Nyāsa of Daṇḍapaṅki and Muṇḍapaṅkinī, as well as the Aṣṭatriṃśatkalānyāsa and Mātṛkānyāsa, one should worship Vidyādeha as being of auspicious complexion, seated upon a lotus throne (padmāsana),
possessing five faces, ten arms, three eyes on each face, and red in color.

On the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet, on the right side, there are the *śūla*, *paraśu*, *khaḍga*, *kuliśa*, and *abhaya* [mudrās]. On the left side, there are these ten weapons: *agni*, *pāśa*, *ghaṇṭā*, *bhujaṅga*, and *aṅkuśa*.
Having meditated upon the divine form of Lord Sadāśiva Svāmī—

who has arisen clothed [in light], together with his five faces beginning with Īśāna, endowed with all ornaments, and possessing whiteness, golden hue, ... (darkness/black), redness, and white radiance ...—
one should thus [worship] the Vidyā-deha with a handful of flowers.

Having worshipped [the faces] beginning with Īśāna for the five faces, and having applied the three eyes, one should thereafter perform the invocation (āvāhana) of Śiva with the root mantra and offer the water of invocation (āvāhanārghya). Then, having recited the prāṇapratiṣṭhā mantra once—

Thereafter, having performed *sthāpana*, *sannidhāna*, and *sannirodhana*, and having offered the *nirodhārghya* water, one should perform the application of sacred ash (*bhasmadhāraṇa*). Then, with the *astra-mantra* ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, one should show the *kālakarṇikā-mudrā*; with the *vāmadeva-mantra*, the *liṅga-mudrā*; with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, the *namaskāra-mudrā*; and with the *kavaca-mantra*, the *avaguṇṭhana*.
Having performed the placement of the mantras beginning with Īśāna (l4),

having performed the ṣaḍaṅganyāsa, and having effected oneness by means of the root mantra, one should offer the dhenumudrā and mahāmudrā. Having offered a flower with the root mantra to Īśāna and the others (l5).
Having meditated upon the qualities of the Saṃhitā mantras and contemplated the relationship between the limbs and the possessor of limbs,
[one should pray]: "O Lord, Sovereign of the entire universe, remain present within this Liṅga with a spirit of complete affection until the conclusion of the worship."

Having made this petition and offered the *svāgatārghya*, at this juncture, having performed the *pañcamukhīmudrā* and subsequently offered the *pādya*, *ācamana*, and *arghya*, one should offer flowers, *dūrvā*, and *akṣata*, visualizing them as either *sāttvika* or *nāga*. Then, [offer] incense and the lamp.
Having offered water for the feet, having offered water for sipping...
while coming for the purpose of the [consecration] bath, having touched the pedestal of the Liṅga with the ring finger and having taken up a flower with the right hand,
[he should offer] the flower previously placed.
After wiping with a cloth, he should wash away the feet with pure water as a *śuddhābhiṣeka*; having performed it likewise with the water of the *viśeṣārghya*,
he should then sprinkle a drop of *viśeṣārghya* water upon the feet with a single flower, wipe them with a clean cloth (*śuddhavastra*), and thereafter— one [flower].
Having offered one flower without a mantra (15) and another flower with a mantra, and then releasing the left hand, at this moment, having applied a small amount of sacred ash (īṣat-bhasma-dhāraṇa),
[he attains] the Great Consecration (mahābhiṣeka) and [the state of] the three worlds... (16) gdhājagattrayaṃ.

"Since they are capable of consuming it, the offering for that time must be given; otherwise, [the deity] would become its master through life-force and power. According to this statement, having offered *pādya* and *arghya*, [he should offer] divine garments (*divyavastra*) with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, a golden sacred thread (*svarṇopavīta*), and subsequently apply anointment of fragrant substances such as musk.
Having offered camphor mixed with snow-white sandalwood paste,

having offered divine ornaments such as necklaces and earrings, having offered fragrant flowers, having offered a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) through the three principles (tattva-traya), and having thus adorned [the deity] with jasmine and other flowers, [worship] eternally in this manner.

Having meditated well upon Śivāsāmin, one should perform the ringing of the bell with the Astra-mantra, the offering of incense with the Śikhā-mantra, and the lighting of the lamp with the Netra-mantra, while changing the service accordingly.

Then, having given the Ācamanārghya, one should give the Manoratha-mudrā, worship the limbs of dissolution (layāṅga), cast one flower with the Mūla-mantra, and proceed to worship the limbs of departure (bhogāṅga).
In the Īśāna-pada of the lotus, one should place Īśāna; in the eastern pada, Tatpuruṣa; in the southern pada, Aghora; and in the northern pada, Vāmadeva.
One should place Satyājāta on the western square, Netra again on the northeast square, Hṛdaya on the southeast square,
Śiras on the northwest square, Śikhā on the southwest square, and Kavaca on the north square; thus, in the four squares starting from the east.

Having worshipped the Astra and each respective limb along with its corresponding meditation, and having thus worshipped Śiva with his limbs, sub-limbs, major limbs, and minor limbs, [one should worship] the five Brahmans beginning with Īśāna.
Having offered the *namaskāramudrā* with the heart mantra for the *dhenumudrā*, *padmamudrā*, *triśūlamudrā*, *makaramudrā*, and *sṛkmudrā* (l4),

having cast a handful of flowers with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, having performed the *mahāmudrā* and the *paramīkaraṇa*, [he should worship] well, accompanied by the respective *aṅga-mantras* (l5).
Having purified [the vessel], one who offers the *naivedya* at this juncture shall do so; or else, having performed the five-fold covering worship (*pañcāvaraṇa-pūjā*), he shall offer the *naivedya*.

Regarding the manner of worshipping the five-fold covering: (16) having worshipped the limbs of Brahmā (*brahmāṅga*) in the first covering (*prathamāvaraṇa*), and the eight Lords of Knowledge beginning with Ananta (*anantādyaṣṭavidyeśvarāḥ*) in the second covering (*dvitīyāvaraṇa*).

In the third enclosure, starting from the east, [one should place] the eight Vidyeśvaras; in the fourth enclosure, starting from the east, the ten guardians of the directions beginning with Indra; and in the fifth enclosure, starting from the east, the ten weapons beginning with the vajra.

Having worshipped with the *tattva-mantras*, he shall offer the *kālakarṇikā-mudrā* to Ananta and the others, as well as to Nandi and the others; and the *triśūla-mudrā* to Indra and the others, as well as to Vajra and the others (13).
Having offered these with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, and thereafter having worshipped Śiva with the *mūla-mantra*, he shall present incense, lamps, and the great food offering (*mahā-naivedya*).
It is said that offering food (naivedya) without white rice yields one unit of merit, whereas offering food with pure white rice yields ten times that merit.
It is said that an offering (*naivedya*) made with a *tina-arici* vessel possesses a hundredfold power, an offering made with a *kula-cennallam* vessel possesses a thousandfold power,
and an offering made with a *godamai* vessel possesses infinite power. Among these, two *nāḻi* measures [of grain] should be husked and weighed.
It is stated in the Kāmikāgama that even a single *marakkāl* may be used for the worship of the Self (*ātmartha-pūjā*), and that it is considered "excellent" (*uttama*);
furthermore, two *nāḻi* is "middling" (*madhyama*), three *nāḻi* is "inferior" (*adhama*), and four *nāḻi* is "lowest of the low" (*adhamādama*).
Thus it is said in the Kāmikāgama.
Since it is stated in the *Kāraṇāgama* that "nine *nāḻi* is the best (*uttama*) and seven *nāḻi* is the middling (*madhyama*)," one should understand this accordingly.

Having prepared [the materials] according to the sixfold division (*ṣaḍrasa-bheda*) by means of the *Mahānaivedya-mūla-mantra*, and having offered the *ācamana*, *pādya*, and *arghya*, one should thereafter perform the *karodvartana* and *mukhavāsa*.

Having offered [these], and having presented betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*) accompanied by camphor (*karpūra*), having given water for sipping (*ācamana*) and water for rinsing the mouth (*ārghya*), and having offered incense (*dhūpa*), [he offers] a single lotus-flame (*kuvalaya-dīpa*) or a flower-lamp (*puṣpa-dīpa*) starting from seven wicks (*saptavartika*).

Having performed the ritual service for the sixteen types of lamps— namely, Nāgadīpa, Puṣpadīpa, Puruṣāmṛkadīpa, Siṃhadīpa, Hastidīpa, Kūrmadīpa, Bhūtadīpa, Padmadīpa, Cakradīpa, Kalpavṛkṣadīpa, Latādīpa, Makaradīpa, Śūladīpa, Nakṣatradīpa, and Rathadīpa—
one should offer the *ācamanārghya* in the center of the inner courtyard.

Thereafter, having offered the *nityapatra* consisting of *dūrvā* and *akṣata* along with the root-mantra and flowers; then, for the sake of pacifying the sins of mind, speech, and body, having offered three handfuls of flowers while reciting the *śivatattvādya*; and thereafter, performing the *nīrājana*, [he offers] the *aṃśukavali* beginning with camphor, incense, and so forth.
Having purified the Ārātrika lamps with the *ṣaṭśuddhi*,

having worshipped them starting from the *digbandhana* and ending with the incense (*dhūpa*) and lamp (*dīpa*), and having lifted them with both hands, one should perform the kavaca [protection] with the Hṛdayamantra, beginning from the feet up to the head, and from the head down to the feet.

Having performed the circumambulation three times with the *tāla-ākāra* (hand gesture), and having offered the *ācamana-nārya* (water for sipping) at the waist-level, one should then place items such as nimba leaves,
dūrvā grass, karpūra (camphor), flowers along with their seeds (*sabīja*), and so forth, into a single vessel, and perform the circumambulation three times while reciting the *kavaca* (armor mantra).
Having performed the exchange of services, one should smear the sacred ash (*bhasman*) around the nostrils with the *mṛgamudrā* gesture, then cast it into the fire.
Afterwards, one should offer the ash to Śiva, [reciting]: "The ash is white, yellow, fragrant, and likewise free from sand."
One should apply the tilaka on the five parts of the face using the thumb and the ring finger.
According to the statement in the Kāmikāgama, "What is the purpose of protection for the middle of the eye on the forehead?
One should cause protection to be bestowed upon the eye above the forehead of Śambhu," one should apply the sacred ash with the root mantra to those respective locations of Śiva.

In the intermediate space, having cast the sacred ash while reciting the mantra for the purification of the hands, one should then assign the mirror, the umbrella, the fly-whisk, the fan, the palm-leaf fan,
and the *ālavaṭṭa* to Īśāna and the other deities, and [assign] the *candana* and other items to Sandhāna and the others.

Having meditated upon Śiva as the one worthy of praise, offer three handfuls of flowers with the root mantra and sprinkle water. Then, having offered [the flowers] with the Pañcamukhī-mudrā, Dhenu-mudrā, and Mahāmudrā using the root mantra, subsequently pray to Śiva and perform japa. Finally, observe the rosary and perform the fourfold purification (catuḥśuddhi) according to the procedure for offering the japa.

Having performed [the preliminary rites] and worshipped with the heart-mantra (l6), taking [the flower] with the right hand and placing the flower in the left hand, covering it with a clean cloth, and having recited the root mantra while listening to the words from the mouth of the Guru, thereafter that... (p45a, l1)
Taking the flower in the right hand and sprinkling the arghya water,
[one should say]: oṃ hāṃ guhyātiguhyagoptā tvaṃ gṛhāṇāsmatkṛtaṃ japam | siddhirbhavatu me yena tvatprasādāt tvayi prabho || oṃ hāṃ || (l2.)
Whatever action there may be, O Lord, whether always well-done or ill-done, that, while I abide in the state of Śiva, do thou enjoy and destroy for me, O Śaṅkara! Om Hāṃ!
Śiva is the giver, Śiva is the enjoyer; Śiva is this entire universe. (3)
Śiva performs sacrifice everywhere; that which is Śiva is indeed myself.

Having recited these verses while kneeling with the knees touching the ground, one should offer [the offering] at the base of Śiva’s feet using the root mantra (mūlamantra) along with the utpavamudrā; thereafter, having performed japa ten times for each of the Brahmāṅgas and having offered [the oblation],
one should perform sādhana.

Having informed Śiva that one intends to perform the mantra-worship (mantra-pūjā) and having received permission, one should worship the mantras of the female forms beginning with Gaurī in the vicinity below the southern petal of the lotus upon which the Lord is seated, and then [proceed] to one's own right side.
Having worshipped the deities of the Mṛtyuñjayādi mantras in the center of the assembly, as well as the Ardhanārīśvarādi mantras, and his own chosen sādhya-mantras according to his capacity—
Having performed japa and offered it to Śiva, one should thereafter worship the Yogapīṭha and Vidyāpīṭha to the west of the Lord, holding the heart-mudrā and añjali.

(Verse 3) "Salutation to the one stationed on the Vidyāpīṭha, who destroys all ignorance, who bestows universal knowledge, and who is the Lord; salutation to Him whose form consists of mind and speech. Thus [one worships] Śiva residing on the Vidyāpīṭha.

Having prostrated, one should worship the sixfold seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*) for the deity within the fire-pit (*agnidhikila*). Having worshipped one’s own guru therein with: "Salutations again and again to the feet of the venerable teacher (*śrīmaddeśika*), together with his Śakti," [and] "Always to Bhagavātman... (l5).
Having offered this hymn with the words, "Salutations, salutations to the causes of awakening," and having bowed to his own guru, he worshipped Śiva with three handfuls of flowers.

Then, praising Śiva with the hymns that had come to him—the foremost of the Śivāgamas—and subsequently rising up, he performed three circumambulations. Finally, he prostrated himself fully with eight limbs.
Having risen and prayed for what he himself desired, if he is unable to perform the *agnikārya* (fire-rite), he should pray to Śiva, saying:

"Be gracious to me, O Śambhu; let fire be obtained. If he is truly incapable, O Lord, let it be accomplished for me with eight flowers. Having thus petitioned, he should hold the vessel for the general *arghya* (*sāmānyārghyapātra*) in his hand.
Having completed the fire-ritual (agnikārya) in the manner that will be described, one should thereafter return to the end of the Śiva-mantra and, while seated upon the throne,
recite: "Whatever has been done and whatever shall be done, all that is your well-performed deed."
O Śiva, you alone are the protector of the universe; indeed, there is no other lord for me.
Whatever merit has been performed by me through acts such as worship and fire-offerings, that fruit, O Supreme Lord, is offered by me unto you.
"Accept this yourself with pleasure; may it be for my sake [the attainment] of enjoyment and liberation.
Having recited these two verses, [he should offer them] upon the palm of Śiva’s right hand with the *bhūmiṣṭhajānuvācaka* [mudrā].

Having offered [the oblation], and then remaining in a comfortable posture, having worshipped with the eight flowers (aṣṭapuṣpa), and having prostrated with the *śiroñjali*, one should worship with the five Brahmans beginning with Satya and with the Root Mantra (*mūla*).
Then, using the Root Mantra ending in *svāhā*, one should offer the *parāṅmukhārghya* for each limb (*aṅgāṅkībhāva*) to the deities of the enclosures (*āvaraṇadevatās*).
The Kāmyadevas,
having bestowed the *parāṅmukhārghya* upon these two, joined them to the *liṅga*. Then, [one should perform] the mantras for the seat (*āsana*),
worship (*arcita*), and so forth, both in their own respective places and upon the pedestal (*pīṭha*).

Having joined [the hands] and worshipped Śiva with the *namontamūla* mantra, and having performed the *rakṣāvakuṇḍa*, one should offer the honey-mudrā (*madhumudrā*) with the *vauṣaḍ-vantamūla* mantra, while holding [the vessel] with hands joined in *añjali*.
O Maheśvara, whatever has been worshipped by me— whether deficient in mantra, deficient in ritual action, or deficient in devotion— may that, O God, become complete for me.
Whatever I have done out of delusion, whether deficient or even excessive,
may all that become complete for me through your grace, O Lord.
Thousands of offenses are committed by me day and night;
considering me your servant, O Supreme Lord, forgive me.
O Master, [this has been done] by me, a wretched servant of impure intellect.
Since you have been gratified by even a mere fragment of devotion, you have been made to feel slighted; therefore, forgive that.
Having thus petitioned Śiva,
he should thereafter join the right wrist and likewise the left hand,
placing the three fingers beginning with the middle finger into the center of their respective palms.
Joining the thumb and forefinger, one should perform the dismissal of the three flowers;
having set aside those flowers with the mudrā called *nirodha*,
one should likewise place the joined palms (*añjali*) upon the head of the *visarjanī* mudrā.
Alternatively, having cast the two excellent mantras into the image by means of the two divine mudrās;
Having formed the *mastakāñjali* gesture, one should offer the *arghya* with the face turned away;
as stated in the words of Aṃsumān, having offered two flowers to the Liṅgamūrti by means of the divine mudrās with both hands, [one performs] the *mastakāñjali*.

Having performed [the rites], and having offered the *parāṅmukha-arghya* with special *arghya* water, one should contemplate it as consisting of light (*tejomaya*) and unite it within one's own heart.
(15) Afterwards, placing the vessel of *sāmānyārghya* upon the palm of the left hand, with that water, [one should sprinkle] the *yogapīṭha* and the *vidyāpīṭha*.
Having offered the *parāṅmukhārghya* to the Guru and the others, he shall join those mantras within his own heart.
Afterwards, he shall wash both hands.
Having properly exchanged the hands and having taken up each image along with its flower,
one should cover it with a cloth and armor and place it at the side of the casket.
Having arranged the elephants according to their respective positions, with the deity in the center,
the preceptor, recollecting the Śiva-mantra, should take hold of the liṅga.
Having wrapped it in a variegated cloth, one should place the image within the central box;

having joined the lid, one should always meditate upon Bhīmarudra. According to this statement from the Aṃśumānāgamavaśana, one should [install] Lord Śivaliṅga together with his retinue of deities in the inner sanctum.

Having risen and closed it, he then performed meditation upon Bhīmarudra for the protection of the *garbhagṛha*—the temple of the womb—reciting: "oṃ hāṃ bhīmarudrāya namaḥ," and worshipped him with a single flower. Having thus petitioned for the protection of the womb (*garbharakṣā*), he then...
Turning to face the east, one should draw a mandala in the shape of a half-moon and worship the form of Sadāśana therein.
[One should worship] Caṇḍa, who is born from the fire of Rudra’s wrath and resembles lampblack.
He holds a trident and an axe, is fierce, and carries a rosary and a water-pot;
he is adorned with a serpent as a sacred thread, has four faces and four arms,
and his twelve eyes gaze upon the great flames issuing from his mouths.
Adorned with a crown of matted hair and a crescent moon, wearing serpent-bracelets,
seated upon a white lotus throne, he is the destroyer of the pride of devotion. Alternatively, he has three eyes, four arms, one face, and is clad in pure white garments.
One should meditate upon Caṇḍeśvara as having his right foot hanging down, endowed with the state of pure consciousness,
his hand shining with matted locks, holding a naṭaṅka in his left hand,
or else with his hands joined in the heart-gesture of añjali.
Having meditated well in this manner,
he worshipped Caṇḍeśvara with all his limbs (sāṅgam), offered the *śivanirmālya*,
and presented lickable foods, dry snacks, drinks, betel leaves, blood, and ointments.
This offering of remains has been bestowed upon you by the command of Śiva.
O Caṇḍa, all this ritual procedure performed by me under your authority—
whatever was done deficiently or in excess through delusion— may that become complete for me.
Having thus petitioned and exhorted Caṇḍeśvara,
and subsequently having joined the mantras residing in the *arghyapātra* within his heart, he performed the purification of the *nirmālya* and went outside.
Having performed the external *ācamana*, having taken up the ashes without water, and having performed the *kara-aṅga-nyāsa*,
one should recite [the mantra] once along with the *mantra-saṃhitās*.
By reciting [this mantra] twenty-one times according to the rule at the conclusion of worship, one obtains the fruit of that worship.

Aghora is spoken by the Weapon (Śastra); there is no other mantra than Aghora for attaining perfection once the Kali age has arrived. Furthermore, he whose mind is dedicated to Aghora is a partaker of liberation; it is not otherwise.
By virtue of this statement from the Kāmikāgama:

having recited the Aghora mantra twenty-one times for the sake of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), and then rising, performing the worship of Kapila, giving a morsel of food to a cow, and bowing to one's own guru—his... (l2)
Having paid obeisance to the Goddess and the Kumāras, and having conversed affectionately with the servant of the Guru, he performs the Śivāgama-pūjā and gazes upon the sun.
(13) Having performed the service of the Śiva temple, he subsequently returns home and engages in the recitation (pārāyaṇa) of the Śivāgamas. Such is the Ātmārtha-Śiva-pūjā.
Know this as the attainment. Verse 85.

(l4) The meditation on Sadāśiva is described specifically in three verses. (l5) [He is] like Īśāna and the other [faces], possessing the brilliance of gold, honey, the moon, and a lovely gem; ever... (l5)

I worship Him who bears five faces, whose body is white, who is auspicious with half-moon eyes, who wears the Gaṅgā and the moon, whose ten hands hold weapons beginning with the spear and ending with the Śakti, who is intent upon the great throne of the Mantra-Yoga, and whose feet and hands are crimson. 1.

In his right hands he holds a trident, a skull-topped staff, a spear, and the gesture that bestows boons and protection; in his left hands he holds a citron, a rosary, a hand-drum, a lordly serpent, and a blue lotus.
Those three spears are the manifestation of consciousness, and that [trident] is the source of all seeds.
"Pūrti is the activity of all the senses; Prakṛti is the entire earth; Mānala is likewise contracted.
Thus [it is said]. The face of Īśāna is milk-colored, the face of Tatpuruṣa is golden-colored, the face of Aghora is copper-colored, and the face of Vāmadeva—
[She] whose five faces are of blood-red color, [and] whose [first] face is Sadyojāta and [the others] are moon-colored;
thus possessing five faces and twelve eyes, with a body of white complexion,
[she holds] Gaṅgā and the Moon.

Displaying ten *śrī-hastas* (auspicious hands), with the objects held in the right-hand [hands] being a trident (*śūla*), a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), a spear (*śakti*), the gesture of granting boons (*varada*), and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*); and in the left-hand [hands],

a citron (*bījapūra*), a rosary (*akṣamālā*), a hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*), a serpent (*nāga*), and a blue lotus (*nīlotpala*)— displaying these attributes— and with the palms of the *śrī-hasta*s and the soles of the *śrī-pāda*s being reddish-brown.
From Śakti up to Śaktimān,
he is seated upon the Mahāmaha-tan-āsana in the lotus posture (padmāsana). Such is the meditation on Lord Satāśivasvāmī according to the Śivāgamas.

Know that it has been stated [previously]. The meditation on the Five Brahmans and the Six Limbs (*pañcabrahma-ṣaḍaṅga-dhyāna*) is set forth in two verses: [One should meditate on] Īśa as white, holding a trident, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), a rosary, and a water-pot; Aghora as yellow, holding a citron, an eye, a sacred thread, and a lotus; Tatpuruṣa as dark-blue, holding a trident, a chisel, a sword, and a staff.

I bow to him who bears the skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), the wooden shield (*kāsthikheṭa*), and the pure *vāmadeva*; and who, with his [other] hands, holds the sword (*khaḍga*), the shield (*kheṭa*), the armor (*varma*), and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhayahasta*). ||1||
One should subsequently meditate upon [the deity] holding a white eye, a triple-stranded rosary for recitation, a water-pot, and a skull-cup; [and likewise] the heart-mantra and so forth,
the moon, gold, fire, a sacred ford, a trident, and a spear, bearing two hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and endowed with lower faces.
The six limbs of Śambhu have been described as reaching the face-lotus and the three eyes. (l3.
Īśāna is white in color and possesses two hands bearing the trident and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya). Tatpuruṣa is the color of gold... (l4.)

In his hands, he holds a skull-cup, a noose, a goad, a lotus, a rosary, a staff, a trident, a drum, a sword, a shield, a bow, an arrow, a bell, a serpent, a conch, and a discus; and it is said that he wears a garland of skulls.
Aghora has one face of a dark-blue hue and eight auspicious hands, which hold a trident, a pestle, a sword, a staff, a wooden drum, a skull-cup, a mace, and a rosary.

Vāmadeva is red in color, and with two hands bearing the *śrī* [lotus] (16), he holds a sword and a noose in his right hands and stands in the form of a woman. Satyasaṃjñāta-mukha is white in color and stands granting protection (*abhaya*) and boons (*varada*) (17).
For all [of them], there is meditation on the five Brahmans beginning with Īśāna according to the three eyes; furthermore, there is meditation on the six ancillaries (ṣaḍaṅga) as follows:
the eye... [color]... and likewise the four faces and the four auspicious hands holding the trident, rosary, staff, and skull.
The heart is red; the face, belly, and the color of the feet, hands, and head are golden; the four faces and four Śrī-hastas are also golden; the crest is the color of a conch shell;
the four faces and four hands are also [golden]; and the armor is blue in color.

One should know that this is the meditation on the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), characterized by four faces, four hands, weapons, and a red complexion; [the deities] bestow the trident, the spear, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), and the gesture of granting boons (*varada*) upon this heart and so forth, up to the weapon-mantra (*astra*). Thus ends verse 90.
Subsequently, it remains as described in the *Pañcabrahma-ṣaḍaṅga-daśāyudha-guṇa* [text]:
"Īśāna is that which shines above all; by virtue of its qualities, Tatpuruṣa is omnipresent."
Then, for the sake of the forest of the left [side], by virtue of the quality of the supreme awakening of the heart of Ghorā,
and immediately by means of the quality of Śiprā— these are the six limbs of Śambhu,
studded with them and endowed with qualities such as existence, just as they are endowed with omniscience and so forth. ||1||
Oṃ! Omniscience, contentment, primordial knowledge, sovereignty, unimpaired infinite power, and the six states beginning with "bho"—these are the six.

Omniscience, complete satisfaction, primordial consciousness, sovereignty, eternal loss of [limited] power, and infinite power—these six are the qualities; such is the sixfold nature (*ṣāḍguṇya*) of the Lord. Furthermore, there are eight qualities:
existence, supremacy, sovereignty, and... [the rest of the line is partially obscured].
Omniscience and invincibility are the qualities of the six limbs respectively. This is an Āgama verse.
It is stated in the *Śrīkāmika* and *Vātula*: "The qualities residing in the ten weapons of Śambhu are declared [as follows]:
by the trident here, the triad of qualities; by the axe, truth; and by the sword, our valor."
The quality of the vajra is indestructibility; the quality of the bell is the grace of bestowing favor; the quality of the fire-tongue (the trident) is the heart;

the quality of the bell is indeed sound; and the quality of the goad is that which is irresistible, being the controller. The meaning of these three verses [should be understood] from the mouth of the Guru.
This should be known as a secret. 92. (l4.
Subsequently, both the sequence of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) and the fruit of the consecration are stated by means of two verses:
"From oil, from the juice of flour and so forth—these three—from below, with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) [and] the product of the cow... (l5.)

Then one should perform the royal bath with milk, curd, honey, and [water] produced from white sugarcane; or with fruits possessing the five tastes, or below that with three fruits, or with water from a bamboo tube.
Afterwards, there is the bathing with sandalwood and saffron, the consecration by means of jars, and the offering of the *arghya*.
By bathing with *śambhara* [water], ten pots [of sin] are destroyed; by a hundred [pots] of milk, a thousand; by a thousand of curd, ten thousand;
by a hundred thousand of clarified butter, a hundred thousand; by a hundred thousand of sugarcane juice, ten times that [ten million];
by bathing with honey, ten times that [one hundred million]; and by bathing with a small amount of water, ten million sins are destroyed.
Indeed, the infinite [merit] arising from bathing with food, sandalwood, and saffron is declared by the wise.

...Regarding the sequence of consecration (*abhiṣeka-krama*) for Mahādeva: first is the oil consecration; second is the consecration with rosewater, coconut water, and mango juice; [then] the consecration with sugar-cane juice; and the consecration with the juice of black jackfruit and breadfruit.
The juice of the *elumiccam* fruit— the *tamāttapai* fruit juice— the *kuḷoñci* fruit juice—
the *kommaḍimātuḷam* fruit juice— the plantain fruit— the mango fruit— the jackfruit—

the coconut water— (l4)— fresh water— the *kaunīr* water— the *annābhiṣeka* (consecration with rice)— the *kuṅkumābhiṣeka* (consecration with saffron)— the *candanakuṅkumābhiṣeka* (consecration with sandalwood and saffron)— the *śatadhārābhiṣeka* (consecration with a hundred streams).

For the sake of others, one who performs the thousand-stream consecration (*sahasradhārābhiṣeka*)—whereby a thousand sins are destroyed—and the special *arghya* (*viśeṣārghya*) consecration according to this sequence for Mahādeva, [attains the following] fruit: what is it? By performing even a single *balantirumañjana* consecration, [one attains the same result].
By performing an ablution with water, one sin is removed. By performing an ablution with milk, a hundred sins are removed. By performing an ablution with curd, a thousand sins are removed.
(17) By performing an ablution with ghee, ten thousand sins are removed. By performing an ablution with black honey, a hundred thousand sins are removed. [Honey...]
Know that it is stated in the *Cintyaviśva* Āgama: "By performing an *abhiṣeka* [sprinkling] with water, a hundred thousand (*lakṣa*) sins are destroyed;

by an *abhiṣeka* with fresh water, ten million (*koṭi*) sins are destroyed; and by performing an *abhiṣeka* with sandalwood paste (*candanābhiṣeka*), saffron paste (*kuṅkumābhiṣeka*), or sandalwood gruel, infinite sins are destroyed. (l2)
The procedure for the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) is set forth in six verses:
"The *pañcagavya* fit for the sacrifice to Śiva consists of cow’s milk, curd, ghee, [urine, and dung]... [Verse 3]
The five nectars (pañcāmṛta) are milk, curd, clarified butter, honey, and the essence of sugarcane; these are the substances placed therein.
Or, in a mandala made from two droṇas of rice,
or according to one's ability with barley as available,
the chambers should be prepared; or else, there are no darbha grasses required here.
Having strewn [the powder], [one should place] the square of the Śiva-tattva in the center. ||2||
One should worship Sadāśiva in the southeast, the Vidyā named Puruṣa in the north,
Kāla in the west, and likewise Prakṛti in the northeast.
Then, the Marutkoṣṭha [should be applied] to the head, and the Anālādi [to the rest of the body]. ||3||

In the center, the vessel is well-established and perfectly tranquil; in the east, it is like fire and restrained, and red... (l6). In the west, the manifest nectar is to be placed; in the southeast, the sun is joined according to the sequence. ||4||

Milk and so forth from the middle [cow] and others, water from *darbha* grass, and flour and so forth from fire and others—these five substances should be established by the wise as the *pañcagavya* using the five mantras, or by means of the *mātrā*, the *śiva*, or the *hṛdaya* and other mantras. ||5||

In this context, the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) should be placed according to the procedure for the products of the cow, while the scented water (gandhodaka) is to be placed in the northeast corner. However, in those corners starting from the southeast (Agni), the three fruits beginning with plantain (kadali) should be placed. (Verse 6) What are the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) suitable for Śiva-pūjā and other rites? (Line 2)

Cow’s milk, cow’s curd, cow’s ghee, cow’s urine, and cow dung—these five are known as *pañcagavya*. As for *pañcāmṛta*, it consists of cow’s milk, cow’s curd, cow’s ghee, honey, and black sugarcane juice or sugar; these five are known as *pañcāmṛta*. Among those, there is *pañcagavya*.
Having measured four *marakkāl* of rice—
or as much as one’s capacity allows— by means of a sieve, one should prepare a circular mandala one span (*muṣṭi*) in length and square in shape,
and therein [mark] the east, west, south, and north. (14–15)
Having drawn sixteen lines and fashioned nine compartments (navakoṣṭha), one should spread darbha grass over each line with its tips pointing eastward and northward.
Then, in the center compartment, one should designate it as the "Compartment of the Śiva-tattva"; in the eastern [compartment], the "Compartment of the Sadāśiva-tattva"; and in the southern...
The Vidyā-tattva compartment is in the south; the Puruṣa-tattva compartment is in the north; the Kāla-tattva compartment is in the west; the Prakṛti-tattva compartment is in the Īśāna (northeast);
and the [Ātman-]tattva compartment is in the Agni (southeast) and the Nirṛti (southwest) directions.

The *Abdatattvakoṣṭha* and the *Vāyutattvakoṣṭha* within the *Vāyudik* (the northwest direction). Having thus performed the worship of the *koṣṭhas*, one should perform the worship of the vessels (*pātra-pūjā*) within this [mandala] as follows:
(l2) the *Supratiṣṭhita-pātra*, the *Suśānta-pātra*, the *Tejovat-pātra*, the *Ratnodaka-pātra*, the *Amṛtātmaka-pātra*, and the *Avyakta-pātra*.
The *vyaktapātra* (manifest vessel),

the *saurypātra* (vessel of valor), and the *saṃyuktapātra* (combined vessel)— having performed the worship of the vessels in this manner, one should wash milk, curd, ghee, cow-urine, and cow-dung in this water.
Having ground together kuśa-water, māka-powder, mañjaka-powder, and pomegranate-powder, and having poured them into those vessels in this manner, [one should perform the rite] at this time.
(15) The five mantras beginning with Īśāna; the Mūla-mantra or the Śivagāyatrī-mantra; and the nine [syllables] consisting of Hṛdaya, Śiras, and Śikhā.
Having worshipped with mantras as well, within this [rite] there are five (16) types,
six types, seven types, eight types, and nine types. Having consecrated it in each of these ways, and having offered incense and lamps, thereafter— each respective...
Having combined the cow dung with cow urine by means of mantras, the cow urine with cow's blood, the cow's blood with cow's bile, and the cow's bile with cow's milk—
and subsequently having added the water of *kuśa* grass and unified it all into a single seat (*kūrca*)— he should again offer incense and a lamp, and then, with his right hand...

He should consecrate [the materials] once with the root mantra and eleven mantras. In the case of an expiation (*prāyaścitta*), he should consecrate them one hundred and eight times with the root mantra. This is the summary for the installation and collection of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
The Procedure: Thereafter, according to the procedure for the consecration with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛtābhiṣeka*), one should grind rice and offer it as an oblation (*koṣṭha-pūjā*).

Then, performing the worship of the vessel (*pātra-pūjā*), one should place the five nectars within it. In the installation of the *kuśa* water, one should also install the fragrant water (*gandhodaka*) and the other three [substances], beginning with fire (*agni*).

In the corner as well, having placed plantains, jackfruits, (15) mangoes, or fresh coconut water, one shall install them with the previously mentioned mantras; this is the procedure for the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
8 verses.
Next,
the procedure for bathing (snapanavidhi) is to be described.
Even when performing worship for one's own sake, a new bath must indeed be performed for the propitiation of Śiva.
In a square measuring two cubits, within a circle of grain one *khārī* in measure,
one should worship in the center a water-pot (*kumbha*) with [the deity] beneath and Indra above; then, in the directions starting from the east,
one who possesses the mantra should worship the eight jars along with the *vardhanī* and the northern *nāsā*, together with Īśa and Ambikā.

Regarding the worship of the Self—according to the view that one may perform the consecration after conducting the bathing with nine jars—if one asks: "Having husked rice grains, [how much] should be taken for both measures of a *mūḻakal*? (l. 2)

Having drawn a square maṇḍala and fashioned a nine-square grid within it, having spread grains upon it, and having placed a water-pot (kumbha) in the center, a vessel for the nose (mūka-karakam)— that is, a vardhanī— in the east and north,
and eight jars on the eight spokes starting from the east, [one should worship] Īśvara within them.
Having invoked Īśvarī and the eight Vidyeśvaras, he shall offer incense and lamps and perform worship. 101.
Afterward, the five-fold offering (pañcāhuti) is not mentioned.

"The fruits are five: the five mango fruits; with three of these five mango fruits, as well as the citron, they say there is a group of five fruits characterized by flavor, beginning with the *kuśa* grass and so forth. Thus it is said. "Fruits" means five. What are those? (l6)

The five fruits consisting of the banana, the mango, the jackfruit, the southern fruit (*dhen-nam-pazham*), and the *kommaṭi* mango; these are the five fruits that provide the primary flavor (*rasa-pradhāna-māna-pazham*).
Next, the five [fruits] beginning with the *elumiccam* (citron): the *elumiccam*, the *nārattam*, the *tamāttam*, the *kuḷoñci*, and the *māṭalam*; thus it is.
Know that there are many [offerings].

102. Here, the five water-offerings (*pañcodaka*) are joined with the fruit, the *bilva* nut, the jewel, the fragrance, and the *kuśa* grass; as well as cardamom, cloves, sweet substances, the five medicinal storehouse-ingredients (*koṣṭhadravya*), and the flower bud. ||1||
And there are five fragrant substances: agallochum, the two types of sandalwood, kāśmīra, bilva, and yellow sandalwood;
furthermore, there are many other fragrances, primarily camphor and musk. (2)
They say there are five types of food: sesame, mustard, sour [grains], mung beans, and again, with black gram—these are the five. (l.

3) Wheat, rice, barley, bamboo seeds, and cooked wild rice constitute the one supreme food, *paramānna*. (l. 3) Thus it is said. Furthermore, there are what are known as the five waters (*pañcōdaka*), the five substances (*pañcadravya*), and the five fragrances (*pañcagandha*). (l. 4)
Furthermore, it is said that fragrant substances (*gandhadravya*) are of many kinds and constitute the *pañcānna*; all these are fit for the worship of Śiva.
What are they? They are as follows:
the five waters (*pañcodaka*), namely, *palodaka*, *bilvodaka*, *ratnodaka*, *puṣpodaka*, and *kandhodaka*. Thus, there are five waters.

The five substances (*pañcadravya*) are as follows: cardamom, cloves, atimadhura, red sandalwood paste, and *śrīkhaṇḍa*—these are the five substances for the unguent (*añjana-dravya*). The five fragrances (*pañcagandha*) are as follows: agaru, Kāśmīra sandalwood, Bilva sandalwood, Haricandana, and excellent sandalwood.
Thus, there are five types of fragrant substances (*gandha*): camphor, musk, sandalwood, and so forth; indeed, there are many such aromatic materials.

Furthermore, regarding what constitutes the "five grains" (*pañcānna*): sesame rice, mustard rice, tamarind rice, millet rice, and black gram rice—these are called the five grains. Wheat is the food of the gods; *śambā* is the food of the ancestors.

Barley is a type of food, green gram rice is a type of food, and jaggery-rice (guḷaśa) is a type of food; thus, there are five kinds of food. Apart from these, there are many other varieties of food, such as *paramānna*, *dadhyanna*, *guḷānna*, *ghṛtānna*, *śuddhānna*, and so forth.
Having understood thus, one who performs the worship of Śiva— (105)—
the fruit that will accrue to me if I subsequently offer water and other articles to Mahādeva is stated in two verses. (106)

Peace shall come from performing the water-consecration; long life from fine incense; the destruction of slander... [from] flowers; and the attainment of prosperity from sandalwood. Incense shall be the remover of sin; victory over death through the lamp; and [fulfillment] through the food offering.
Through betel nuts (*pūgaphala*) and the like, the kingdom yields meager fruit; through unbroken grains (*akṣata*), there is the destruction of enemies.
(L6) Durvā grass removes the path of brothers; through the worship of *nīla* flowers, the path of Brahmins perishes.
Through *droṇa* flowers, there is indeed the loss of cattle and the destruction of one's mother; the *māraśvadha* flower destroys injury.

The *arka* flower destroys the sin of approaching another's wife, while the blue lotus (*nīlotpala*) accomplishes eloquence; furthermore, saffron (*kuṅkuma*) burns away other faults as well as the affliction caused by the nine planets.
Thus [it is said]. Śambhu, the Great God.

It is said that by performing the *ruk-tirumañjana* (anointing with medicinal herbs) and *abhiṣeka* (consecration bath), peace (*śānti*) shall prevail; by offering fragrant substances such as *taṭṭuppūgu* (a type of fragrant root), one shall attain a long life; and by worshipping with excellent flowers while uttering the word "Kodu," the defect of the household being ruined shall be removed. Furthermore, [by... excellent...

By offering incense (*sāmprāṇidhūpa*), many sins are destroyed; by applying sandalwood paste (*candana*), there shall be prosperity; by offering a lamp (*dīpa*), there is the destruction of sin and the destruction of untimely death; [by offering] excellent nectar (*amṛta*)... (14)
It is said that by offering *naivedya* (food offerings), one attains a kingdom; by offering *tāmbūla* (betel leaf), one gains manifold prosperity and beauty.

By scattering *akṣata* (unbroken rice grains), enemies are destroyed, and by throwing parched grain (*aru*), the fault of hostility toward kinsmen is removed. Through the worship with sesame seeds (*tila*)...
By worshipping [the deity] with *brahmahatyā* flowers, the sin of killing a Brahmin is destroyed.
By worshipping with *droṇārccana* flowers, the sin of killing a cow is destroyed. By worshipping with *koṇṭai* flowers, the sin of killing one's mother is destroyed.
By worshipping with *vellerkkam* flowers... (17)

It is known that by reciting [the mantra] while worshipping with a *nīlotpala* flower, the fault of approaching another's wife is destroyed; and by applying saffron (*kuṅkuma*), the afflictions arising from the nine planets are destroyed. Know that this is stated thus in the *Cintyāgama*. 107.
The fruit that results from offering flowers to Śiva thereafter is described by these two verses:
dhūrdhūraṃ karavīrajātivakulaṃ mandārapadmekabakaṃ punnāgaṃ... (l3)
The kuravaka, nandika, kuṭaja, droṇa, and others, as well as the mādhavī—
this entire white [flower] is said to be sāttvika and bestows liberation.
Following that, [flowers] equal to the kalhāra, ambuja, paṭṭa, and pāṭala, as well as those like the palāśa and nīpa, [are rājasa].
O Ajita, red [flowers] are said to be of the nature of *rajas*; through their worship, they grant all worldly enjoyments (*bhoga*).

O Kuṣṇa, that which is black is entirely fit for those of the nature of *tamas*, except for the *kuthaphala*. Yellow [flowers], such as the lotus, the *āragvadha*, and the *campaka*, are of the nature of *sattva* and *rajas*.
And that which begins with *dhūr-dhūra* and so forth, even when it is of the nature of an instrument (*karaṇika*), bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. ||2||

Indeed, dark-colored [leaves] belonging to the *tāmasa* and *rājasa* qualities—such as the leaves of *tulasī*, *bilva*, and others, as well as *hrībera*, *maruka*, *damanaka*, and *dūrvā*—[are used] for the sake of the two types of *siddhi*. Thus it is said.
White *madhumattham-puṣpa*, white lotus, *picchi*, *śephālika*, *makhī*, and white... (l7)
Mandāra, śvetatāmarasa, kokkeraka-mandāra, punnāga, kurava, vellērukka, nandyāvarta, mallikā,
kuḍa-mallikā, tumbu, mullai, and all other such white flowers are known as *sāttvika* flowers; by worshipping Mahādeva with these, [one attains the fruit].
It is said that liberation exists; furthermore,

all red flowers such as the *śoṇaka*, the *raktatāmarasa*, the *raktapāṭali*, the *raktapaṭṭī*, the *raktapāṭalī*, the *raktapalāśa*, and the *raktakadamba* are known as *rājasa* flowers for Mahādeva.
It is held that while offering worship brings merit, all other pungent flowers except for the *nīlotpala* are *tāmasa* flowers;
therefore, these are considered unfit for the worship of Śiva. [Such flowers include] the *koraṇṭaka*, *campaka*, *puṃnāga*, *mallikā*, and so forth.
All noble flowers are classified as either rājasa or sāttvika; by worshipping Śrī Mahādeva with an abundance of these, both worldly enjoyment and liberation are attained. (15–16)
The bilva leaf, raw tulasī, and the two types of vella; marukkoṟuntu, aruku, and kaṭirpaccai—these and other such leaves that grow wild, all these are tāmasa and rājasa leaves and flowers.
If one worships Śiva with these, both worldly enjoyment (bhoga) and liberation (mokṣa) shall be attained. Thus...
Know that this has been stated in the Ajitāgama (p56b, f52a, l1). 109½. Thereafter, the relative gradation of the flowers is set forth in one hundred and one verses.
From a thousand *karavīra* flowers, [one obtains] a *bilva* leaf; from a hundred [of those], a white lotus;
from that, a hundred-petaled lotus; and from that, an *apāmārga* flower.
Therefore, the darbhasamudra is equal to a mālati; from that, the vyāghāta; from that, the baka; then the dhūrdhūra; then one thousand more than that is the droṇa; then the śaṅkha;
then fifty more than a hundred padmas is the droṇa; [and] the bṛhat is the utpala.
"For the flower of devotion is said to be superior to everything in the *Kālottara*. [1½] Thus it is said.
Regarding the offering of flowers to Śrī Mahādeva, the excellence of the flowers is for Śrī Mahādeva himself, while the *durvā* grass is for his son Kumāra. [5]

Furthermore, by the scriptural statements of the Āgama known as the *Skandakālottara*, as well as the subsequent statements of the *Mahāmaulāgama* which express the grace of Maheśvara, one comes to know the superiority of the *puṣpadhārā* (the stream of flowers).
To explain how that is so: there is a single *erukkam* (a specific measure) consisting of ordinary flowers.
More than a thousand of those is a single *alari* flower; more than a thousand of those is a single *vilva* flower; more than a thousand of those is a single *vilva* branch with three buds;
more than a thousand of those is a single *veṇṭā-maraippū*; and more than a thousand of those is a single hundred-petaled lotus.

In that [number], one red lotus flower (*śvetāmbuja*) in excess of a thousand; in that [number], one *nāgakesara* flower in excess of ten thousand; in that [number], one *darbha* flower in excess of ten thousand; and in that [number], one... in excess of ten thousand.

A single jasmine flower; (l3) more than that—a single small *śephālikā* flower; more than that—a single small *tumbī* flower; and more than a thousand of those—a single white *kākaṇī* flower; (l4) thus it is said.
In that regard, ten thousand more than that is one *vellirukkambū* flower; ten thousand more than that is one *peruntumpai* flower;
ten thousand more than that is one *ceṅkazuṉīr* flower; and ten thousand more than that is one *nīlotpala* flower. That [last mentioned] lasts for one year.

Know that there is no impurity [in these offerings], and among the various types of flowers, the blue lotus (*nīlotpala*) is the most excellent... among the types of *traja* garlands, it is the most excellent. Among those, the *marukkoṇḍu* is the most excellent; and among those, know the *bilva* leaf to be the most excellent.

"By worshipping Śambhu once with a *bilva* leaf, one obtains that fruit which is gained by performing ablutions in the waters of the Gaṅgā for ten thousand years"—according to this statement from the *Śivapurāṇa*, there is no equal to the *bilva* leaf. Furthermore, since devotion itself is the most distinguished among all flowers, this establishes the supremacy of flowers (*puṣpa-dāratmya*). Moreover:
Know that this has been stated in the Śivāgamas:
"The Bilva leaf may be used for one year, as may the Aśvattha and Tulasī;
the Bakula flower [is effective] for six months, while the Karavīra is [effective] for three days. (12)
Having washed the Tulasī leaf, the Bilva leaf, the Palāśa leaf, and the golden [leaf],
one should worship the Supreme Lord again and again.
By the statement "ye" (ya + e), it is understood that one may worship Śrī Mahādeva by offering *tulasī*, *bilva*, *palāśa*, and golden flowers (*suvarṇapuṣpa*), having first washed them clean;
furthermore, the five *bilvas* (*pañcabilva*) are: *vilva*, *kīlavai*, *māvilaṅgai*, *viḷā*, and *nāyūruvi*.
Alternatively—
These [flowers] growing on the *noccil* tree constitute the five *bilva* fruits. Knowing this, one who performs the worship of Śiva should gather other flowers day after day;
thereafter, he should offer *dūrvā* grass.
The mantra verse is stated as follows:
"O Goddess Dūrvā, who possesses a thousand tips and is manifested with a thousand petals;
you who are held upon my head, remove the sin accumulated by me throughout infinite births."
"Grant me beauty and prosperity; destroy my enemies. [Thus he says.
O Dūrvā goddess, who possess a thousand feet and a thousand petals, with my head...
By wearing [this], may all the sins accumulated throughout my many births be dispelled,
and may great beauty and greatness be bestowed upon me.
Having said, "Grant me sovereignty and destroy all my enemies," he shall offer [the earth]:
"O Vasundharā, trodden by horses, trodden by chariots, and trodden by Viṣṇu!
Being borne upon my head, protect me at every step. (3)
This is the verse for worshipping Viṣṇukrānti:
O Aśmantaka, great tree, king of trees, salutations be unto you!
Grant me pure food and bring about the destruction of my enemies. (4)
This is the mantra verse recited by Kāṭṭiyai at sunrise; it has remained unspoken since the time of Tuḷasīkīlāḍan. 111.

On the twelfth lunar day, during eclipses, at the two junctions of day and night (*saṃdhyā*), on the full and new moon days (*parvan*), and also at night during the *pāta*, the wise man should not, out of negligence or error, step over *tulasī* when the sun is situated in the asterism of Śravaṇa or on the days of Āditya, Indu, Kuja, Asura, Ārya, or Iṣṭa.

"For him, no expiatory rite has been prescribed other than the cutting off of the tuft of hair on Viṣṇu's day. This refers to Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, the seventh lunar day (saptamī), the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), a lunar eclipse, and the Śravaṇa asterism.
At dawn, at dusk, and during the five festival days— namely,

the eighth day of the dark fortnight, the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, the new moon, the full moon, and the month-birth (māsaja)— as well as during the vyatīpāta yoga and the night; in these times...
A wise person should not pluck a *tulasī* sprout. If one plucks a *tulasī* without wisdom, it is equivalent to having caused the decapitation of Viṣṇu’s head.
Know that for such a person, there is no atonement. (112)

On this point, there is a statement from the Smṛti: "Those who pluck Tulasī on Sundays, Saturdays, Tuesdays, on the twelfth lunar day, or during the five festival days (parvan), they cut off the head of Hari. One should discard leaves, flowers, or fruits brought by hand, brought on a cloth, fallen upon the ground, or brought on castor-oil plant or arka leaves."
If, however, worship is performed by them out of negligence, that worship is always fruitless due to sin. Hereafter follows the instruction regarding the five festival days (*parvan*):
"The fourteenth and eighth days of the dark fortnight, and the sun's transit (*saṃkrānti*)—these are declared by the sages who know the scriptures to be the five festival days. (l6)
Next, the meditation on the Vedic fire (vaidikāgnidhyāna):
They say the Vedic fire has one face, a red heart, two mouths, and four [arms].

One should meditate on Śṛṅgin, who has seven feet and seven hands, who holds in his right [hands] a sacrificial ladle (*sruk*), a spoon (*sruva*), a spear (*śakti*), a rosary (*jāpa*), and a water-pot (*ghaṭikā*), while in his left [hands] he holds a sickle (*kṛnta*), a winnowing fan (*śūrpa*), and a vessel containing clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*); he knows the seven tastes and possesses the eyes of a woman and the ears of a goat, and he resides in a ram.
Thus it is said.
[He has] a body of blood-red color, one neck, two faces, six eyes, four ears, four horns on both faces, and three humps. (12)

In its hands, and specifically in the right hand, it holds the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles; in its trunk, it holds the trident, the rosary (*japamālā*), the *valla* (?), the *vṛttaviśiri*, and the *ājyapātra* vessel—carrying these with those seven hands, it stands upon the bull.
Thus, it is described as having the form of a Vedic fire (*vaitāgnirūpa*) in the Śivāgamas.
Know that it has been so stated. 113.

(l4. One should meditate upon the Fire-god, who is three-eyed, seated upon a lotus, red as a hibiscus flower, possessing a face and hands like those of Śambhu, and holding a forest and a speech-organ in his hands.

"In the upward-facing [lotus], there are three tongues—Kanaka and the others, as well as Hiraṇyā and the rest—extending toward the directions starting from the west; one should meditate upon that auspicious child with two feet. Thus it is said.
One should perform the meditation on Śivāgni (the fire of Śiva) in this manner. It is red.
Because he is Śivakumāra, his body and his lotus-posture (padmāsana) are such that he possesses five divine faces and ten glorious hands;
on the central face there are three [eyes], and on the other four faces there are four hoods beginning with Hiraṇyā; furthermore, he has two feet facing westward and is of youthful age (bālavayassa).
On each face there are three eyes (l2),

or else one auspicious face with four Śrī-hastas; in those [hands] are the Śakti, the rosary, the gesture of granting fearlessness (abhayamudrā), and the sword— thus is the nature of Śivāgnisvarūpa (l3).
Know this clearly.
114. Kāmikā—In the case of installation, [the deity] should have the form of an elder; however, during a festival, it should be in the prime of youth.
In the initiation (dīkṣā), the form of the child is indeed declared to be the threefold form of Agni.

At the time of the installation (pratiṣṭhā) of Śivāgni, one should conceive of Agni as being in the form of an adult; at the time of the festival (utsava), in the form of a youth; and at the time of initiation (dīkṣā), in the form of a child.
Thus [one should regard] Agni.
He shall purify. This is the word of the Āgama:

"The seven tongues [of fire] indeed—Matimukhī, Abdhā, Kṛṣṇā, Suprabhāsī, Paurvī, Hiraṇyā, and Raktā—enter into the mouth [of the sacrificer] in the form of gold and other precious substances, with Ratnodakā at the front. (16)
Thus it is said.
Furthermore, Agni has seven tongues. If one asks what they are: 1. Adhiraktā, 2. Bahurūpā, 3. Kanakā, 4. Suprabhā, 5. Kṛṣṇā, 6. Raktā. (p60a, l1)

7. Regarding the seven tongues of fire: because there is one named Suprabhā in the eastern face, Kṛṣṇā in the southern face, Raktā in the northern face, and Hiraṇyā in the western face, the names of the seven tongues of Agni are thus [assigned] to these faces.
Knowing that [the deity] is present, one should perform the homa.
As for the mudrā in the homa, it consists of the sacrificial ladle brought into contact with the ring finger of one's own right hand.
The little finger is joined to the thumb, while the index and middle fingers are raised to the height of four [finger-breadths].
Next, the *homadravya* (substances for the fire-oblation) and the *homaprakāra* (method of the oblation) are described by three verses:
"One should offer rice and other grains with the five fingers, and sesame seeds with the hand. (*mudgā* is corrected to *mudgān*).
Kubjā herself [offered] curd up to the ladle, as well as parched grain and milk-rice;
likewise, whatever substance was in liquid form, such as milk, honey, and ghee, up to the sacrificial spoon—whatever edible thing, even just fruit as it was prepared with its various parts. ||1||

Food is measured by the mouthful; fruit is four finger-breadths in length. The measure for roots and varieties of cakes is one handful, as is appropriate for pieces of sugar and the like. Here, a *guḍa* (molasses) piece is like a chickpea, while a piece of *gulat* is like a jujube stone.
Or else, one may use guggulu and other substances as prescribed in the Kāmika-tantra, or clarified butter weighing one niṣka.

"Fuel sticks (*samidh*) the size of a span, *ikṣu* stalks, and creepers of every kind, even as if with a banner; food, barley, and so forth, should be offered from the conch-seal (*śaṅkhamudrā*)—thus indeed are the bonds of the fire-oblation (*homabandha*). This refers to how all sacrificial substances are offered. As for that: *saṃbhā-* [line 2].
One should perform the *homa* with rice, green gram, sesame, *kadalai*, *tuvarai*, *avaraī*, *kaṭuku*, *koḷḷu*, and so forth, using all five fingers;
one should perform the *homa* with *mudga* beans using the *mṛgīmudrā*;
one should perform the *homa* with curd using the *kuñcikā* hand; and one should perform the *homa* with nectar (*amṛta*) in a single portion.

Having said, "Perform the oblation," [he should offer] all varieties of old fruit measuring four finger-breadths; having said, "Perform the oblation," [he should offer] all varieties of *kiṅkirāta* (citron) measuring one handful;
and [all varieties of] *paṇiyāra* (pumpkin gourd).

Having instructed that the homa be performed by cutting large tamarind fruits into small pieces, and having instructed that the homa be performed with sandalwood the size of a finger-joint, and having instructed that the homa be performed with ghee—
using items such as split black gram, turmeric, and so forth, only the size of a jackfruit seed or a single handful— he [prepared] the sacrificial fuel sticks (*samidh*).

"One should perform the homa with one *sāṇ* measure of molasses, wood, and *koḍirūpa* by means of the *padākaimudrā*; furthermore, all those who maintain the doctrine of primordial non-existence (*ādyanāstika*) should perform the homa by means of the *śaṅkhamudrā*.
Thus [it is stated]. (p61a, l1)
Know the sequence for performing the homa.
(118) The fruit of the homa is stated in two verses:
"Success through cows [is attained] by means of milk; great sovereignty through ghee; [prosperity] through sugar and water... (l. 2)

Through curd, there is the fulfillment of all prosperity; through mouthfuls of jewels, food, and wind-seeds (mustard), fame; through sesame and unbroken rice, wealth; through honey, one's desired object; through the rays of the moon (silver) and auspicious flowers, a beautiful garment; and through excellent betel-leaf, both beauty and eloquence shall be attained. (1) (l3.)

Through lotuses, one gains subjugation over kings; through blue lotuses, the king’s wife becomes submissive; through a fire-offering of white water-lilies, one becomes a minister; and through an oblation of the *bodhi* tree and other such trees, one gains mastery over the twice-born.
Furthermore, by using salt combined with a specific visualization, one truly wards off forced labor.
"By constantly offering oblations with effigies and the like, one shall subdue all human beings.
(L5) This means that by performing the homa with milk, cattle will abound; and by performing the homa with beef fat, (L6)

It is said that by performing oblations with mahā-dhānya one attains great sovereignty (aiśvarya); by performing oblations with śakvara one attains good fame; by performing oblations with tadīya one attains all prosperity (sarva-samṛddhi); and by performing oblations with food (anna), one attains excellent meals of divine food and the like.
It is said that by performing a *homa* with parched grain (*lāja*), one attains fame;
by performing a *homa* with a mixture of rice and *māṣa* beans, one gains great strength;
and by performing a *homa* with honey, one attains the state of a god.

It is said that if one performs *homa* with *kusumbha* flowers, one will possess divine garments; if one performs *homa* with white *veṇṭalai* (white mustard), one will possess excellent beauty and excellent poetic talent;
and if one performs *homa* with lotus flowers...

By performing *homa* with *rājavaiśyamuṇḍa*, there is the subjugation (*vaśya*) of the king; by performing *homa* with blue *utpala* flowers, there is the subjugation of the king’s wife; by performing *homa* with *āmalaka* flowers, there is the subjugation of the minister; [and] with *aśvattha* fuel-sticks (*samidh*), etc. (14–15).
By performing the *homa* with *nattināl*, Brāhmaṇas and others will attain prosperity (*vaiśyam*);
by performing the *homa* with *vahalavañci*, there will be rain;
by performing the *homa* with *nīr vañciyan*, there will be rain; and by performing the *homa* with *puttalyādika* and so forth...
"Know that the fruits of the oblations (homa) beginning with 'All men shall be submissive' and 'The head [shall be won]' are as follows.
(120) Next, the eighteen substances for the oblation are set forth.
Clarified butter, milk, curd, *sallāṭaka*,
and so forth; likewise, mung beans, cakes, balls, groats, honey, *nīvāra* rice, black gram, barley— these, along with the *caru* cooked with sesame, are suitable for the fire offering (*homa*).
"For in this world, even though all substances are equal, it is well known that what is pure is fit for consumption.
(l2) These are as follows: wood used as fuel, clarified butter, milk, curd, parched grain, coriander, long pepper, sacrificial fuel, and rice.
The sacrificial materials for the *homa* are eighteenfold: *paṇiyāram*, *vellam*, *porimā*, (l3) honey, *kuḷac-cennal*, *uḷuntu*, *sampānelu*, rice, and *caru*.
In addition to these, all other substances may also be used for the *homa*. (l4)
"So it is; thus know these to be the substances for the oblation (homadravyas).
121. Now, regarding the fire-altar (agnyāyatanam): where the smoke rises together with the flames, that is the place perceived by the nose and the eye."
If the sacrificial fuel is only slightly ignited, there will be a fire in the house;
if it is offered while the flame is rising, there will be the destruction of the village and so forth.
If the offering is made when the smoke rises, there is suffering for the nose and likewise for the head; however, an offering made upon the crest of the flame is auspicious.
Thus it is said.

Regarding the manner of performing *homa* in places such as *kuṇḍas*: if one performs *homa* in a place where there is only firewood, it is called *manoduṣkara*; and if it is performed in a place where there is only a small amount of fire... [it is called] *cakṣuṣya*. In that regard—
It is said that by performing a *homa* sacrifice, the path of fire (*agnipatha*) will come to one's own dwelling;
furthermore, it is said that if one performs a *homa* in a place where sand is being sprinkled, the path of fire will come to the house where one currently resides.
Therefore...
The one who performs the homa [should do so] with the tongue of Agni, which is the crest of Agni’s flames... 122.
Subsequently, the auspicious and inauspicious characteristics of the disciple are described by means of four verses (13).

The signs for a person fit for initiation are to be known by the auspicious or inauspicious attainment of fire-marks and fluids; furthermore, color, sound, fragrance, and flame, as well as smoke in battle—
these are the six petals, and likewise the eleven colors.
Then there are five *dhānās*, thirteen kinds of fragrances (*gandhas*), and five types of crests (*śikhās*). ||1||
Furthermore, smoke here is indeed of four kinds; and here, from the *Raṇa-rāśi*, the calculation of the characteristics of the fire that has arisen is fifty, as stated in the *Āgama*.
This which was spoken in the *Dīpta* [chapter] has indeed been forgotten in the *Kālottara* due to its manifoldness.
Thus, both [the *Śatasāhasrikā*] and the one of twenty thousand verses have been declared by me to this extent.

(2) Indeed, for the killer of a Brahmin, the violator of the Guru’s bed, the slayer of a twice-born, the killer of a cow, the ungrateful, and the drinker of liquor—[for these] fire is black, and the earth, when its fragrance is stolen, becomes like poison. (3)

O Lord, if it trembles when placed on the cheek of one who has killed a woman, he becomes pure; if it shakes when placed near a thief of gold, he is purified; and if it bursts open when placed near a killer of a fetus, he is declared by the Lord to be cleansed of that sin.
If the fire resembles the *bandhūka* flower and the like, or is similar to a *sumendra* fruit, it is auspicious;
one will be powerful in this world and the next when the fire crackles like the sound of a lute.
When the fire is fragrant with camphor, agallochum, sandalwood, and so forth, its crest brings constant happiness.

"If the flame moves toward the east, north, upward, or the west, and the smoke is white, [then] there is a king. (4) If one asks what the meaning of these four verses is: it is that there are six types of characteristics for the fire in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). What are they? They are: color, sound, smell, and the flame.

Furthermore, it is of six kinds— namely, *dhūma* (smoke), *tūma*, and *yīraṇa* (l4); within that, color (*varṇa*) is of eleven kinds, sound (*śabda*) is of five kinds, and fragrance (*gandha*), which is scent (*parimala*), is of thirteen kinds (l5).

The characteristics of fire (*agnilakṣaṇa*) are stated in the Dīptāgama as follows: there are five types of flame (*śikhā-jvālā*), four types of smoke (*dhūma*), and twelve types of piercing (*vedhana*);
thus, the characteristics of fire amount to fifty kinds. Furthermore, [this is followed by] the Kālotara...

Know that this has been stated in the Upāgamangas. Furthermore, for one who commits the murder of a Brahmin, the murder of a guru, sexual intercourse with the wife of a guru, or the slaughter of a cow—the merit [accumulated] perishes; and for the drinking of intoxicants—these are the defects.
Regarding the earth: "We shall burn him with fire," and for one who steals land, it is said that he shall be "milked by fire" (agnidugdha); and for the killing of a master...
...that fire will burn for one who has intercourse with a Śūdra woman; fire will scorch for the theft of gold; fire will lick for the killing of a child;
and fire will be indifferent toward the destruction of a fetus.
One will know this gradually, just as one perceives the colors of flowers such as the *ucchis-chilantaka*, or like the color of this *koppa-pūcci* insect.

If fire is present in the *śivamudrā*, it indicates that this person undergoing initiation (*dīkṣā*) is a most excellent individual. [Furthermore, there are signs such as] camphor, agallochum, sandalwood, and musk.
If there are good fragrances such as sandalwood and the like, they will live happily; and if there are good sounds such as the lute of Rudra and the like, they will be supreme in every respect.
If the flame of the fire leans toward these directions—north-east, west-south, and north—he will become a great lord;
if the smoke is white, he will become a king. Having thus understood these signs of the fire, the excellent teacher...
One who bestows initiation upon a disciple; one who performs penance (prāyaścitta) if there are unfavorable signs. 126.
Hereafter, the characteristics of the five seats (pañcāsanalakṣaṇa) are described in two verses.
Know that the fivefold seat of Śambhu consists first of Ananta, then a triangle, then a lion-throne, and another square; this is the Yoga-āsanā.

The lotus is circular, pure and six-cornered for the rite of bathing; the lion-throne and the infinite [seat] are for worship with cloth, sandalwood, and so forth; and two stainless [seats] are for the rite of grace. (1) Thus the five seats have been described, included within the seat of the Supreme Lord.
Then, from the covering [of the petals], there is the infinite [series] beginning with Dhāriṇī and ending with Hari, as well as Dharma and the others;

likewise, from the bulb (kanda) and the knot (granthi), there is another Yoga[-system]; from the petal (dala) and the pericarp (karṇikā), there is the Lotus; and the pure Sārakarṇikā is shown in the Yoga[-system]. (2) Thus it is said.
Regarding the statement that there are five seats for Śambhu, the illustrious Mahādeva— namely, the Anantāsana which is triangular (trikoṇa),
the Siṃhāsana which is quadrangular (caturasra), and the Yogāsana, which is also quadrangular (caturasra)— [15–16].
The *mṛdu-āsana* is circular, the *padmāsana* is circular, and the *vimalāsana* is hexagonal; thus, during the time of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), these are known as the five seats (*pañcāsana*).
Furthermore, both the *anantāsana* and the *siṃhāsana* are for the purpose of meditation (*marśana*). Afterward, one performs the circumambulation (*parivarta*) starting with the sacred *melappūcu*.

For all occasions of worship (*pūjā-samaya*), one should worship the *yogāsana* and the *padmāsana*; for the occasion of worship intended to bestow grace (*anugraha*), one should worship the *vimalāsana*.
In this manner, the method of worshipping the five seats (*pañcāsana*) is as follows.
Furthermore, it is understood that this Pañcāsana is also included within the Śivāsana; specifically, from Ādhāraśakti up to Anantāsana is called Anantāsana (3);
from Dharma up to Ūrdhvacchadana is called Siṃhāsana; and from Kaṇṭha up to Granthi is called Yogāsana.

Having understood that the fivefold seat (*pañcāsana*)— consisting of the *upatala* (foundation), the *karṇikā* (pericarp), the *padmāsana* (lotus seat), and the *vimalāsana* (pure seat)— is subsumed within the *śivāsana* (the seat of Śiva), one should perform the worship of Śiva (*śivapūjā*).
Know that this has been stated in the Śivāgama known as the Yogaja-tantra, according to the *Ceyvāṉi* [tradition].
127. Hereafter, the sixteen-fold ritual service (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) is described.
(l6) It remains.

The enumeration of the sixteen modes of service (*upacāra*) has been declared: first, the triad beginning with water for the feet (*pādya*), then worship with the *śamabhorasa*, followed by bathing, the seat (*āsana*), and the invocation (*āvāhana*);
then the offering of fragrance and so forth (*gandhādi*), the food offering (*naivedya*), and below that, incense (*dhūpa*), the lamp (*dīpa*), and the oblation (*āhuti*).

"Two [offerings], water for the five [senses] with a handful of flowers, then praise, incense, and the worship of Caṇḍa. Thus it is said. If one asks what the sixteen services (*upacāra*) for the worship of Śiva are: (p65a, l1) water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), worship of the door-deities (*dvārapūjā*), the consecration bath (*abhiṣeka*), worship of the seat and the image (*āsanamūrti*), invocation (*āvāhana*), offering of scents and other articles (*gandhādisamarpaṇa*), and the food offering (*naivedya*).

The offering of incense, the offering of lamps, the performance of the daily fire-ritual (*nityāgnikārya*), the offering of water in the hollowed palms (*culukodaka*), the hymn of praise (*stotra*), the worship facing away from the deity (*parāṅmukhārcana*), and the worship of Caṇḍeśvara— these constitute sixteen [services], totaling 128. (l3.)
Roots, fruits, perfumes, flowers, food, and so forth belong to the earth element;
milk, curd, water, sugar, clothing, ornaments, and gems belong to the water element;
the lamp belongs to the fire element; and the wind is below. (v. 4)

Incense and the like, the fly-whisk, the bell, and the sound of songs—these five offerings are known as celestial (nābhasa). (Thus it is said. Nutmeg, mūla, bala, sandalwood, flowers, and nectar—all these and so forth [are included]. (15)

Earthly offerings (*pārthiva*) include items such as water, milk, curd, holy ash (*vibhūti*), sugar, and betel nut; luminous offerings (*taijasa*) include ghee lamps, ornaments, gems, and so forth; and aerial offerings (*māruta*) include incense, yak-tail fans, and the like.
Bells, songs, the mukhavīṇā, and so forth—all these are known as *nāpasam*, and thus one should understand them as the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*).
129. Hereafter, the procedure for the monthly worship (*māsapūjā*) will be described.

Indeed, there is the worship with ghee during the month of Sāhasa; with honey during Madhu; a woolen blanket during Tapaka; worship with curd in Phālguna; Damanaka in Caitra; and sandalwood from elsewhere in Vaiśākha;
the three fruits in the month of Jyeṣṭha; milk from a cow that has killed its calf in Āṣāḍha; and sugar in Śrāvaṇa.

"In Bhādrapada, the sacrifice of cakes, meat, and excellent food; in Kārttika, the worship with lamps. Thus it is said. Furthermore, for each of the twelve months, one should perform the respective rites under their corresponding lunar asterisms: for the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, an ablution with ghee (*ghṛtābhiṣeka*); for the month of Tai (Māgha), an ablution with honey (*madhvabhiṣeka*); and for the month of Māsi (Phālguna/Caitra), the offering of a "ghee-blanket" (*ghṛtakambala*).

For the month of Paṅguni, the offering is the consecration of the *vintayir* (a type of grain) from the Vaḍikkaṭṭin cattle; for the month of Cittirai, it is the *sāttava* of *marrukozuntu*; and for the month of Vaiyāśi, it is the *sāttava* of sixty *tirumeṟpū* flowers. (15)
It was stipulated that for the month of Āni, three types of fruit should be offered; for the month of Āḍi, jaggery and milk; for the month of Āvaṇi, rice and sugar;
for the month of Purattāsi, tiruppaṇiyāram; and for the month of Aippasi, śambā-amudu.
It is understood that one performs the monthly worship (*māsapūjā*) for all twelve months in this manner, offering the *sāttavam* and the lamp-garland (*dīpamālā*) for the month of Kārttika. 130.
Subsequently, it is stated that there are eight kinds of *Ratnalingas*. (p66a, l1)

The *liṅga* made of jewels is of eight kinds; first, it is said by Viśvakarman to be born of diamond (*vajra*), ruby (*māṇikka*), lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*), crystal (*sphaṭika*), coral (*pravāla*), emerald (*nīla*), komeḍaka, and dark stone (*śyāma*). (l2)

[They] bestow, respectively, the destruction of enemies, prosperity, sons, the remaining supernatural powers (*siddhi*), self-mastery, wealth, splendor, and excellent enjoyments. Thus it is said. Furthermore, there are eight kinds of *ratnaliṅga*; what are they? [They are: *vajraliṅga*, (3) ...
The eight types of jewel-liṅgas (*ratnaliṅga*) are: the māṇikya-liṅga, the vaiḍūrya, the sphaṭika-liṅga, the pavāla-liṅga, the indranīla-liṅga, the gometaka-liṅga, and the marataka-liṅga.
As for the fruits obtained by worshipping them: by worshipping a vajra-liṅga, there is the destruction of enemies; by worshipping a padmarāga-māṇikya...
It is said that by worshipping a Vaiḍūrya liṅga one gains sovereignty; by worshipping a crystal liṅga one gains all prosperity;
and by worshipping a coral liṅga... (16)

It is said that by worshipping the *Sakalavaśya* [Liṅga] one gains subjugation (*vaśyatā*); by worshipping the *Indranīla Liṅga* one gains other [powers]; by worshipping the *Komedaka Liṅga* one gains beauty;
and by worshipping the *Marataka Liṅga* one attains excellent yoga—thus are described the fruits of worshipping the *Ratna Liṅgas*.
Know that this is stated in the Āgama known as the *Cintyaviśva*, which was spoken by Īśvara (p66b, f22a, l1). 131.
Subsequently, the procedure for the metal liṅga (*lohalinga*) is described as being of eight kinds.

The liṅga is of eight kinds: ... [one] made of iron, one of gold, likewise one of silver, one of copper, one produced from bell-metal, one fashioned from brass, one of tin, and one of steel. [These result respectively in] prosperity, sovereignty, excellent sons, acquisition of people, enmity with others, and subsequently, eradication.
The *Sūkṣmāgama* states that the fruits of worshipping [the deity] beneath such [a liṅga] are manifold.
As for the eightfold classification of *lohaliga* (metallic liṅgas), they are as follows:
