the golden liṅga (*svarṇaliṅga*), the silver liṅga (*rajataliṅga*), the copper liṅga (*tāmraliṅga*), the bell-metal liṅga (*kaṃsaliṅga*), the tin and lead liṅga (*tuttināgaliṅga*), the iron liṅga (*ayoliṅga*), the brass liṅga (*pittalailiṅga*), and the steel liṅga (*āyasaliṅga*). These constitute the *lohaliga*.
If those eight types [of lingas] are worshipped, what are their respective fruits? The worship of a golden linga bestows wealth; the worship of a silver linga grants a kingdom;
and the worship of a copper linga—(16)
It is said that worshipping the Satpuṭra-liṅga grants a virtuous son; worshipping the Kāma-liṅga causes enmity with people; worshipping the Tūthi-nāga-liṅga causes expulsion;
worshipping the Yī-liṅga brings disease;
worshipping the Pitṭai-liṅga grants longevity; and worshipping the Āyasa-liṅga brings about death.
Thus, understand that the fruits of performing the worship of the *lohaliga* have been described in detail in the *Sūkṣmāgama*.
132. Subsequently, [the worship] of the sixteen-fold momentary *liṅga* (*ṣoḍaśavidhakṣaṇikaligapūjā*) is explained by means of three verses.
It remains unspoken.

Here, at the outset, the sixteen types of lingas are momentary: first, the sand linga, then the rice-grain linga, then the food linga, then the one fashioned from fish, and afterwards the one made of cow dung. (3)

One should use butter derived from cow's milk for *navanītajam*, a paste of sandalwood fruit for *phalapaiṣṭe*, a brush (*kūrcaka*) for *cāndanam*, a garland of *sumana* flowers for *rakṣākṣe*, two types of water for *gulajale*, and sprouts for *kāraṇe*.
Next, its fruit is described in Aṃśumān: liberation and the sequence of enjoyment;

longevity, purity of self, freedom from disease, firmness, happiness, the splendor of the eightfold nourishment, fortune corresponding to each [planet], the destruction of sin, equality with the Lord, and constant joy.
Knowing that sovereignty on earth is attained through virtuous qualities, one should worship the beloved Śambhu.

(5) O Brahmin, among those [offerings] mentioned which are momentary, rice-grains and cooked rice should be placed upon the sacrificial mound (*dṛṣad*), while the earthly [mound] is prepared with cow-dung. (6)

The Vaiśya should use a new tooth-stick that is suitable and effective, made from either *piṣṭa* wood or sandalwood (*pāṭīra*); and for the Śūdra as well, there is the triad consisting of a tooth-brush, a rosary, and [a staff] made of *gaula* wood. (3) (l7) Thus it is said.

The momentary liṅga is of sixteen kinds. What are they? They are: the sand liṅga, the rice-grain liṅga, the food liṅga, the clay liṅga, the cow-dung liṅga, the butter liṅga, the fruit liṅga, the flour liṅga, the sandalwood liṅga, the tuft of grass liṅga, and the ash liṅga.
The Rudrākṣa-liṅga, the Puṣpamālā-liṅga, the Gulaliṅga, the Jalaliṅga,
and the Pallavaliṅga— these sixteen types are known as the kṣaṇika-liṅgas. As for the fruit of worshipping them, it is said that the worship of the vālukā-liṅga bestows liberation (mokṣa).
It is said that the worship of a liṅga made of rice flour brings enjoyment; the worship of a liṅga made of food brings longevity; the worship of a liṅga made of clay brings purity of the self;
the worship of a liṅga made of cow dung brings freedom from disease; the worship of a liṅga made of fresh butter brings firmness of the body; and the worship of a liṅga made of fruit...
It is said that the worship of the *piṣṭaliṅga* brings about desired objects;
the worship of the *candanaliṅga* brings about beauty; the worship of the *kūrcaliṅga* brings about splendor; and the *bhasmaliṅga*—(l6) [brings about]... [auspiciousness].
Among these— wherein it is said that worship of the *bhū-liṅga* brings fortune, worship of the *kuḷa-liṅga* brings joy, worship of the *jala-liṅga* brings sovereignty,
and worship of the *pallava-liṅga* brings virtuous qualities— it is the *vāluka-liṅga* among the various types of *kṣaṇika-liṅgas*.

The worship of these three liṅgas— the wooden liṅga, the stone liṅga, and this [metal] liṅga— is appropriate for the Brāhmaṇa Śaiva; likewise, the worship of these three liṅgas— the earthen liṅga, the cow-dung liṅga, and the butter liṅga— is [appropriate] for the Kṣatriya Śaiva.
The three types of liṅga worship— bāṇaliṅga, piṣṭaliṅga, and candanaliṅga— are suitable for Vaiśya Śaivas; furthermore,
the three types of liṅga worship— kūrcaliṅga, puṣpamālāliṅga, and kuḷaliṅga— are [suitable] for the Caturdaśaiva community, such as Vellāḻar and others.
Know that it is stated thus in both the *Aṃśumānāgama* and the *Kāraṇāgama*: that [this] is suitable, while all other [rites] are common to everyone. 135.
Next, the characteristics of the worship of the *pāṇaliṅga*.

The greatness of the Bāṇaliṅga, which arises simultaneously with its origin, is declared in three verses; this [greatness] has been stated in the Śrīkāmika, and having heard it, its status as an Āgama was then proclaimed.
When Bāṇāsura arrived, he performed terrible penance; pleased by that penance, Maheśvara granted him fourteen crores of *liṅgas*, which were then installed. ||1|| (l7)

Having worshipped [the deity] and enjoyed incomparable sovereign pleasures for the duration of his entire reign, he then, by the command of Śambhu, at the end of time, rendered these [powers] common in certain excellent locations—
namely, on Śrīśaila, within the belly of the celestial river (Gaṅgā), and in the great place of Ālam.
And in the womb of the Kālindī, within the wombs of sacred rivers, and in the hermitage of a maiden; ||2||
Free from defects such as lines, spots, stains, roughness, fissures in the head, flaws on the sides of the stone, cracks, eruptions, or extreme density; pleasing to the sight of those who behold it;
devoid of various colors; a beautiful and auspicious pedestal like a water bubble—[such is the stone].

"...the excellent *kāra-liṅga*... ordained and auspiciously bestowed by one's own preceptor. (3) As for how the *bāṇaliṅga* came into being: there was a king named Bāṇāsura, who [was well-versed] in various kinds of *śāstras*, *purāṇas*, and *āgamas*.
(14) Having requested the elders to read, while listening to various meritorious narratives, he said with great affection, "One day, please tell me the *Śivaliṅgamāhātmya*. (15)
Upon hearing this, he felt a profound sense of devotion that impelled him to perform the worship of Śiva; thus, for a long time, he performed penance directed toward Mahādeva.
(16) By virtue of that penance, Mahādeva became exceedingly pleased and appeared before him in person to ask what he desired.
At that time, although Bāṇāsura possessed both hands and eyes,
and although he maintained great devotion toward the worship of Śiva, he was also driven by the desire to conquer the ten worlds.
When he requested ten billion Śivaliṅgas, Mahādeva, at that time, went to the banks of the Gaṅgā near the Himavat mountain;
there, taking his own hosts of attendants (pramathagaṇas),
he fashioned excellent images, squeezed them with his hands, gave them to the demon Bāṇāsura, and [instructed him on] the worship of Śiva.
Having spoken thus, he ascended to Kailāsa and remained there.
(13) After that, the demon Bāṇāsura performed the worship of Śiva in that very manner and enjoyed all those royal pleasures for many crores of years;
thereafter, Mahādeva— (14)
According to His divine will, those ten billion Śivaliṅgas are located in Śrīśaila, within the womb of the Gaṅgā river,
in the principal Śiva-sthalas such as Nīlakaṇṭha and Mukala, within the belly of the Yamunā river, and furthermore, within the hearts of the sacred rivers.
He also established [it] at Kanyāśrama. As for how that most excellent Liṅga exists there at this time: it is like a line, a fissure, and the northern...
Gaṅgā.

The black *śirā-citra* (vein-patterned) *ucchikkuḻi* exists as the *aśma* (stone-like) *parukku*; the *pārśva-kṣata* (lateral wound) exists as the *pakka-tirruḻampu* (side-thorn); and the *sphoṭa* (eruption) exists as the *kurutti*.
It is exceedingly heavy (*kanat-tirukkuri*) and exceedingly painful (*noy*). Without these and other such defects, and without being of many colors—

Like a mango fruit upon a liṅga, like a wave in the waters of Māyā, it remains firm everywhere; like a ripe karuṇāval-pazham, O Mother with the broad chest, you are the Dṛṣṭipriya for your own Ācārya, whose name is Pārkuṟa. (ll. 2–3)
Therefore, know that the Bāṇaliṅga alone, which was given by him, is the most excellent. Know that "Bāṇa" refers to the beautiful Bāṇaliṅga; all of this has been stated in the Kāmikāgama. 138.
The greatness of the Rasa-liṅga is expressed by three verses: "Who here, other than a madman, can describe the weightiness of the liṅga made of mercury? (l. 5)
By merely giving a proper sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), one destroys all evil;
by worshipping him for only two or three days, all sovereignty comes to pass—oh, how marvelous! Whatever desired perfection (*siddhi*) there may be, worship alone bestows it swiftly. (1) (l6.)
As many lingas as there are in these three worlds, so many have been worshipped;
if there is any fruit from this worship, let it be that.
Once performed, it bestows everything right here [in this world].
(2) It destroys the merit of a thousand Brahmin-slaughters incurred by worshipping a phallus made of mercury;
furthermore, the mere sight of it quickly destroys many tens of millions of cow-slaughters. (3)
Thus it is said.
As the greatness of the Śivaliṅga produced by means of *rasa* has been described in the Śivāgama known as the Vātūla, so too [it is described] for others. (12)
If it is argued that this has not been stated well, and if one asks how that is so—it is because it is said that by merely beholding the Rasaliṅga, all sins perish at that very moment;
and that by merely performing the worship of that Rasaliṅga for two or three days, all forms of sovereignty (aiśvarya) shall come to pass. (3)

The worship performed on a single day will itself grant the fulfillment of one's desired wishes; furthermore, if one were to worship every single Śivaliṅga that exists throughout the three worlds— however many there may be— (15)
It is said that the worship of this Rasaliṅga for even a single day bestows such fruits, and furthermore,
that the worship of the Rasaliṅga destroys many great sins (mahāpātakas), such as the killing of a Brahmin or the killing of a cow.
Thus, know that the greatness of the worship of Rasaliṅga has been declared in the Vātulāgama. 141.
Next, the majesty of Swayambhūliṅga [is described] by means of two verses.
It remains unspoken.
If the self-existent *liṅga* is indeed seen on earth, it is according to the *Kāmika*:
"By virtue of the trembling of the infinite heads of Kālāgnirudra..."
It is said that from that [fire] there would be smoke; above it, thick sparks went forth, and those masses of sparks became threefold through the process beginning with their uprooting. ||1||

However, that linga which is submerged in water, rooted out, and supported by the immovable [earth], is called *samūha*; furthermore, that which is known through the words of authoritative tradition (*āpta*) on earth is called *samūla*. Moreover, whatever other lingas there are, such as those made of white stone and so forth, they likewise abide in that same manner.
Therefore, how can the greatness of Svayambhū, endowed with manifold doctrines, be described?
||2|| (l4) Thus, one should properly understand from the mouth of the Guru that the Svayambhū-liṅga exists in three forms. 143.
Subsequently,
(15) the power of the *tattvamūrti* is described as it is taught in the *Vātulāgama*:
"The power of the *tattvamūrti* and the chariot— this which has been declared in three ways in the *Vātula*..."
In that regard, the reality there is indeed both partless (*niṣkala*) and with parts (*sakala*), and their form (*mūrti*) has been so described.
That which is yoga is indeed power (*prabhāva*); such is the state of Śaṅkara, who is eternal, and here his form consists of twenty-five [principles].
"Indeed, these are the forms of Sthāṇu"—thus it is said. One should understand this great secret well through the oral instruction of the Guru. 144.
Subsequently: *vyaktaliṅga*, *avyaktaliṅga*, *vyaktāvyakta*. (p71a, l1)
This definition of the three types of *liṅga* has been stated:
"The *liṅga* may be of three kinds—manifest (*vyakta*), unmanifest (*avyakta*), and both;
among these, the manifest consists of twenty-five principles, for it is explained that your bodies are those [twenty-five]. (L2)

"The unmanifest (avyakta) here is partless (niṣkala), and that too is said to be endowed with the name Śiva; then there is the Sādākhya, the Liṅga-pīṭha, and the three-fold Liṅga which has a dual form. Thus it is said. (Verse 3.
As for the manifest Liṅga (vyaktaliṅga), it consists of the 215 forms beginning with the body of Candraśekhara, which originated within Maheśvara.
The *avyaktaliṅga* is said to be "without parts" (*niṣkala*), while the *vyaktāvyaktaliṅga* is described as having both a body and a *liṅga*.
In the Śrīkaṇṭhāgama, the *sthaṇḍilaliṅga* is also referred to as the *vyaktāvyaktaliṅga*. This is [the point]. (15)
Know that this is stated in the Vātulāgama.
145. Subsequently, the twenty-five-fold division (pañcaviṃśativigraha) is described by means of two verses. (16.
Candrālaṅkṛtaśekhara, Tuma, Amitra, and Vṛṣārūḍhaka...
The dancing [form] with auspicious attire, the bestower of boons upon Arjuna, and the seventh is the wandering mendicant;
then Kālāri, Purajit, Jalandharari, Mātaṅgabhañjana, Bhadraka, he whose form is half-lion and half-woman, and the other, Kairātaka, and Kālakau. (7)

O Hari, who subdued Caṇḍa, bestowed grace upon Anugraha, and removed the Kālakūṭa poison; O Lord, who gave the discus to Viṣṇu and are skilled in awakening the secret of Vighneśa; O Moon; O Guha; and O One-footed One—furthermore, who else is there who dwells in a blissful posture, namely the illustrious Dakṣiṇāmūrti?
Thus, together with the *liṅga*... [it consists of] twenty forms (*vigraha*). (l.
2) If one asks how there are twenty-five forms: [they are] the form of Candraśekhara, the form of Umāsahāya, the form of Vṛṣabhārūḍha, the form of Nṛtta, and so forth.

(l3) His form is beautiful and auspicious; his form is one that bestowed the *pāśupata* weapon upon Arjuna; his form is that of wandering for alms; his form is that of the slayer of Time (*kāla*); his form is that of the destroyer of Tripura;
his form is [that of] the water... (l4)
The Vigraha [image] of the slaying of Mātaṅga; the Vigraha of Vīrabhadra; the Vigraha of Haryardha; the Vigraha of Ardhanārīśvara; the Vigraha of Kirāta; the Vigraha of Kaṅkāla;

the Vigraha of the bestowing of grace upon Caṇḍeśvara (l5); the Vigraha of the removal of the Kālakūṭa poison; the Vigraha of giving the discus to Mahāviṣṇu; and the Vigraha of the bestowing of grace upon Vighneśvara—20.
The form of Soma-Skanda, the one-legged standing form, the form seated in the posture of ease (sukhāsana), the form of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the form of the pillar of fire, and the Ākāśa form.
25. Thus. (l7)
Know that Mahādeva possesses many distinct varieties of forms. 147.
Subsequently, the gradation in the devotion to the worship of Śiva is stated:
"In the *Aṃśumatī-āgama*, a gradation even in worship is proclaimed. (p72a, l1.)

The worship of the Lord residing in the lotus of one's own heart is the best; after that, the maṇḍala; after that, the momentary [image]; from that, the fruit; from that, the painting on cloth; from that, the painting on a wall; from that, the image; from that, the liṅga; and after that, the formless (niṣkala). Thus it is said.

If you ask how one performs Śiva-pūjā: among all forms of worship performed as an internal sacrifice within one's own heart-lotus, that which is performed internally is the most excellent. Among those, the maṇḍala-pūjā is superior, and even more excellent than that is the kṣaṇika-pūjā. (ll. 3–4)

Furthermore, it is said that among those, the worship with many flowers is superior; among those, the worship with variegated garments is superior; among those, the worship with variegated food-offerings is superior; among those, the worship of the image (bimba-pūjā) is superior;
among those, the worship of the Śivaliṅga is superior; and that which is superior even to that is this very [worship]. Thus...
Know that the gradation of Śiva-pūjā is as described in the Āgama known as Aṃśumān. 149. The moment called Vīkṣā [is when] the fire becomes dry by the gaze of the sun upon Śiva. (l7)

The moon-like gaze [of the deity] is the burning away [of impurities], and the sprinkling [of water] is the act of providing a flood of nectar for its fulfillment. Having performed the service of waving the fan of the lotus-stalks of the living beings situated in that reality, and thereafter having performed praise, salutation, and circumambulation... the fire-rite (*agnikārya*).
Having petitioned Śiva, saying "I shall perform [it]," and having received permission, he should place the *sāmānyārghyapātra* in his right hand, go near the site of the *homa*,
and sit upon the seat facing north.

1. Placing the *sāmānyārghya-pātra* to one's right from the [seat of] existence. 2. In the middle of the *kuṇḍa*, using a single blade of *darbha* grass and the *astra-mantra*, scratching three lines pointing toward the north and one line pointing toward the east. 3. Taking *darbha* grass with the *astra-mantra* for the purpose of sprinkling water (*akṣapāna*).
3. Distributing [the offerings] in many ways; 4. Placing a seat for the Goddess as a throne for the gods; 5. Invoking and worshipping Vāgīśvarī and the Vāgīśvaras. (l6)
6. Afterwards, bringing the fire into the fire-pit; 7. Taking one fragment of fire (*agniśakala*) as the *rākṣasāṃśa* and setting it aside;

8. Performing purification through inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) and other rites; thereafter, (l7) striking [the fire] with a flower, taking the consciousness (*caitanya*) of the fire, and merging it once again with one's own *jāṭharapāvakāgni*.
Having gathered the fire situated in the vessel... (p74a, l1) ...one should worship it with the *saṃhitā* mantras.
9. Protection and sprinkling; performing the *deṇu-mudrā*, one should worship with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, lift the fire with both hands, and [place it] in one part of the *kuṇḍa*. (l2)
10. Circumambulating to the right, prostrating fully, and standing facing the deity within the sanctum, perform the *pātraka-udvāsana* (the ritual dismissal of the vessel).

11. Afterwards, offer two pieces of cloth as the *vastra-dakṣiṇā* (sacred gift of clothing). 12. For the purpose of purification and pacification (*śaucāśamana*), offer water for the *arghya* three times from the heart center.

12. By means of these [mantras], one should cover the fire with the Astra-mantra and cause it to blaze with the Kavaca-mantra. 13. One should worship the Garbhāgni. 14. Thereafter, one should worship it with the five mantras beginning with Satya.
15. With sesame seeds. (l5)
16. Offering five oblations (*pañcāhuti*) with the root mantra, ending with *svāhā*. 17. Subsequently, meditating upon [the fire] as being born from the fire-god (*agnijanittha*).

18. Worshipping Brahmā and others in the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), and Indra and others on the sacrificial grass seats (*viṣṭara*). 19. Reciting the protection formula for the son of Agni (*agnikumāra-rakṣaṇa*). 20. Performing the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*) for the fire.

21. Offering the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). 22. Performing the ritual dismissal (*udvāsana*) of the ancestors. 23. Worshipping Śiva within the lotus of the heart-fire (*agnihṛdaya-kamala*) using the seat-mantra (*āsana*), the form-mantra (*mūrti*), and the root-mantra (*mūla*).
24. Offering one hundred oblations (*śatāhuti*) with the root-mantra, ending with *svāhā*. (p74b, l1)
25. Performing the Daśāṃśahoma for the Brahmāṅgas: In the Kāmika [Tantra] it is said:
"One hundred, half of that, or half of that again—namely twenty or ten—[should be offered], either with the sesame seeds used for the daily homa or with whatever materials are available. * * (L. 2)
26. Performing the *pūrṇāhuti* offering; taking the *sruva* ladle, perform three oblations (*āhutis*) with the root mantra for the sake of the *naivedya*.
27. Having given *ācamana* and *arghya*, perform the *gandha-homa* and *tāmbūla-homa*; then perform the *rakṣābandhana* and offer the eight flowers (*aṣṭapuṣpa*). 28. Afterwards—

29. Joining Śiva, who is the fire within the Śivaliṅga; 30. Performing the homa in the fire with the pūrādimantras; 31. Offering bali to Brahmā and others, as well as to Indra and others; 32. Having consumed the oblation, [attains] the supreme.
32. Thus, the invocation of Agni; 33. The invocation of Indra and the other deities by Brahmā and the others;
34. The loosening of the knot of the *viṣṭara* grass. (16) [This is] from the *Sūkṣmāgama*.
Taking the fire with the *niṣṭhurā* mantra, one should worship it at the root-liṅga;
then, taking the seat (*viṣṭara*) and releasing the knot, one should dismiss it.
Having brought the sacrificial grass for strewing, one should indeed sprinkle it with clarified butter;
then, taking a single blade of darbha grass, one should burn the remainder starting from the tips.
Having cast one of them into the fire, make a tilaka-mark with those ashes.
The wearing of those ashes increases the lifespan, prosperity, and fame of men;
it grants victory, destroys disease, and bestows the fruit of all desired objects.
One should apply that ash as a tilaka on the forehead using the Netra-mantra.

By this statement, why is it that the offering of clarified butter (*ājya*) is performed in the *homa*? 35. Thus concludes the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*). Afterwards, having risen, one should offer the merit of the *homa* into the right hand of Śiva, and thereafter perform the worship of Śiva (*śivapūjā*).
Having gone to the site and remained there, he shall complete all other rites up to the conclusion of the worship of Caṇḍeśvara. Thus ends verse 159.
In the Kālottara:
"By a single sprinkling alone, the consecration of the sacrificial ladle (sruk) is accomplished. (4)
The vessel for the arghya offering should be filled with ghee and water.
Endowed with all conditioned qualities, he becomes worthy of performing all ritual actions.
Thus ends the procedure for the daily fire-ritual (nityāgnikāryavidhi). (L5.
Hereafter, the procedure for the inner offering (antarbalividhāna) is stated in one śloka:
"In the case of an offering and worship performed for one's own sake, both the internal and external offerings are prescribed."
To the east of the pit (*kuṇḍa*), there is a square mandala; then, in the eight directions starting from the east, the Rudras, the Mothers, the Gaṇas, and the Yakṣas are to be worshipped.
The Planets (*graha*) are in the northeast; those belonging to the gods, Rākṣasas, and Uragas are in the three corners beginning with the southeast.

"In the center of the mandala, one should worship the hosts of stars in the directions of Īśa, Vahni, Nirṛti, and Viśve; below them, the gods, and likewise Varuṇa in the north and the Kṣetrapa. Thus it is said. (p75b, f71a, l1.

The four types of confusion—1. confusion regarding the preceptor, 1. confusion regarding ritual action, 1. confusion regarding verbal instruction, and 1.

confusion regarding doctrine—must be avoided at all times, whether in obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), or optional (*kāmya*) rites, as well as in matters concerning the self (*ātmartha*) and matters concerning others such as festivals (*utsava*).

otherwise, if the fault of confusion (*sāṅkarya*) arises due to a failure to avoid it, the elders will abandon him, knowing him to be fallen. 165.

Now I shall describe in detail the supreme lineage of gurus in the Śaiva scripture.
A certain leader of mantras, having come from Kailāsa for a specific purpose,

One should impart the knowledge of Śiva to the immortals who are without distinction.

he presides over the empowered mantra belonging to the dualistic faction of Śakti and Śambhu.
Turning his back on indifference toward the eight supernatural powers beginning with *aṇiman*,

being entreated by Cemuṣi— departed for the southern direction.
And he imparted the knowledge of Śiva to the multitudes of yogins dwelling there.
He had three disciples who had crossed to the further shore of the ocean of the Śiva scriptures:

"Nīlakaṇṭha" is one [of them], the promoter of the knowledge of the one Śiva. "Ugrajyotis" and others—these five were the most eminent disciples of the Guru. This is known from such statements as: "Those born in Gauḍa, Saurāṣṭra, Kaśmīra, Mahārāṣṭra, and so forth."

In former times, this rule regarding a Śūdra was never established anywhere due to public censure. [However,] thinking, "I shall not perform an improper act even out of a desire for great wealth," it is therefore said that in the Kali age, the rites of initiation and so forth may be performed by a preceptor born of his own respective lineage. 2.

While performing [the rite], one should impart the instruction of the mantra (mantrōpadēśa) after making the disciple understand that secret (rahasya) by saying "In this manner" into his ear;

Having transcended the state of a Śūdra (l2),
one should not think "I am a twice-born" nor "I am a portion of Rudra"; rather, one must cultivate the realization of oneness between the disciple and oneself (l3).
Furthermore, not otherwise: in the *sthānīyabhāga*, one portion (*kalā*) is for Maṇḍaleśvara-Kaulla;

and one portion [is for others]. After the Śivadīkṣā is completed, having seated this disciple along with [the others] in a single row—
Thinking, "I must provide food," and likewise, "All this must be done for the disciple by the Brahmin preceptor," he considers that alone to be appropriate.

If one does not act according to the [standard] procedure, the following six types of initiation may be performed: Cākṣuṣadīkṣā, Sparśadīkṣā—which is the contact of Śiva’s hand with the head—Vācikadīkṣā, Bhāvanādīkṣā, Śāstradīkṣā, and Yogadīkṣā. Furthermore, according to the ritual of Homa...

The Brahmin preceptor performs for them what is improper, and that which is not approved by the elders; (3) even the great former teachers did not perform the funeral rites (*antyakriyā*) regarding Śūdras in any place whatsoever, out of fear of public censure.

The Śaiva mantra-word, the phoneme, the vowel, the reality (*tattva*), the category (*kalā*)— of these six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) proclaimed in sequence, when is the counting of the "desirous one" (*kāminī*) desired?
Indeed, for the teacher who knows the three [paths], that which is the measure of the palm-beat (*tālamāna*) is like a timid woman.

"Having known the six paths of the Guru below... (l5) ...the Śiva-āgamas are the preeminent among the eighteen branches of knowledge; thus, in this matter, there is no Dvāpara age, and even reasoning is said to be acquired. So it is said.

"The Teacher is everywhere; he alone is eternal among the other forests [of doctrines]. For that reason, among all scriptures, it is the Śiva-scripture alone which is the scripture proclaimed by him as 'this is what should be studied. (p80b, f76a, l1) Thus it is said.

"Everywhere" means: there is no other deity who instructs all the worlds—the Prākṛta-bhuvana, the Māyā-bhuvana, and the Mahāmāyā-bhuvana—except for the Great God (Mahādeva) known as Hara. Among the eternal ones (nityas), that... [text ends].
Mahādeva is eternal; however, among other deities there are none who are eternal. Therefore, even though it is said that this was spoken by a god who exists as the Lord (Śāstṛ) everywhere, (l4)
Know that among all the scriptures handed down to the world by these two types of beings, the Śivāgamas, known as the Śivaśāstra, are the most preeminent. (15) 171.
Subsequently, regarding the dream-omens during the disciple’s sleep on the initiation bed for nirvāṇa-dīkṣā, they are described by two verses:

One should behold milk, sugarcane, meat, curd, wine, honey, and water, as well as flowers and other auspicious things. ||1||
Among men, the twice-born and the king are to be honored; among birds, the parrot and the swan are to be honored;
among wild animals, the elephant and the lion [are to be honored]; and likewise the bull, the milch-cow, the white serpent, and the [white] snake. (2) (p81, l1)
Regarding the fruit of the disciple’s auspicious *adhivāsa-śayana* (consecrated bed):
(l2) To see a royal umbrella, a lotus flower, a bull, cattle, a peacock, a horse, milk, curd, green sugarcane,

behold the excellent kings. Among birds, behold the Cakora and the Śatapatra; among wild animals, behold the elephant and the lion.
"Behold—within the forest of the city (l5)—behold the all-white serpent; know that this and the rest are what one perceives as 'good'. 173.
Now, the sevenfold initiation (saptavidhadīkṣā) is being described. (l6.)

"Opening his eyes," the Guru, thinking "I am Śiva," out of compassion for the disciple whose heart is wounded, performs the rite of initiation known as *cākṣuṣī*—which is indeed like [the healing] of one bitten by a serpent with a mantra. ... Having worshipped his own hand with the thought that it is the Hand of Śiva, he [touches] the disciple with that very hand.
If the teacher touches [the disciple] on the head and other parts, while his own feet remain untouched, that is the initiation of touch (*sparśanādīkṣā*).

(p81b, f77a, l1) "I am he" through such contemplation, according to the *Śivatantra* taught by the Guru—that indeed is the verbal initiation (*vācikīdīkṣā*), as stated by Ratnavācaka in the *Vajrakatāmocana*.
(2½) For that teacher is meditation itself. (l2)

Mental initiation (*mānasī dīkṣā*) is indeed that which is called *bhāvanā*, like [the perception] of a tortoise regarding an object; whereas scriptural initiation (*śāstrī dīkṣā*) consists of the study and instruction of the Śaiva Āgamas and the practice of yoga, and it should be well-observed through the six substrata (*ṣaḍādhāra*). (3½) Thus it is said.

Furthermore, there are what are known as visual initiation (*cākṣuṣadīkṣā*), tactile initiation (*sparśadīkṣā*), verbal initiation (*vācikadīkṣā*), initiatory contemplation (*bhāvanādīkṣā*), and scriptural initiation (*śāstradīkṣā*).
(14) Thus,
Śivadīkṣā consists of eight types, namely Yogadīkṣā and Hautrīdīkṣā;
among these, Sākṣuṣadīkṣā is as follows— (15).
The Guru, maintaining the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) "I am Śiva" (*śivoham*), fully opened his eyes and, perceiving the disciple— who was a practitioner of mantras—
as a serpent through the contemplation of Garuḍa, awakened that disciple by means of the *Śivabālaka* mantra, just as one would dispel poison.
It effects liberation from bondage (pāśavimocana), namely, the initiation by sight (sākṣuṣadīkṣā). As for the initiation by touch (sparśadīkṣā):
the preceptor, having meditated upon his own hand as the Hand of Śiva (śivahasta), [performs it] in that very manner. (l2)
After performing the worship, the touching of all the limbs of the disciple, beginning with the head, is called *sparśadīkṣā*.
As for *vācikadīkṣā*: the preceptor, maintaining the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) "I am Śiva," causes the disciple to chant the sacred names of Śiva while instructing him in their recitation.
And also what is called the Vāśikadīkṣā.
(14) If you ask how that is so—it was Maṇikka Vācakānār who, having proclaimed the sacred names of Śiva, destroyed [the bonds] and bestowed [them] upon Rājākumāra-ttiyar. (15)
Know that it is like removing a cataract— this is the initiation through contemplation (*bhāvanādīkṣā*).
Just as a hen breaks her eggshell and brings forth the chick, so too does the Guru, through the mental activity of the contemplation of "I am Śiva" (*śivoham-bhāvanā*), [liberate] the disciple.
Contemplating [this], one effects liberation from sin; this is called *bhāvanādīkṣā*. As for *śāstradīkṣā*—it consists of [the study of] the Śiva-śāstras and the Devāra Tiruvācakam.
The preceptor who is free from error imparts to the disciple what is known as *śāstradīkṣā*. As for *yogadīkṣā*:
the preceptor [perceives] the *mūlādhāra* as a lotus with four petals, the *svādhiṣṭhāna* as a lotus with six petals, and the *maṇipūraka* as a lotus with ten petals.
The twelve-petaled lotus of Anāhata, (l3) the sixteen-petaled lotus of Viśuddhi, and the two-petaled lotus of Ājñācakra— having thus [taught] these six ādhāras to the disciple, (l4)

It demonstrates it as follows: there is the initiation of yoga (yogadīkṣā), and the initiation of the Hotṛ priest (hotrīdīkṣā), which consists of being joined with the sacrificial pit, the maṇḍala, and the altar (kuṇḍamaṇḍalavedikā).
Thus, having identified these seven kinds of initiation, [the text concludes at verse 176½].
Thereafter, the *hautrī-dīkṣā* is described by means of three verses:

"In this context, the *hautrī* [initiation] consists of the construction of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and the mandala; it involves the manual actions of the preceptor and is accompanied by the purification of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhva-śuddhi*), beginning with the common [purification]; for that indeed is the initiation leading to liberation (*nirvāṇa-dīkṣā*). (16)

In the group of six, the mantra-words, syllables, worlds, principles (*tattva*), and digits (*kalā*)—their number is proclaimed slowly with meritorious words, auspicious grass (*kuśa*), and the deep resonance of heavy cymbals. ||1||
The initiation performed by the true Guru according to the *hautrī* [tradition]— which reveals purity through the four absorptions (*laya*), removes committed sins, bestows good fortune,
grants the six qualities, and is incomparable— is the giver of the eightfold supernatural attainments (*siddhi*).
This very initiation, placed at the very summit of merits, is the bestower of liberation.

(2) A physician does not effect the release from disease through meditation or anything else; everywhere it is action alone that effects the removal of cataracts and the like by means of a surgical instrument. (3)
It is observed that the purification of copper occurs through acid, not by mere thinking;
therefore, for the removal of the self’s fetters, the *hautrī* initiation alone is sufficient—enough of this ignorant activity!

(4) The *hautrī* initiation consists of: the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the altar for the Lord of the Maṇḍala (*maṇḍaleśvara-vedikā*), the altars for the water-jar and the *vardhanī* vessel (*kumbha-vardhanī-vedikā*), and the altar for the chosen Liṅga (*iṣṭaliṅga-vedikā*).

Together with the five medicinal altars (*pañcauṣadhavaidika*), the five-pitcher altars (*pañcakumbhavedika*), and the altars for the retinue deities (*parivāradevatāvedika*), you performed the extensive manual rites of the true preceptor (*sadācāryahastakriyā*). Furthermore, you conferred the various types of initiation (*dīkṣābheda*) consisting of consecration (*abhiṣeka*) accompanied by the purification of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvaśuddhi*) according to the specific rules of the tradition (*samayaviśeṣanirvāṇa*). In this manner, it constitutes the sequence of ritual action (*kriyāpaddhati*).
Know that it is also called *hautrī-dīkṣā* and *nāmadīkṣā*.

The six paths (*ṣadadhvan*) are: the path of mantra (*mantrādhvā*), the path of words (*padādhvā*), the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvā*), the path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvā*), the path of principles (*tattvādhvā*), and the path of limited powers (*kalādhvā*).
Thus, know that these are the six dvādaśakas: eleven mantras, eighty-one words, fifty-one phonemes, two hundred and twenty-four worlds, thirty-six principles, and five arts (kalās).
As for how that *hautrī-dīkṣā* is performed, it is as follows: by means of the true guru, along with the extraction of the arts (*kala-śodhana*).

That which is to be performed; that which dispels all accumulated sins; that which bestows the eight supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇimā*; and in whatever manner it may exist in this world—(15)
Not only does this merit exist, but it is superior to all other merits, bestowing liberation directly;
furthermore, its greatness is as described in the Kāmikāgama: "Whosoever, at whatever time, [his own]..."
If one were to satisfy one's own hunger by killing and eating a sacrificial goat with a spear (paṭṭi), liberation could not be attained without this Śivadīkṣā.

If those who are blind from birth, those with speech impediments from birth, and those without any other assistance were able to wander everywhere as they desired, then it would follow that liberation could be attained even without this Śivadīkṣā, and that one could know it [without it].

If anyone, without performing the *oḍḍu* and other preliminary rites, were to carry the great *asamudra* vessel low in their hand across [the fire], then it is said that one may attain liberation even without the initiation of Śiva (*śivadīkṣā*).
Thus says Vaidya. (14)
