The meaning of this is clear. Hereafter, the purification of the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*) and the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is described by means of two verses:
"Inspection, sprinkling, striking, digging, raising, and filling..."
Leveling, sprinkling, pounding, sweeping, smearing, the fashioning of the decorative arts,
winding the thread, worship, the three lines on the ground, and the placement of the *vajra*—
these are declared to be the ninefold purifications of the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*), along with the scattering of parched grain and other items. (Verse 1)
Now, the purification of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*):
inspection, sprinkling, striking, digging, lifting [the earth], and filling.
Leveling, sprinkling, pounding, sweeping, smearing with plaster, the fashioning of decorative designs,
winding with thread, worship, and the removal of flaws by scraping— these,
along with the work of the diamond-tool and the laying of the four-footed [foundation], are the purifications appropriate for the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). ||2||

Inspection, sprinkling, striking, consecration with water, digging, lifting up, filling, leveling, pouring, pounding, sweeping, smearing, and the arrangement of the ritual arts such as the rites of withdrawal (*nivṛtti*) and so forth.

The consecration of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa-saṃskāra*) consists of eighteen [steps]: wrapping with thread (*sūtrāveṣṭana*), worship (*arcana*), laying down four lines (*rekhācatuṣṭaya-dhāraṇa*), making it adamantine (*vajrīkaraṇa*), and the scattering of substances such as parched grain (*lājādi-dravya-vikṣepaṇa*).

(l3) Excluding the scattering of divine substances such as parched grain, one should understand that the consecration of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa-saṃskāra*) consists of eighteen [steps] including the offering at the crossroads (*catuṣpathārpaṇa*).
Thereafter, the names of the Maṇḍapa-devaras remain unmentioned.
Śānti, Nandi, Mahāsita, Indratapana, Avahni, Vidyā, and Kalā.
Bhṛṅgin, Bhāsya, Yamāśva, Vāstu, Nirukti, Viṣṇu, Nivṛtti, and Vṛṣa;
(l5) Skanda, Pāśi, Ramā, Anila, Ibhavada, and Ana; the goddess Pratiṣṭhākalā; and Caṇḍa, Yanādhipa, Ārya, and Bhava—these twenty-seven are to be worshipped. ||1||
There exists another text that expresses a slight variation from this verse (17):
"Nandīśa, Atimahāsita, Indratapana, Avahni, Bhṛṅgī, and Kalā..."

Vidya, Bhāsya, Yamau, Vāstunirukti, Viṣṇu, Vṛṣa, Vṛttikā, Skanda, Paraśira, Mānilebha, and Vadana; the Goddess Pratiṣṭhākalā is to be worshipped, as well as Caṇḍa, Dhana, Dhāpārya... [and others]; these are the deities in the maṇḍapa.
Thus it is said.
Regarding the names of the twenty-seven deities who constitute the enclosure (*āvaraṇa*) of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), they are as follows: Nandin, Śāntikalā, Mahākāla, Indra, and Sūrya. (13)
Agni, Bhṛṅgin, Vidyākalā, Vināyaka, Yama, Vāstupuruṣa, Nirṛti, Viṣṇu, Vṛṣabha, Nivṛttikalā, Skanda, Varuṇa, Mahālakṣmī, Vāyu,
Mahāgaṇapati, Devī, Pratiṣṭhākalā, Caṇḍa, Kubera, the Seven Gurus, Īśāna, and Brahmā— [these are] from the east (l4–l5).

Know the names of the twenty-seven Kalāśadevatās who are situated in the first circumambulation (pradakṣiṇā). 210. Hereafter, the sequence of the Maṇḍapa for Śivadīkṣā is described: one should take refuge in the Sūrya-toraṇa, and then the four doors and their guardians.
The eighth lunar day of Kaitra is lost; it is inauspicious for the installation of a flagstaff, elephants, and the like, as well as for activities near a well.
Hasta is the asterism for the acquisition of wealth, the construction of a pavilion, the consecration of a site, and the worship of Indra with a water-pot.
"Śāpa, āyudha, kumbha, vardhanī, Gaṇeśa-arghya, the eight altars, and the fire. Thus it is said.

First, there is the worship of the Sun (sūryapūjā), the worship of the archways (toraṇapūjā), the worship of the doors (dvārapūjā), the worship of the eight banners (dhvajāṣṭakapūjā), the worship of the eight elephants (gajāṣṭakapūjā), and the worship of the eight auspicious symbols (aṣṭamaṅgalapūjā).
(13) Remaining near the altar and performing the *śivahasta* rite;

(14) the placement of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), purification of the pavilion (*maṇṭapaśuddhi*), worship of the site deity (*vāstupūjā*), worship of Mahālakṣmī, worship of the guardians of the quarters (*dikpālapūjā*), worship of the ten weapons (*daśāyudhapūjā*), and worship of the stable seat, the water-pot (*kumbha*), and the prosperity-vessel (*vardhanī*).

The worship of Gaṇeśvara, the worship of the seven Gurus, the worship of the *iṣṭaliṅga*, the great worship of Maṇḍaleśvara, and the commencement of the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*). Thus, understand the sequence of the pavilion worship (*maṇḍapapūjākrama*). 210. (The second time the number is mentioned.)
Next, the characteristics of the archway (toraṇa) are described:
one made of banyan wood is for the east, that of udumbara wood for the south, that of pippala wood for the west, and likewise that of plakṣa wood for the northern direction. (6)
It is as high as the height of the door, bound with three planks across the transverse [beam],
and like the previous [structure], it has nine vertical spikes above and below, measuring [so many] finger-breadths and possessing the splendor of the sun.

For the pavilion of the Śivadīkṣā, there are four archways: the Nyagrodha archway for the eastern entrance, the Udumbara archway for the southern entrance, the Aśvattha archway for the western entrance, and the Plakṣa archway for the northern entrance. Within these four archways... (13)
As for the length, it is the width and length of each respective door;

as for the length and thickness of the nine *śūlas* placed above the *toraṇa*, know that they are stated in the *Aṃśumānanāgama* to be seven *aṅgulas* in length and the thickness of a large betel-vine stem.
Afterwards, the eight auspicious characteristics (*aṣṭamaṅgalalakṣaṇa*) have not been mentioned.

Now, the construction of the fruit-bearing panel for the eight auspicious signs of the initiation pavilion (*dīkṣāmaṇṭapa*) is described: [It should be made] from copper or other materials, or from wood, with a height of eight times the width of nine fingers (*aṅgula*).

That [measurement] should be made with two finger-breadths thick; now, following the sequence beginning with the venerable *Kāraṇa-tantra*, I shall state one characteristic in accordance with the words of the illustrious *Kāmika-tantra*.
That single measurement of Rudra-fingers is increased by one finger-breadth by this [method].

Up to twenty [types of jewels], decreasing by one at a time, there may be varieties of gems. With that [material], an auspicious eight-sided pedestal should be made everywhere according to the measurement-fingers; its height should be well-spread out to half [the length], and its thickness should be two finger-breadths less than that. ||2||
Having divided that [space] into three parts for the path, one should then draw the pedestal (*pīṭha*) in two of those parts,
containing a mirror, a full water-jar, and a bull, as well as two fly-whisks with you [the deity] between them;
thereafter, a svastika, a conch, and a lamp— whatever has been declared [elsewhere] as inauspicious.
Then, one should contemplate that entire [universe] as being sustained by the three [qualities], beginning with *paśya*, which are free from attachment. ||3||
As for who they are, the host of gods spoke thus:
Menakā, Rambhā, Tilottamā, Sumukhī, Sundarī, and Kāminī;
one of these increases desire, and then one should worship Skanda and Lambodara.
Dara, Bhadra, Jahnusutā, Kamalā, Rudra, and Śaśāṅkāmbikā among them;
[this is] the golden plaque of the eight auspicious symbols for the initiation pavilion. (16)

It may be made of silver or copper, or it may be made of wood; its height is sixteen *aṅgulas*, its width eight *aṅgulas*, and its length two *aṅgulas*. Thus, it is stated in the *Kāraṇāgama* that one should fashion eight such slabs, or else not otherwise.

It may be made with a width of eleven aṅgulas and a length of nineteen aṅgulas; or, according to the rule that the length should be half a kalā more [than the width], it should have the measurement of two big toes (pradeśinī) in thickness (kha[gha]na).
Thus, as stated in the Kāmikāgama, one should divide the length of the plank into three parts and write the pedestal (pīṭha) in one part; in the other two parts, [one should write] the mirror,
the full pitcher, the bull, the pair of chowries, the śrīvatsa, the svastika, the conch, and the lamp.
These signs (15) are to be written upon eight wooden planks; as for those who bear them— Urvaśī, Menakā,
Rambhā, Tilottamā, and Susukhī (16).
It is attended by the eight [deities] known as Sundarī, Kāminī, and Kāmavardhanī. Regarding which deities are to be worshipped among the eight maṅgalas:
(l7) Skanda in the *darpaṇa* (mirror), Vināyaka in the full water-pot (*pūrṇakumbha*), Vīrabhadra on the bull (*vṛṣabha*), and [the deity] in the pair of fans (*yugma-sāmara*).
[One should place] Gaṅgā on the Śrīvatsa, Lakṣmī on the Svastika, Rudra on the conch, and the Goddess on the lamp.
It may be made from materials such as wood or copper; indeed, it has been stated here that "the depth is three finger-breadths," and for this reason, the ten weapons must be fashioned.
Is it not the case that [the vessel] made of copper and other materials yields the desired fruit according to the manual? This is another alternative view. ||1||
Furthermore, as stated in the *Kiraṇāgama*, the various weapons are indeed threefold;
[the first] is that which is raised by the hand, the five [others], and the remaining five weapons... or [the tree] beginning with the *āmra* tree up to the *yajña* tree...

In the *Kāraṇāgama*, it is stated that there are two types [of measures]: one is sixteen *aṅgula* in length and [the other] is [eighteen] *aṅgula* in width; and that [the measurement] from the head to the base of the neck is [twelve] *aṅgula* in length—and taking half of that [for the other part]—thus it is described in two ways.
(p. 97b, f. 93a, l. 1; the other side of the folio is not clear).
(l2) Regarding the lotus and the wheel—within this five-finger-breadth [measurement], it may be taken as one span in length or half a span in length; thus it is stated in the Kiraṇāgama...
having understood this well, the preceptor [should prepare] the ten-thousandfold [mandala].
"...he shall prepare... (l4) thus it remains unsaid.

"I shall describe the characteristics of the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) and the dipping-spoon (*sruva*); the handle (*guṇḍikā*) of the ladle, however, should be made according to the rule, as required. (l5)
The *arghya* vessel is prescribed for Taṇḍi;

it should not be made of liquids. At its base, one should fashion a circular pit, which is deepened by the [number of] groups [of deities], four times [the measure], and [shaped] like a *śravaṇa*. ||1||
By whom, however, was the remainder proclaimed as being of the lotus-form?
This [remainder] is said to be the head, consisting of three times eight, according to the count of the flowing [vowels].
The back [of the pillar] is rounded; its belly is like a foot placed upon the surface of the mud, and the *gaṇḍikā* is the staff. 3. What...?
Regarding the characteristics of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles:
(30) [The length] of the handle is said to be six *aṅgulas*, and the thickness of that handle is four *aṅgulas*. Within those four *aṅgulas*, there is one *kalaśa* for that handle. (15)
At eight *aṅgulas* from that [point], a square altar (*vedi*)...
(l6) ...three *aṅgulas* in width... (l7) ...to be trimmed; above that, three *aṅgulas* long... at the tip, three *aṅgulas* wide, and the elephant... (p98b, f94a, l1)

Above the hand, it is like a variegated whip; likewise, in the Śruti... (l2) ...twenty-four aṅgulas, and its... (l3) ...at the end of the second aṅgula-measure... in the mud, like the trembling of a man...
Know that a single *kaṇḍikā* has been stated [in this section] measuring two finger-breadths (15). 220.
Hereafter, the characteristics of the *pariti...* [and] the *vardhanī-kalaśa* (16).
It remains unspoken through fear, expressed by means of verses.
............... The enclosing-stick is made of *pālāśa* wood; its measurement is thus two hands, as well as [the length of] fingers. (l. 7)
The *rujaśyāma* is straight and free from defects;
it consists of thirty blades of *darbha* grass and is known as the *viṣṭara*. This is considered the auspicious measurement for the tip of the ear, according to the tradition of the *mataṅga*.

The *uṣṇīṣa*... the most excellent... [with] eight fingers... that too is spread out by one side. In length... or else it is spread out; the upper garment (*uttarīya*) is half the size of the *uṣṇīṣa*, or else it is radiant... with thirty-six thin [lines], having the form of a lute-player, and the tip is perfectly complete.
Alternatively, it is stated that the cause is the extension of mindfulness (*smṛtyāyatana*). By means of the grasping of the two streams of water, the *kumbha* should be prepared;

for that purpose, however, the measurement of the jar (*kalaśa*) as taught in the *Śrīkāmika* [Tantra] is to be followed. The nature of the *kumbha* is as follows: [it should be made of] gold, silver, copper, iron, or clay; or else, in the case of a distinction, [it may be made of] thread, a vessel, a jewel, white cloth, bone, or a brush (*kūrca*).

"What are the appropriate items for the leaf, the matted hair, the life-mantra, the sage’s grain, and the seat? [If one asks] "How so?", [the answer is: "One may take a *palāśa*, *koma*, or *pāṭala* leaf according to its length; in terms of weight, it should be as much as a cow-hair or a fine thread of *vīta*.
And how is the *viṣṭara* [prepared]? [The answer is: 30... [line 3].
...and ending with two *iṛaṇḍa*-units (*aṅgula*). The tip is one *kāla*-unit ...
(l4) Just as the headband (*veṣṭi*) that encircles my head is polished white, so too—(l5) being one-fifth part wide and four *pi...* polished white ... (l6)
If one asks how it is so, [it is] on the uṣṇīṣa...
as much as the width is less—alternatively, one-third of the northern...
from the southern limit of the uṣṇīṣa... If one asks how the sword of knowledge (jñānakhaḍga) is so: (l2)
...therefore, like the posterior part of the body, it is the posterior part...
(l3) ...it is said that the nīla is nine *aṅgulas* long, and that the hair on the head (*mūrdha*) is two *aṅgulas*... as if to reach [the crown]...
(l4) ...in this regard, the length from the heel to the top of the head... the length of the hair, or else eighteen *aṅgulas*... (l5)

...and eighteen *aṅgulas* in length; such is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the sword of knowledge (*jñānakhaḍga*). As for the characteristic of the water-pot (*kumbha*), if one asks what it is: it is that which supports the pillar of the water-pot, measuring sixteen *aṅgulas* in length, or else twelve *aṅgulas*.
The neck should always be four *aṅgulas* in height, and the mouth should be four *aṅgulas* wide, or else six *aṅgulas*; it should extend downward from the base for two *iṇḍa-aṅgulas*.

Such are the characteristics of a *kumbha* (vessel). Furthermore, it is said that the *karaka* (water-pot), which serves as a *vardhanī*, is fixed [to it], and its spout (*mūka*) is four *aṅgulas* long.

It is three finger-breadths in width and long; thus it is the characteristic of the *vardhanī*, and it is held by various scholars to be its defining mark—this indeed is its superior characteristic. Thus [it is said]. (l. 3)
Without blackness, without being smeared with ash, and without the *kaḷaṅkam* (mark/stain), O Mother, [you are] the *kumbhavardhanīkalaśa*.
Having made [it so], ... [regarding] the true nature (*svarūpa*)—if you ask how, it is thus:
in the earth, that which is worshipped as a deity is [conceived as] flesh upon the sand within the *kumbha*; and upon the *kumbha*...
The impure earth is called blood; the water within the jar is called marrow; and all the threads encircling it are ten thousand human sinews.
The gem that is placed within is called *śukla*; the seat (*kūrca*) is neither bone nor tongue, nor is it the mouth.
(7) Above, the skin of the belly is spread out, and the head-hair of the maiden is tied up together with a coconut.
The head is [the mantra]; the seven grains placed below are the seat; the mantra is the vital breath—thus is the nature of the *kumbha*, and thus... (l2)
Having understood the forms [of the deities], the Guru shall bestow the Śivadīkṣā.
225. Subsequently, regarding which trees are suitable for the *dīkṣā* sacrifices, it has been stated as follows: (13).

In this [work], ten sacrificial wood materials are taught in the *Aṣṭakiraṇa* or the *Suprabheda*, as well as in the *Bilvapaṭu*: the *śamī*, the two types of *khadira*, the *cūta*, the *vaikaṅkata*, the *hemakṣīra*, the *palāśa*,
the *candana*, the *kujā*, and the tree named *śārdūla*.

Furthermore, the Aśvattha and Śamī bricks are mentioned as twelve in the Śrīkāraṇa; the sacrificial trees are said to be eight in the Kiraṇāgama and ten in the Suprabhedāgama, while in the Kāraṇāgama—
Regarding the twelve:
what are they? They are the bilva tree, the āla tree, the vahni tree, the karuṅkāli tree, and the mango tree.

Know that the twelve sacrificial trees (*yajñavṛkṣas*) are: the *narmuṟukka* tree, the *atti* tree, the *palāśa* tree, the *mandāra* tree, the *veṅgai* tree, the *arasa* tree, and the *vākai* tree. (226)
Subsequently, it is stated that trees are not designated as female, male, or neuter.
(l. 2) "All trees may be of three kinds; among them, those with pith in their bark are of the female species.
Those trees whose inner core consists of pith are male, while those devoid of both [the aforementioned types] are neuter. (l. 3) What [is this]?

All trees that are like diamonds within are called *pumān-vṛkṣa* (male trees), all trees that are like diamonds upon the surface are called *strī-vṛkṣa* (female trees), and all those that belong to neither of these two categories are called *napuṃsaka-vṛkṣa* (neuter trees); thus, all trees are male, female, or neuter.
Know that the female organ (liṅga) is likewise divided into three types: the straight, the curved, and the crooked. 227.
The characteristics of the sacrificial fuel (samidh) have not yet been stated.
The sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*) made of *pālāśa* wood should be fashioned at the measure of a span (*vitasti*), five [in number], joined, and auspicious;
furthermore, there are sixteen fuel-bundles (*idhma*) here, likewise measured by long hands and fingers.
For the purpose of initiation (*dīkṣā*), seven scattering-substances (*vikiradravya*) have been declared: parched grain (*lāja*) and sesame (*tila*).

"Siddhārtha, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), ashes, darbha grass, and flowers—these [are prescribed] in the Kālottara. Thus it is said. Fuel-sticks (samidh) that are joined with the *śīraṇīla* [plant], which are small...
[as described above], and which are found on the palāśa tree or the mango tree—such fuel-sticks as these, even though... [they are accepted].

The *idhma* (sacrificial fuel) is that which exists on those two trees, having the thickness of a thumb and a length of sixteen *aṅgulas*; such is the *idhma*, and there are sixteen such *idhmās*— these are the *vikṛti-vyaṅgas*.
In the south—fried grain (lāja), sesame, long pepper (kaṭuka), unbroken rice (akṣata), sacred water (tīrthodaka), darbha grass, and flowers—these seven are known as the vikira-dravyas.
Know that they exist thus within the Ātamattam called Kālotthara. 228.
The characteristics of the seven grains:

"They say there are seven grains: rice (*vrīhi*), *kulattha*, sesame (*tila*), black gram (*māṣa*), pigeon pea (*siṃbā*), white mustard (*siddhārtha*), and green gram (*mudga*); however, for the pedestal of the jar (*ghaṭāsana*) and for the fire-oblation (*homa*), every category of grain may be used. Thus it is said.
The grains are said to be of seven kinds; what are they? They are:
rice, millet, paddy, foxtail millet, sorghum, lentils, and mung beans—these are the seven varieties. These are used as the seat for the worship of the water-pot (*kumbhapūjā*).
Know that all varieties of grain, whether they are fit for *homa* or not, are suitable for *homa*. 229.
Next, the procedure beginning with the five medicinal herbs (*pañcauṣadha*) is stated.
The five medicinal herbs are known as the Devikās; likewise, the Bhadra, the Vaikaṅkata, and the Ekapatra;

the Krānti, the Śālī, the Yava, the Kodrava, the Nīvāra, the Śyāmāka, and the Yava—these are the five [grains]. (1) Furthermore, there are five types of earth here: from a mountain, from the ocean, from a pond, from the horn of a bull, and from the earth dug by a boar. (2)
In the Śiva-kṣetra, however, for the sake of the teacher (*ācārya*), these materials [are required], beginning from the roots of *kuśa* grass: (l3) ...
[the earth] from a cemetery, from a crab’s carcass, from an anthill, from a river, from the base of *darbha* grass, from the mud of a pond, from a heap of soil, from sap and so forth, and stone. (l4)
And the wife, suitable for initiation, [is one] born from a Jambu, Udumbara, Cūta, Pippala, or Paṭola tree...

The five medicinal herbs (*pañcauṣadha*) are: Śītādevī, red *kāñcanī*, *kuṃbhi*, fragrant *mūrkai*, a single petal of a lotus, and *viṣṇukrānti*—these are the five herbs. (l6) Furthermore: *Sambāneḷḷu*, *vālneḷḷu*, *varaku*, *kulaśenṉal*, and *muṅkilariśi*—these are the five grains (*yava*). Mountain soil...

There are five kinds of earth: earth from the ocean, earth from a pond, earth from the horn of a bull, and earth from a Śiva temple. Together with these, there is also earth from the Nanduvallī creeper, earth from the tusk of an elephant, and earth from a crossroads.

"Three," and "rasādi" refers to five: *rasa* (mango), *kēntaka* (jasmine), *jāti-liṅga* (clove tree), *aridāra* (citron), and *manōśilai* (pomegranate). "Duttam," "duru," and "saptadhātu" refer to seven.
(l3) Regarding "pañcatvakkū"—that is, the five *ballava* trees: *nāval*, *atti*, *mā*, *aracu*, and *āl*; these are the five trees from which the *paṭṭai* is obtained.

As stated in the *Kāraṇāgama* regarding its chapters (paṭalas): "All these are the objects of application (*viniyoga*) in the consecration of the practitioner (*sādhakābhiṣeka*), as well as in initiation (*dīkṣā*) and installation (*pratiṣṭhā*).
Know this as "la.
232. Hereafter, the characteristics of the *kūrca* (grass-bundle) are described. The formation of the *dīkṣākūrca* should be made with thirty-six blades of *kuśa* grass in five ways.
On one side, it is twenty *tithis* long, with twenty-four qualities (*guṇas*) as its lower part;
it is seven finger-breadths in length, and its tip is four finger-breadths [long] according to the seasons (*ṛtus*), while the lower knot (*adhogranthi*) measures two finger-breadths;
the stalk below, however, is twelve finger-breadths.

What is it? As for the characteristics of the *kūrca* (grass seat): a *kūrca* may be completed with thirty-six blades of *darbha*, twenty-five blades, fifteen blades, nine blades, seven blades, five blades, three blades, or even a single blade of *darbha*.
—Know that the characteristic of a seat (*kūrca*) is as follows:
its tip should be four *aṅgulas* long, and its other length twelve *aṅgulas*, making eighteen *aṅgulas* in total.
If it consists of a single blade of *darbha* grass, know that the end-tuft (*muḍiccu*) is not required. 231.
The ritual procedure for the pacification of the site (vāstuśāntividhi) has been described by five verses.
The location for the pacification of the site (vāstuśāntisthala) should be within the sacrificial pavilion (dīkṣāmaṇṭapa), performed by the officiating priests (hotṛ).
Then, once a mound of earth has been fashioned upon that circle of rice as an altar,
the worship of Vāstupati according to that sequence is first, followed by the worship of Vighneśa.
It has also been stated that even the people who increase the worship of the water-jars [perform their rites] without the worship of that [deity].
By proceeding with the placement of the altar-pads in the sequence of sixty-four,
one should worship the Vāstupuruṣa, who has the luster of gold, in the center upon the four altar-pads.

With a face [shaped like] a conch, hands, eyes, a rosary, and a staff, bearing the earth upon his upraised head, and with a pair of feet constantly eager to rest upon the ground— [this form] was instantly raised by his memory.
At that moment, the six steps here were traversed by him, yet he neither fell nor did he remain.
To the west was Garhya, and to the north Mitra; then Dharaṇīdhara.
Following the sequence of the two corner positions, there were Savitṛ and Sāvitra;
then Indra, Tarja, Rudra, Tarjaya, and Surā, [and] Āpāpa...
Thus, having previously come together according to the fivefold rite, those eight gods— six and seven [in number]—
beginning with the Lord of the Thirty-three (Tridaśeśa) and others,
[are established]; afterwards, outside of that, in the eight directions, likewise the four beginning with Carakī.
Then, four [deities] beginning with Ṣaḍānana and ending with Bilipiñcha are to be worshipped in sequence. ||4||

According to the calculation of the three ages, fifty [years] have passed; having worshipped all those [deities] upon the lotus-ground of the site with mantras joined [with offerings], [one should perform the rite] below the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).

"One should indeed perform the entire rite of *homakarma* ending with *svāhā*, and then, outside the pavilion, [perform] the offering of the *balis* and food upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) using *kuśa* grass.
Regarding the meaning of these five verses in the context of performing the *dīkṣā* and *mānavāstuśānti*:
Within the area of the initiation altar (dīkṣāmaṇḍapa),
inside the fire-pit, there is a single maṇḍala made of either rice flour, parched grain flour, or clay, measuring one span in length and three finger-breadths in height.

Having measured that [space] and laid out sixty-four squares in the manner of a frog-leap (*maṇḍūka-padakrama*), one should worship Vāstupuruṣa-Brahmā in the center, within the forty squares, after having also drawn the diagonal lines (*karṇasūtra*).
As for his meditation (*dhyāna*): he has four faces and four hands, and in those hands—

One should meditate upon Vāstu-Brahmā as having a rosary (*japamālā*) and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) in his two hands, seated upon a lotus (*padmāsana*), with a golden complexion, and resting upon the *nābhi* [navel].
Having instructed him to perform meditation, he further directed him to worship the deity named Marīci in the sixty [units] to the east;
Vivasvān in the sixty to the south; Mitra in the sixty to the west; and Dharitrī in the sixty to the north.
For the purpose of worship— starting from the southeast (agnikoṇa)—
in all four corners, for each corner [the deities are]:
Savitṛ, Sāvitra, Indra, and Indrāṇī.
One should worship eight persons— namely Jaya, Rudra, Rudrāṇī, Śaṅkara, Śaṅkarī, Mṛḍa, Mṛḍānī, and Bhavānī— and circumambulate them. Then,
at thirty-two stations surrounding that [area], one should worship the thirty-three deities beginning with Īśāna, and circumambulate them.
In the four directions starting from the east— namely Sarakī, Vidārī, Pūtanā, and Pāparākṣasī— and in the four corners starting from the southeast corner— (l5)

One should worship these four—Skanda, Aryaman, Jṛmbhaṇa, and Balipiñjana—in this manner, and perform the fire-oblation (homa) for that location; having performed all other rites according to the procedure prescribed for Vāstuśānti, one should bring it to completion. This is the [instruction].
The ritual procedure for the pacification of the site (*vāstuśāntividhi*). 238.
(p105b, f101a, l1) The ritual procedure for the offering of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇavidhi*) is set forth in six verses.
One should also adorn the auspicious sprouts during initiation (*dīkṣā*), just as in the case of the primary cause (*kāraṇa*). (l2)
Then, in the interior of the initiation pavilion, either in the south-western direction or from the north-east,
on one or two spots as available, [the teacher] should prepare a square mandala with lines and lotuses, measuring one and a half cubits across, using barley or rice grains. ||1||
In that [diagram] divided sixteenfold, in the central four-square area, one should place the *kumbha* by counting from here and there; the auspicious *pālikās* [are likewise placed].
In the *bhāvya*, [one should place] the moon with its full body and single face upon the water-born [lotus] situated in the water of the *kumbha*.
One should meditate upon the pair of arms shining like white water-lilies and the two white eyes;
then, as a cause for the delight of the worlds, one should worship Rohiṇī together with Kṛttikā. Thereafter, one should worship the Sun in the offering-bowls situated at the edges, as follows:

Having bound the omentum, which has been held together with *darbha* grass, on the outside with three-pronged [needles] or with seven planets and days, and having joined it with leaves of *aśvattha*, *śirīṣa*, and *bilva*, as well as *dūrvā*, turmeric, and *kuśa* grass;
||3|| in the middle, a vessel for the entrails, and likewise with the powders of cloud-earth and forest-stone—
And with an anthill from the ground whose belly is filled with fine sand, having placed these small vessels upon them, one should worship the twelve [deities] along with Sumihara;
thereafter, the worship of the supporting Śaktis should be performed in another vessel, such as a shallow bowl. ||4||
Then, having filled two *prasthas* of milk, Yavana threw into it seeds of barley, sesame, *niṣpāva*, and half a *śimbā* of peas; and here he added mung beans,
black gram, and *kulattha*, [weighing] either seven or five *vasus*.
Having mixed [the ingredients] with water and washed them three times with milk, one should offer them to the Self who is like pure crystal.

Having thus worshipped and consecrated [the seeds] seven times, one should thereafter perform the sowing of the seeds with auspicious rites, with the intention of bringing about prosperity, until the sprouts appear in due order—
either after five days at the minimum, or after seven days (the number of sages), or after nine days.
"Or else, having observed other auspicious and inauspicious signs, or having understood them, the wise man should cast [them] into the water. (6) Thus it is said.
At the time of performing the Śivadīkṣā, the first step is the offering of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*).
If it is asked how this should be done: for the period of initiation (*dīkṣā*), it may be nine days, five days, three days, one day, or that very day.
(12) It is also stated that the *aṅkurārpaṇa* (the rite of sowing seeds) must be performed; and if it is asked where that should be performed: within the initiation pavilion (*dīkṣāmaṇḍapa*). Niruti.
Having gone toward the northeast (īśāna-dik) from the northeast direction,
the preceptor (ācārya), following the path established by the gods, should, with the span of his hand, draw a single mandala that is one and a half cubits in length and breadth,
and square in shape.
Having divided that into ten compartments, one should form a four-compartment lotus seat (padmāsana) in the center; therein, one should place the moon-pitcher (candrakumbha),
and in the other twelve compartments,
twelve pilasters with doors closed by crossbars, using three lines of thread— 5.

7. With a lute, having encircled and bound it with a leaf of *arjaka*, a leaf of *vāka*, a piece of *bilva* bark, *aruṣkara* resin, cow’s urine, and *kuśa* grass—having pierced these [with the needle]...
Having filled [the vessel] with powdered conch-shell and a little sand along with the sand brought previously according to the aforementioned rule,
and having placed it on the right side,
one should worship the Moon in that vessel and the twelve Ādityas in the bowls (*pālikās*), using the root-forms of the deities as their seats (*āsana-mūrtis*) in conjunction; thereafter, one...

Having placed [the offerings] in the *caru* vessel, in the *navapātra*, and in the two *nāḷi* measures of rice, along with those [add the following]: green gram, black gram, *tuvarai*, *kaṭalai*, *kaṭukku*, pigeon pea, *ulundu*, and cowpea;
thus [it is done].
Having combined eight substances, seven, or five substances with rice, he should wash them with milk while reciting mantras; then,
after performing the three-fold worship and consecrating them with mantras, he should place that fried grain into twelve milk-pots accompanied by auspicious musical instruments.
(16) Here, one sprinkles with water from the moon-pitcher (*candrakumbha*). This concludes the procedure for the offering of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇavidhi*).
From the nineteenth day after the initiation (*dīkṣā*) has concluded, [the period lasts] for seven or five days. (p107b, f103a, l1)
Having understood the auspicious and inauspicious results of the sprouts, one should perform the expiatory oblation (*prāyaścitta-homa*).
244. Next, the procedure for binding the protective thread (*rakṣābandhana*) is described: the Guru, facing north, [places] unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) in a vessel.
Having placed betel, areca nut, the *sadobhalaphala*, and a protective cord (*rakṣāguṇa*), one should—
using a golden cord with three strands, or a yellow cotton cord with five strands—
wipe it [the head] three times with the *astra-mantra*, excluding the thumb of the artisan, and then bind it. ||1|| Thus it is said.
When bestowing the Śivadīkṣā,
the preceptor, having performed the binding of protection (rakṣābandhana), stands facing north and instructs the disciple to stand facing east.

Having placed vibhūti in a vessel made of copper or other materials, one should place within that vessel either a protection for gold by means of a single, three-stranded, or five-stranded thread, or a protection for a thick golden thread that has been spun together;
having consecrated it with mantras, thereafter...
[that] in the vessel.

The one who has become the Guru, having taken up the protective book (kāppunūl), shall, excluding the thumb and using the other fingers, form the *mukhakoṇa* with the *astra-mantra* and bestow it upon the disciple’s right hand with the *śivamantra*.
Afterwards (l2),
the sequence of the Śaiva initiation and fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) is described by twenty-five verses.
Regarding the specific fruit of the ritual in the initiation-fire, it occurs after the kindling (l3).

Herein is the worship of the fire within the womb; then that bracelet, which has the luster of sound, should be placed on the left hand of the Goddess. Through the offering of clarified butter from the goat and the ewe, [the mantra] ending with the three days of resonance... *maḥ śiraḥ* is as before. (l4.)

For the sake of the parting of the hair (*sīmanta*), one should perform [the rite] with the *aghora* mantra and the crest-mantra (*śikhā*) for the sake of its birth; likewise, with the face-mantra (*vaktra*) and the armor-mantra (*varman*) at the proper time, for the sake of subduing the evil-mindedness within the womb.
Then, there should be the blazing of the armor-mantra from the weapon-mantra (*astra*), followed by sprinkling with water offered as the *arghya*. Again—
Taking that bracelet, which was fashioned from the embryo and possessed the brilliance of blazing fire, she departed. ||2||

A particle of gold should be offered, and worship performed with the heart-mantra for the sake of removing the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*). Then, there is the sprinkling with water from the *arghya* vessel for the sake of Śiva;
furthermore, there is striking with *darbha* grass while reciting the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), and the sprinkling with water while reciting the *vauṣaṭ* mantra.
With *darbha* grass, one should perform the removal of the ashes; furthermore, the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and other items should be set down. ||3||

Then, with the heart-mantra, one should offer five oblations of ghee into the mouth of the fire to remove the saliva; thereafter, one should offer the head-oblation with the *asmṛta*-mantra. One should worship Brahmā and the others at the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), and the lords of the lower directions within these [enclosures].
The Noble One should state that [the purification] of the mouth and hands must be performed first;
thereafter, the purification of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles is included here within the fourfold purification:
[the purification] of the upper and lower parts of the face and the left hand together with the *kuśa* grass, all at once.
One should sprinkle the water for the *arghya* with the Astra-mantra, sprinkle it while reciting the Kavaca-mantra, and then conceal it.
Furthermore, for the purpose of preparing the seat of the wooden staff, one should heat it slightly at the heart and at the tip.
(L5) Therein, starting from the front, one should touch the palm of the hand along with the *kuśa* grass in sequence; thus, together with the weapon, the seat is prepared in three ways.

Regarding the procedure for circumambulation toward the pure one, [one should perform it] before those two, in between them, and at their feet. Having placed the object of worship—the triad of its Lords—below, one should subsequently place Śakti and Śiva here.
Then, by means of the threads that effect the state of identity with That, one should establish the presence within the heart using darbha grass.

Thus, the purification of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, beginning with the inspection [of the clarified butter] like the crescent moon and ending with the worship of the heart, as well as the purification of the clarified butter (*ājya*) in its entirety, is now described. The clarified butter, having been purified by means of the inspection and other rites, is then whirled below over the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
Having established the fire upon the head of the threefold [sacrifice], I, the priest (hotṛ), shall likewise perform the rite. ||7||

Thus, having slightly stirred the clarified butter with the tips of darbha grass while reciting "To Brahmā, svāhā," this is the placing [of the vessel] upon the fire; then, having lifted it off, one should pour the two ladles together. Having offered the oblation consecrated with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should then place the kuśa grass into the pure [butter].
Then the rite of the *pavitraka* for the sake of success, as well as the *nīrājana* and the lighting of lamps [should be performed].

(L4) Having cast into the clarified butter two blades of *kuśa* grass with knots in the middle, with tips, one span (*vitasti*) in length, and with their points directed toward the north, then the right-hand [blade] and the middle one [are placed].

Having meditated upon the Suṣumnā together with Piṅgalā, one should offer the clarified butter from the left side with the ladle; this, however, should be offered into the fire during the moment of initiation for one who is white [in complexion]. ||9||
In that [oblation], with the mantras "svāhā" and "vaha," one should likewise offer the clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) into the left, the middle, and the fire;
then, by the preceptor, this triad should be offered to Soma joined with Agni and to the Moon.
In the vessel—namely the right, left, and middle—one should take that threefold portion of ghee with the *sruva* ladle.
Then, at the mouth of the ancestral fire, the oblation of clarified butter must be offered by Manu. 10.

But in the case of Kṛṣṇa, it is the reverse; there, the rite of consecrating the clarified butter (*ājya*) is performed below. This is the *saṃhitā*. Now, the *tāla*-counts, the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*), and the cow-seals (*gomudrikās*) should be given according to the greater or lesser [scale]. Then again, that worship is performed from the root mantra.
The twenty-five purifications (*śuddhi*) that must not be omitted here have been described.

(11) Thereafter follows the rite of offering the oblation into the mouth of the fire (*agnimukha-abhighāra*), the joining of the faces and their subsequent unification, and then the act of offering the oblation to the tongues of fire.

O auspicious one, for the purpose of uniting that [deity] and bringing about its single-minded absorption, perform the worship of the Lord with the Name and the Artha-mantra using the Weapon-mantra; or else, O Śubhā, you are the fire of Śambhu—[perform it] with five oblations or three.
Having spoken thus, and having worshipped the parents while turning away that vajra of Īśa,

the experts in taste should then apply the same ritual procedure for this sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). Indeed, there is a fivefold consecration ending with the topknot (*cūḍā*), and then the *pūrṇāhuti* for the sake of fulfillment.
But there, by means of the *rdeyā* [mudrā], one attains the accomplishment of the *tantra*, as well as the rites beginning with the *upaniṣad*. ||13||
Having performed that, the preceptor who knows its efficacy must indeed offer the *pūrṇāhuti*;
for it has been stated even in the *Dīkṣādarśa*, and all of this is approved by me.
Furthermore, for the sake of purification, there is the removal of the fragments of the fire-altar that have fallen away from all its parts, as well as the act of replenishing it.

Then, having meditated upon the sixteen *ṛidhmas*, each measuring sixteen finger-breadths, as the auspicious gods of the fire, according to the previously stated method— following the worship of the Lord in the mind— one should then contemplate the unification of the mouth of the fire with one's own face, and likewise the two junctions within the channels (*nāḍīs*).

The supreme teacher Kumbha offered two hundred and ten root-mantra oblations (*mūla-homa*) for the sake of fulfilling the disciple’s common [deficiencies], consisting of the nature of light; he then performed the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). (Verse 15) [End of] the book—260.
After this, (Line 4)
The procedure for the initiation into the *samaya* is set forth in three verses: "Then, for the sake of a favorable time,
place, and auspicious signs, and for the pacification of obstacles,
one should offer a hundred oblations with the root mantra alone and perform the *pūrṇāhuti*."

Thereafter, having performed the satiation (tarpaṇa) and the kindling (dīpana), he here performs the offering of the cooked oblation (sthālīpāka) three times for Śiva and the others; then, from the Sun (Dinakara) down to Āryā, there is worship through recitation (japa). ||1||

Subsequently, for the sake of expiation, there is a tenfold fire-offering (*homa*) with missiles; when completed, the notification regarding the corpse, the summoning of the disciple, his entry, obeisance to the maṇḍala, and the instruction on the excellent vows follow in sequence.
Furthermore, therein, the disciple, the preceptor, the master of the jar, and the fire-guardian [are established] in order.
This is the procedure for the junction of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhi-vidhi*), which one should perform in connection with the path of the sacrificial grass (*kutha*).

(2) By means of grasping the root and the tip, for the sake of establishing the performance of the *saṃpāta-homa* upon the palm of the disciple, one hundred oblations at the root and ten oblations below that should be offered. (3)

"For the sake of atonement, one should perform one hundred and eight root-mantras with the *pūrṇāhuti*; together with the *pūrṇā*, this constitutes the sequence of initiation with its light (*sālokadīkṣākrama*), consisting of the offering of the *kevalasaṃhitā* along with the essence. ||3|| (l4) Thus it is said.
Having performed the *nāḍī-sandhāna* (joining of the channels), he should perform two hundred oblations with the root mantra for the purpose of general and specific satiation (*tarpaṇa*).

Then, having performed oblations ten times the portion [of the root mantra] with the Brahma-mantras and limbs (*aṅgas*), and having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, he should conclude by performing all subsequent rites according to the sequence of the *paddhati*.
Next, the meditation on the deity Pāpabhakṣaṇa is described:
One should meditate upon Mahābhairava himself, who is intent on devouring unbearable sins,
licking with the tip of his tongue, granting fearlessness, and possessing the luster of a mountain of split collyrium.

Three-eyed, clothed in red garments, with faces and eyes turned toward all directions, invincible, with matted locks of red hue, holding the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness, and bearing a trident, sword, and a single face. (264)
Subsequently, the sixteen sacraments (*ṣoḍaśasaṃskāra*) are described.
First is the union during menstruation (*ārtavasaṅgama*), and likewise the rite of conception (*dhāraṇasaṃskriyā*).
Then follow the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), the birth rite (*janikriyā*), and thereafter the rite known as the naming ceremony (*uddhāpakriyā*).

"The fetching of the funeral cake for those free from desire, the taking up of the [Vedic] section, the ignorance [of the ritual], and likewise the marriage—these sixteen rites have been proclaimed by those devoted to the Āgamas. Thus it is said; know that this refers to the sixteen great rites (*mahākarma*). 265. Vaidika.
The sacraments (*saṃskāra*) remain to be described.

Here, they are as follows: conception (*garbhādhāna*), the two [rites] during the period of pregnancy (*sūcana-sīntau*), the rite called birth (*jātāhvaya*), emerging from the womb (*niṣkrāma*), the tonsure (*khikhaṇḍaka*), initiation (*upanayana*), the final rites (*ānantyeṣṭi*), and also the cremation with wood (*dārvī*).

Afterwards come the Bhautika and Saumika rites; following those, the Godāna, the marriage, the Aṣṭakās, and further the Pārvaṇika rite; then the monthly prescribed Śrāddha, as well as the Śravaṇa rite.
(1) After that comes the Āgrayaṇī, which is the twentieth; then the Caitrī and the Āśvayujī. And then—
Then the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*), the fire-sacrifice (*agnihotra*), and finally the full-moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsa*) and the new-moon sacrifice (*darśa*);
the four-monthly sacrifices (*cāturmāsya*), the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*), and furthermore the sevenfold *sautrāmaṇī*;
then the *agniṣṭoma*, the *atīṣṭi*, and the most beloved *ṣoḍaśin* following the sacrificial pavilion (*maṇḍapa*). (2)

The *vāja-peya* sacrifice, joined with the *atirātra*, has been attained through the path of the *āmikṣā*. One who has renounced the world (*parivrāj*) should perform the *prastha* rite accompanied by the word "drinking" (*pāna*), as well as the funeral rites (*antyeṣṭi*). Indeed, for those seeking initiation (*dīkṣā*), these must be performed according to the Vedic tradition.
"These forty rites are likewise Śaiva, just as they are Vaidika. [3] Namely:
*garbhādhāna* (conception), *puṃsavana* (ensuring a male child), *sīmantonnayana* (parting the hair), *jātakarman* (birth-rite), *nāmakaraṇa* (name-giving), *upaniṣkramaṇa* (first outing)... [5]

The nine [rites] beginning with *niṣkrāmaṇa*, *annaprāśana*, *caula*, and *upanayana*; the four *vedavrata*s known as *aiṣṭika*, *dārvika*, *bhautika*, and *sautika*; the two [rites] *godāna* and *vivāha*—these constitute fifteen [rites]. Then there are the *pākayajña*s: *aṣṭakā*, *pārvaṇi*, *māsikaśrāddha*, *śrāvaṇi*, *āgrayaṇi*, *caitrī*, and *āśvayujī*.
7. The establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*);

the fire-oblation (*agnihotra*); the new- and full-moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*); the *āgrayaṇa*; the four-monthly sacrifices (*cāturmāsya*); the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*); and the *sautrāmaṇī*. These are the *haviḥ-yajñas*. 7. The *agniṣṭoma*; the *atyagniṣṭoma*. (l2)

The Soma sacrifices are: the Uddhāttha, the Ṣoḍaśika, the Vājapeya, the Atirātra, and the Aptoryāma—these are the seven. The Vedic rites are forty: Medhājanana, Vānaprastha, Parivrājya, and Antyeṣṭi. (L3) Thus, there are forty Vedic rituals. 268.
In the *Bhinnam*, the names of the twenty-eight Āgamas are stated by means of two verses:
"First are the *Kāmika* and *Yogaja*, and likewise the *Cintya* and *Āgama-kāraṇa*."
Following that are the Ajita and the Dīpta; then the Sūkṣma, said to be a thousandfold like the sun;
then the Suprabheda and Vijaya; the Niśvāsatantra which is self-existent; and those known as the Pāvaka, Vīra, Raurava, Makuṭa, and Vaimala. ||1||
Then his [disciples] were Candrajñāna, Bimba, and so forth; likewise Lālita was proclaimed, and he who was called Siddha was said to be below him, along with the two lineages mentioned by Śarva.
After that, indeed, were the two Pārameśvara and Kiraṇa, and Vātula by number.
There are twenty-eight Āgamas; among them, ten are Śaiva and the others are Raudra.

The venerable Śrīmat Sadāśivasvāmin— [the Lord] whose five faces are Īśāna-mukha, Tatpuruṣa-mukha, Aghora-mukha, Vāmadeva-mukha, and Sadyojāta-mukha— revealed the twenty-eight divine Āgamas concerning the supreme essence from his sacred mouth.
Know these by reciting their names as well. 270.

Know that herein Śaiva is of ten kinds and Raudra is of eighteen kinds. Subsequently, these twenty-eight (28) divine āgamas are described by means of three verses concerning the manner in which they constitute the very body of Mahādeva.
It remains.
From the feet arises Kāmika; from the ankles, Yogaja; then Cintyāgama [arises] from the shanks;
then Kāraṇa from the toes; and Jita from the knees.
The pair of thighs is radiant, the subtle secret organ is arisen, the hips are a thousandfold, the back is like the sun, the navel-lotus is the differentiation, and the victory is the belly. ||1||
The breath is Svāsa, consisting of the nose; the pair of breasts is Agneya;
the throat is Vīra; the pair of ears is Raurava; then the head is Makuṭa;
the flood of hands is Vimala; then Candravidura; then let there be another ornament, Vāsanta.
The Vātula, the Kālottara, the Ghrāṇapa, the Pāyu, the Mālya, and the Upāgama—
these are all the Siddhāntas, which are the very form of Śambhu’s Āgama;
they are declared in the Makuṭa [Tantra] in the form of Naṭeśa.
For Śrī Mahādeva, *kāmika* consists of two *śrīpāda*s;
*yogaja*, two *kaṇikāla*s; *cintya*, *pādāṅgulī*s; *kāraṇa*, two *kada-kāla*s; and *ajita*, two *muṣṭi*s. (14–15)
Tāla is the two thighs; Dīpta is the secret place (guhyasthāna); Sūkṣma is the region of the hips (kaṭisthāna);
Aṃśumān is the head; (16) Suprabheda is the navel-lotus; Vijaya is the belly; Niḥśvāsa is the nose; Svayambhuva is the two...
The *Sthana* [Tantra] is the breasts;
the *Agneya* is the eyes; the *Viragama* is the face; the *Raurava* is the ears; the *Makuta* is the crown of the head; the *Vimala* is the two hands;
and the *Candragnana* is the sacred feet.

The *Bheda* is the face; the *Prodgīta* is the serpent; the *Lalitā* is the two earrings; the *Siddha* is the nose; the *Sandhāna* is the two ear-ornaments; the *Śārvokta* is the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*); and the *Pārameśvara* is the pearl necklace. The *Kiraṇa*...
The twenty-eight Āgamas known as the Tiruvāparaṇam and Vātula-tiru-p-parivattam, with the exception of these, [include] the Kalottara Āgama known as the Tiru-mērpūcchi;
All the Upāgamas are considered as fragrant substances (parimala-dravya) and flowers (puṣpa), while the Śaivasiddhānta is considered as the food offering (naivedya). Thus,
the twenty-eight Divyāgamas beginning with the Kāmika, and the two hundred and seven Upāgamas beginning with the Kālottara, [are offered] to Lord Taṇḍaveśvara Svāmī.
Know that it is stated in the *Mahāgama* that [the deity] remains endowed with all those very limbs. 273.
Thereafter, the enumeration of the *upāṅgas* is not mentioned.
Three, five, and six; the ascetic, however, [remembers] one beyond the jewel, and the sun [remembers] one; eight, the elephant’s eye, and the six directions; not Manu;
half a month, the digit of the moon, the three Vedas, the sages, the elements, the ocean, the apertures, and Aruṇa.
Having combined them, he [obtained] two hundred and seven arising from the sequence of numbers:
three (3), five (5), six (6), seven (7), four (4), nine (9), one (1), and five (5).

Heat (3), one (1), eight (8), elephant (8), two (2), eye (2), Smara’s lunar day (13), six (6), eye (2), Tamu (16), Manu (14), half-month (15), Indra’s arrow (5), three (3), Veda (4), sage (7), element (5), ocean (4), cavity (9), Aruṇa (12)— thus, by the phrase "having struck," there are two hundred and seven Upāgamas.
The meaning is that there would be a number [of tantras]. [They are]: Kāmika, Bheda, Yogaja, Cintya, Kāraṇa, Ajita, Dīpta, Sūkṣma, Sahasra, Aṃśumān, Suprabheda, and Vijaya.
Niśvāsa 8, Svāyambhuva 2, Āgneya 2, Vīra 13, Raurava 6–9, Makuṭa 2, Vimala 16, Candrajñāna 14, Bimba 15, Prodgīta 16, Lalita 3, Siddha 4,
Santāna 7, Śārvokta 5, Parākhyā 7, Kiraṇa 9, Vātulāgama 12— such are the divisions.
Know that the divisions of the Mūlāgama are the Upāgamas. 274.
Subsequently, the enumeration of the Āgamas is stated by means of five verses.
The first is *parārddha*; the next is *dvilakṣa*; the next is *lakṣa*; the next cause is *koṭi*.
Another is *ayuta*; *niyuta* is *dīpta*; *sūkṣma* is *padma*; and *sahasraśaṅkha* indeed [is the next]. (1)

The *Ravitantra* is said to have five hundred thousand [verses]; the *Bheda* has thirty million; the *Vijaya* has thirty million; the *Śvāsa* has ten million; the one called *Svayambhū* has thirty-five million; and the *Nala* has thirty-three million. (L5) 2.
In the Vīra[tantra] there are ten lakṣas; Raurava has eight koṭis and Makuṭa has one lakṣa.
The Vimalāgama consists of three lakṣas of verses, and Candrabodha is likewise three lakṣas. (3)
Then there is the Bimba and the Mahābja; furthermore, the Gītatantra consists of one hundred thousand verses, while another is three times eight thousand.
The Siddhatantra consists of ten million five hundred thousand verses, and the Santānatantra consists of twelve thousand verses. (4)

The Śārva [Āgama] consists of one hundred thousand verses, while the Parama [Āgama] consists of one million; the Kiraṇāgama consists of fifty million, and likewise, the number of verses in the Vātula Āgamas is said to be one hundred thousand, as declared in the Makuṭāgama. (Verse 5) Thus it is stated. Having thus stated the numerical count for the twenty-eight Āgamas, [the author says: 279.
These twenty-eight Āgamas are also stated to consist of [a total of] fifteen lakṣas of ślokas.
Beyond a parārdha, there are ten lakṣas, one koṭi-lakṣa, one koṭi, three tripas, and one koṭi.

The number of verses for the twenty-eight Āgamas, including the *Varṇottalakṣa* and the *Sahasrahārāgama*, is as follows: the total number of *granthas* is eleven lakhs (*lakṣa*) plus one hundred thousand (*parārtha*).
The *Koḍi* is the 30th, and the *Koḍi* is the 51st; the 50th is known as the *Lakṣa* *grantha*. 280.
Subsequently, the connection with the *Śivāgama* is said to be sixfold. (l3)

And there is a sixfold relationship between Śrīkaṇṭha and Devendra: namely, *para* (supreme), *śambhavīśayoga* (the union with the Lord of Śambhu), *mahān* (great), *īśa* (lord), *māpātika* (beyond measure), and *antarāla* (intermediate). O Lord of Gods, [this is] the divine [relationship]; furthermore, among those sages, it is the piercing (*vedhana*).

That which is called "divine and non-divine" refers to the flow of wealth; the "non-divine" therein is the Tantric [tradition]. (5. If one asks how the Śivāgama exists in sixfold divisions, it is as follows: there is the relationship between Sadāśivasvāmin and Ananteśvara. (p116a, l1)
The great relationship between Īśvara and Śrīkaṇṭha; the intermediate relationship between Śrīkaṇṭha and Devendra;
the divine relationship between Devendra and the Ṛṣis;
the super-divine relationship between the Ṛṣis and human beings; and [the relationship] for human beings...
Know that for humans there is a connection with extreme longevity, and (l3) thus there is a connection with the Śivāgamas as they arrive.
281. Subsequently, it is not told in eighteen thousand (aṣṭādaśa-sahasra) Purāṇas, but in one thousand five hundred (1½) verses. (l4)
It stands thus: first, the Brāhma Purāṇa is declared as one; likewise the Pādma, the Vaiṣṇava, the Śaiva, the Bhāgavata, then the Bhaviṣya, and thereafter the Śrī-Nāradīya. (v. 5)
Then there is the Mārkaṇḍeya and the Anala; after that, the Brahmakaivartaka and the Laiṅga; following that is the one named Varāha, then the Skānda, and thereafter the Vāmana. ||1||

Then [the Purāṇas] are the Kaurma, the Gāruḍa, the Brahmāṇḍa, the Skānda, and the Śaiva—these two [the latter two] consisting of two hundred thousand [verses each]; the others are said to consist of two hundred thousand [verses]. Thus, there are eighteen [Purāṇas], totaling one million three hundred twenty thousand verses. These are the sources.
It remains unsaid.
Manu, Atri, Viṣṇu, and likewise Hārīta, Vasiṣṭha, Śaṅkha, Likhita, Āpastaṃba, and Saṃvarta—these are the various authorities here. (Verse 3)

Kātyāyana, Bṛhaspati, and then Vyāsa—his father, O dear one; furthermore, Vyāsa, Śaṅkha, and likewise Likhita, Dakṣa, and Gautama. (v. 4) Know that these are the authors of the eighteen Smṛtis. 283½. (Second time).
Next, the procedure for the eightfold binding (*aṣṭabandhana*) is described according to the *Dīptāgama*: "Regarding the eightfold binding for one's own sake, the procedure is as follows:
eight jars, including the *kumbha* and the *vardhanikā*, should be placed around [it], just as in the mandala."

Based on the [specific] signs, one should perform the worship of Śiva, Śivā, and the Vidyeśvaras in those [liṅgas] respectively; then, having adorned them and bound [the thread], there follows the sprinkling with water and clothing. ||1||

Having performed the bathing with products of the cow and so forth, and having completed the rites of invocation and the like by the potter and others, one should then place the *liṅga* upon that auspicious pedestal (*bhadrapīṭha*).
After respectfully offering the food oblation (*naivedya*) and other items, one should [proceed] with that [liṅga] using the *aghora* mantra.

In this case, one should likewise perform an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) or a fire-oblation (*homa*) a thousand or a hundred times. (2) This is the procedure for the eightfold binding for one's own sake. 285½. Next, the thirty-two characteristics are to be described. (3)
Indeed, there are thirty-two marks; [the following] are long due to the five nectars:
the nose, the space between the breasts, the knees, the neck, and the shanks. (L4) Furthermore, the back, the anus, the nails, the throat, the teeth, and the joints of the fingers are short.

The five [parts] are subtle; the six elevated parts are the abdomen, the two shoulders, the shoulder-blades, the nose, the armpits, and the forehead. The seven reddish parts are the eyes, the palate, the penis, the lower lip, the palms of the hands, the soles of the feet, and the nails. Furthermore, three parts are broad: the hips and two others. (1–1½)

In these four [verses] (16), learn the thirty-two characteristics of a person (puruṣa). 287. Subsequently, the signs of a devotee of Śiva (śivabhakta-liṅga/siṃha) are described by means of four verses. (p117b, f113a, l1.)
The collection of marks for the devotees of Śambhu consists of ashes, the triple-tilaka, the wearing of Rudrākṣa ornaments, matted hair and so forth, bearing the insignia of the Lord of Servants,
and the glorification of the greatness of the stories of Śiva— all of which have Śambhu as their sole creator.
Dancing by reciting praises of His name and meditating upon the five-syllabled mantra. ||1||
Wearing saffron-colored upper garments, being girded with a white cloth, shaving the head,
wearing ritual hand-marks (*mudrā*), reciting the *Āgamas* and other scriptures, the thorough study of those [texts],
the occasional worship at the abodes of Śiva and so forth, and devotion to the work of service (*kaiṅkarya*).

To think, "I am the servant of Śambhu, the Master," is the true worship and service of a devotee. (2) [The worship of the illustrious Maheśvara consists in: always acting for the benefit of all living beings;
speaking words of grace with a mind moistened by compassion; and constant subordination to Śiva. (3)

Wearing the belt of the Oḍyāṇa and Tulā mudrās, bearing the staff of the khaṭvāṅga, constant trust in the words of the guru and the scriptures, and always possessing a kind disposition—(these are the marks of a true yogin). 3.
The alms-bowl made of a gourd, the begging bowl, the patched garment, eating by begging, eating one’s own food,
constant devotion toward the qualities of those who protect oneself, self-knowledge, the worship of Śambhu,
the sacrifice to Gaṇeśa, the worship of Skanda, and [the worship] of Pārvatī.
Performing the fire-ritual for Śiva before the image of Śambhu and constant association with the virtuous—know that this is the description of the marks of a devotee of Śiva. 291.
Afterward, the [verses on] the three [sages] who know the truth... (l2)
The assembly: 9 plus 72. The name of the one who possesses a changed name has not been uttered.

Among the Śaivas, those who have attained liberation are the Brahmins numbered by the sun (twelve), the four Śiva-Brahmins, the physician-twice-born, the earth-lord, and the ruler of the six and five boundaries. (Verse 3)

There are five Vaiśyas, then thirteen Mahāśūdras—beginning with the potters and ending with the low-born—and the nine-pallava Kulajā; [these] six, multiplied by three, make sixty. (1) For each one indeed consists of the Kila, the Āla, the Dhīvara, the Paṭīkṛt, the Vyādha, the Nāga, the Garbha, and the Tī.
"...and those who wear the faces of the *drākṣāṭana* and *kārivakra*; thus nine have been mentioned.
And if the wise say that there are also nine *vyūha*s and nine *ketu*s, then with the eight thousand [deities] beginning with Padma and Sadbhava, the total would be one hundred and seventy."
Know that this work (16) is according to the *Periya Purāṇam*. 293.
A verse from the *Saundareśvara* [Purāṇa].
Born in the village of Jambū, blazing with the power of meditation on the state of Śiva,
bearing the *lālījaṇḍu* [emblem], supremely devoted to others, and having taken the hand of Kalyāṇā;
he who offers praise to the various forms of the abode of Śiva and is a mine of the jewels of beauty.
I pay homage to Sundaradeva, the lotus-born Brahmā, who is beloved by the devotees of Tyāgeśa. 294.
Homage to Śivaguru. The procedure for the Cūrṇotsava festival is set forth in thirteen verses.
The Cūrṇotsava should indeed be performed on the day the pilgrimage site of Śambhu is completed;

furthermore, this [festival] is to be performed for one initiated by Śiva immediately after the departure of the vital breaths. If it is asked why it must be performed here [at that time], it is for the sake of auspiciousness once again.
Furthermore, because it is proclaimed in the Śiva-āgamas, the Cūrṇotsava is ordained; as follows: (l5.

When the group of five has departed, for the sake of purifying the deceased among those residing in the Śiva-āśrama, then, according to the Vātula [Tantra], the cremation of the body on the path is appropriately to be performed above the neck.

Afterwards, when the corpse has been bathed with fresh water from the heart-lake by those who have themselves bathed, using oil and other substances, and has been laid upon a bed or a wooden plank smeared with ashes and the like; ||2||
Following that, on the southern head [of the altar], to the east of that, there is a platform (*vedi*) made of rice by means of two hands and the eight [fingers]...
[for the purpose of the essence of rice]... with those [grains] and rice-flour, a mandala is then [drawn] below that eastern [section].
Just as [one prepares] rice, in the very same way one should prepare the threefold circle of the hand-essence. ||3||
Having established the water-jars (*kumbha*), the mortar (*ulūkhala*), and the drum (*bherī*) with their attendants,

one should place them in sequence within the lotus-diagram drawn with lines in the western direction; therein, the placement of the jar is prescribed in the center, and then in the four directions starting from the east.
There should be ash, an *alamallaka* vessel, and [the remains] of the *di...* [rite]; then, from the oil for betel;
(4) in the jar, the worship of the deity of the *pāśupatāstra*; this is the traditional transmission (*sampradāya*).
Without this, there is no way for anyone to attain non-attachment (*alagnigati*); indeed, that is the cause, the very cause. (5)
Having visualized [the deity] as red or white, with fierce ornaments and eyes, with tawny matted hair shining upwards,
three-eyed, and holding a sword, a rosary, a mace, and a shield in his four arms—
one should then worship the supreme Lord of Mantras (Astra-īśvara).

Having offered the food offering (*naivedya*) and so forth to the Wielder of the Thunderbolt (*vajrin*), the Lord of Wealth (*dhanapati*), the Lord of Sea-monsters (*yādodhipa*), and the Ender (*antaka*), as well as incense, another lamp, and the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) for the purpose of cessation,
he should remain for a moment; having uttered this, the Guru, holding the *arghya*, should then rise.
One should begin by beating the drum; having placed it here wrapped in cloth as desired, one should sacrifice here in its center and on its sides to Rudra,
Viṣṇu, and Aja, according to the seven musical notes within the seven kalās.
With the two circles of its wheels as the earth, the moon as the serpent, and Guha at the corner as the rope.
The meditation on Bherī is here described as it was taught in the Siddhāgama:
"Pure, with three faces, elevated, bestowing the [six] flavors, having three legs, resembling the Japā flower,
bearing a conch, a discus, a mace, a rosary, a trident, and an axe, and seated upon a lotus."
One should strike the drum with a weapon while reciting its own name, "Bherī Deva. ||8||
Afterwards, the worship of the mortar has been described; next, one should worship the Support-Energy (Ādhāra-śakti).
Above that, one should worship the Lotus-Seated One (Kamalāsana), and below that, Acyuta. In its cavity, one should worship the Earth, and upon the pestle, Meru, which arises from the Haridrā [tree].
Then, having placed the very element of earth (*pārthivatattva*) into that powder within her womb,

the Master himself, together with the Śiva-attendants, the Rudra-attendants, and the groups of servants, while reciting the mantra of the *pada*, should personally take up the pestle and crush it into three parts.

Then follows the recitation of the Drāviḍa-gāthā, the raising of all [the images], the sprinkling of the *preta* with water from the *kumbha*, and the filling [of the vessel] with oil and powder; such is the Powder Festival (*cūrṇotsava*). (l3.
The verse regarding the great drum-beating remains to be told.
Now that the season for the powder festival has arrived, and for the purpose of bewitching the Piśācīs,
I, the Guru, strike the kettledrum three times with the weapon-mantra.
(L4) [I do so] even for the sake of summoning my Maheśvara-like kinsmen, and for the sake of summoning others as well.

For the sake of pacifying great suffering, I now beat this drum for the planetary deities. (2) Having cast off his wandering through the mortal world and its enjoyments, he has now set out on the journey to the realm of Śiva; because of the proclamation of the auspicious *pratyamṛta* and other hymns, I now beat this drum. (3) Thus [ends] 13.

The summary of the powder festival (*cūrṇotsava*) is stated [as follows]: (p120b, f116, l1) At the beginning of the powder festival, the worship of the *kambha* is performed by the *amṛtajana*; then, in the east, north, west, or south directions, there is ash, a loincloth, and betel. (l2)

There should be an offering of oil and worship of the desired lords of the four directions; thereafter, the striking of a kettle-drum, the powder, the rubbing, the head of a corpse, and the offering of water from a jar and so forth. ||1||
Thus, 14. (l3.

Hereafter, beginning with the description of the pavilion for the rites of the funeral ceremony (*antyeṣṭikriyāvidhānamaṇḍapalakṣaṇa*), it is set forth in eight verses. Having made the funeral pavilion square, with red [threads]... (l4.)
In the center, at the station of Brahmā, the digging of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and the ritual (*kratu*) are performed as prescribed for initiation.
There is a single girdle (*mekhalā*) one finger-breadth high; or else, with the earth excavated [from it], [the altar] is prepared.

Then, on the altar (*vedi*) and in the fire (*anala*), this place is toward the southwest and northwest, with the sacred thread (*śruti*) [extending] eastward and westward, and subsequently [marked] by fragrance.
The excavation should be one hand-deep, and the altar (vedikā) should be made of earth in the cardinal directions; beyond that,
the railings (vitardī) for the Vajra and other [deities] should be ten tālas high,
and the pillars (śaṅku) should be sixteen, twelve, eight, or twenty-four units in height.
Indeed, among the four gates, the southern gate is the most excellent even for all ritual activities.

When the site is divided into twenty-five parts, one should place Brahmā upon the yellow earth in the central five squares; then, in the north, one should place Acyuta upon the white [earth] in five squares.
One should worship Hutavaha and Rudra in the red four-square [section] of Fire; then, in the black four-square [sections] of Wind, one should worship Vāyu, Īśvara, and Āvīśa.
(3) Furthermore, in the four dark-blue squares, one should worship Gaganatattva and Sadākhya.

In the speech-cavity [of the mandala], which is joined with red, white, black, and yellow jewels, Kubera and the others are to be worshipped; their sequence is stated here as follows: then, with water from the *vardhanī* vessel resting upon the shoulder of the preceptor—who has bathed and is positioned to his left—the [preceptor] should enter that pavilion by way of the left.
Having entered through the southern door... having gone there also to the south of Kutala, [he should proceed] to Mārutave... he should dwell on the right side. Having placed the Vardhanī...
having then requested Gaṇapa upon the Ku... seat, the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is performed with a simple mental resolve.
The withdrawal of the offering water (arghya) is appropriate, as well as the ground from within the elements. ||5||
The designation of excellence, purification, and then the non-utterance of one's own [name];

the hand... [and] the act of sprinkling with cow-products; then the sprinkling of the study-hall and the sprinkling of the cows; ...the eightfold and tenfold purifications, the scattering of the *vikira* offerings, and the wiping (*mārjana*).
Then follows the preparation of the vardhanī vessel and the seat, as well as the worship of Vāstu with the funeral pyre and the vardhanī rite.

After the worship [of the deity], the worship of the ten weapons (*daśāyudha*) should be performed; then the oblation for the worship of the water-pot (*kumbha*), followed by the procedure for the kindling of the mantra. Then the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), and then the food offering (*naivedya*).
Then, with the mantra, an oblation of sacrificial porridge (*caru*) should be made into the fire; and thereafter, in that same place, four or three [oblations].
Then, the piercing with a stake during the worship of Indra and Agni according to the Śrauta rites, as well as the entry of the deceased [into the body], likewise [are described]. ||7||

Then, having fashioned a corpse out of a doll, the initiation should be performed with the Great Net (*mahājāla*). After that, one should perform the worship beginning with the entry into the self, followed by the vein-joining (*sirā-sāndhika*).
Having performed a hundred oblations for the violation of the prescribed conduct, this is the common procedure.
The worship of Vāgīśā, the joining of the disciple, the consecration of the site, and the entry into the house. ||8||
Understand the meaning of this according to the *Paddhati*. Verse 212:
The definition of *puṣpitā* has not been stated.
The effigy should be made from *kuśa* blades according to the [number of] principles (*tattva*). The hair should be [made with] four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) [in length].
It should have two joints; the head is formed by three [fingers], and the shape of the neck by rows of *kuśa* blades on the sides.
The arms are eighteen fingers long, while the middle [of the body] is twenty-six [fingers].
"By its stability, O child, it is called *paṇḍikāṭya*; thus that pair is the sixfold foot.
As for how the arrangement of the hair (*darbha*) is performed:
beginning with "the hair is one *aṅgula*" and ending with "two *aṅgulas*," and [mentioning] the head and below that the neck, three *aṅgulas*—
Below that, by means of five *vaṃśas*, there are two *kaikas*; the length of each of those *kaikas* is eighteen *aṅgulas*.
Regarding the *maṇikkaṭṭu*:
The length of the little toe is six *aṅgulas* each; the length of each phalanx is thirty-four *aṅgulas*;
by twenty-six *puḷ*s in the middle, the chest, abdomen, waist, and thighs are fifteen *aṅgulas* long; and by thirty-three *puḷ*s each, the two [thighs]...

Having cut out the legs, therein (l2), the length of the thighs including the calves shall be six *kula*s, and the length of the lower leg, including the knee and the toes, shall be six *kula*s; thus is the head (l3).
Know that the length from the hairline to the knees is thirty-eight aṅgulas. 315. Here is the scriptural authority in support of this:
"The head is said to be forty [aṅgulas], while the neck shall be twenty;
the heart is said to be twenty, and the abdomen is declared to be twenty."
The two arms are said to number two hundred; the penis is proclaimed to be eight [finger-breadths];
the scrotum twelve; and the feet forty respectively.
Thus, the measurement of the statuette is three hundred and sixty [finger-breadths].
The procedure for the installation of the stone slab (*pāṣāṇasthāpanavidhi*) is described hereafter in eight verses (l6):
"The pavilion for the placement of the stone slab should be situated in the cremation ground, in a human habitation, in a courtyard, or by a river..."
Or else, on the bank, according to one's convenience, [one should construct] a gateway toward the direction of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) with various enclosures.

In its center, there should be a square altar-platform (*vedi*) possessing a height and width of one cubit (*kara*), provided with two rims (*nemi*) and a surrounding trench (*khāta*) one cubit deep and circular. ||1||
Regarding the installation of the stone jar:
one should worship Mahādeva, known by the name Rudra, who is seated upon the central altar within the excellent jar;
he faces north, has the luster of the rising sun, is accompanied by his retinue, and is endowed with the limbs of enjoyment (*bhoga*). One should worship him together with his limbs.
Afterwards, one should perform the worship of the rear enclosure (āvṛti), starting from the northeast (haradig) and proceeding counter-clockwise (vāmakrama);
then, the wise one should again worship the eight Rudras on both sides.
Regarding the installation of the stone:
the taking up of the stone by one belonging to the Śiva-āśrama is the single, supreme [requirement]. That too must be a stone possessing its original form, or else it may be a brick.
Of the two bricks mentioned as superior, one should be appropriately bathed by the agent in the pit.
How is that bathing performed? That man, having bathed, should wear only a single garment made of liquid. ||3||
The speaker, previously positioned facing west, wearing his garment over his left shoulder,
should take the deceased— who has completed the two initiations— near the water-pot; having anointed him with oil, *amlaka*, and so forth, he should place him well-seated here facing north.
Then one should also invoke Skanda and Caṇḍagaṇādhipa; even then, this is appropriate.

Furthermore, if [the disciple] has been initiated into the two upper [levels], then one should invoke these three—the one called Sadāśiva, the Peaceful One—according to the traditional teaching, by name. Then:
Having anointed [the image] with perfumes and the like, and having adorned it properly with divine flowers,
the Guru should then offer incense and other offerings here, omitting the striking of the bell; thereafter,
he should present the *bhūtabali* consisting of various side-dishes and food appropriate for that occasion.
Having offered that [water] with his name, water for the bath (vāsudaka) and sesame-water (tiloda) should be given.
Or, for one who has died on the same day, water should be offered three times until the end of the period of impurity; if there are ten days of impurity, then thirty times water should be offered. 6.
For one day, there is the offering of sesame-water; for ten days, this triad [of offerings] increases by one each day, totaling twenty-five. Furthermore, three rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) are to be given:
the offering of a rice-ball in the morning is indeed the *bali*, while that in the evening is the minor one, according to their respective counts.
The funeral cakes, the row, and the bali offering—these ten should be given once the ritual actions have been completed. ||7||
In the pavilion established upon stone, first is the construction of the altar...
[then] the placement of the water-pot (*kumbha*), the pouring of water upon the stone below it,
followed by the offering of the *bali* for its stability, and likewise the offering of sesame and rice.
Three times the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*), the giving of the ten seats (*daśapīṭha*), the giving of the *daśabalyā*, and the ritual bathing (*āplāvana*).

On the sixth day, having placed [the deity] upon a litter or a cart, one should proceed with the powder festival (*cūrṇotsava*).
(l1) Having performed [the ritual] as before, and having smeared [them] with water made from saffron, safflower, turmeric, and so forth—or otherwise—sprinkle them all.

(l2) At night, [anoint] the elephant; on the seventh [day], the chariot; at night, the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpataru*); on the eighth, the palanquin. At night, having mounted the horse, at the time of departure...
Mounted on horses...

[they], equipped with weapons and shields, accompanied by all ornaments, and joined by the attendants of Rudra and courtesans, should proceed around [the site]. In the meantime, having suppressed the wicked and protected the virtuous, and having caused [them] to hear all matters of dharma and adharma, he should cause them to enter the temple. At the ninth hour, the men... [on] a palanquin... with shields; at night...
Then, on the tenth day, having placed the deity upon a jeweled lion-throne, [he performed] the circumambulation of the city and other sites... [at the tip of the banner] the Fanged One (Vikṛtānta)...
